positions.position: Abu ʿAli explains fatḥa as circumstantial (“not in a state of being angered”), exceptional (“except those angered”), or an implied “I mean”; al-Khalil is reported to agree.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA-FULL reporting أبو علي: Abu ʿAli explains fatḥa as circumstantial (“not in a state of being angered”), exceptional (“except those angered”), or an implied “I mean”; al-Khalil is reported to agree.

positions.position: ʿUmar and Ubay read ghayr before both “those angered” and “those astray,” with reports varying between accusative and genitive on each.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA-FULL reporting عمر بن الخطاب وأبي بن كعب: ʿUmar and Ubay read ghayr before both “those angered” and “those astray,” with reports varying between accusative and genitive on each.

positions.position: Al-Sarraj says ghayr becomes definite when its definite complement has one known opposite: the favored people are the ones other than those under anger.
positions.reasons: TABRISI reporting أبو بكر السراج: Al-Sarraj says ghayr becomes definite when its definite complement has one known opposite: the favored people are the ones other than those under anger.

positions.position: The word maghdūb need not be pluralized because the plural pronoun in ʿalayhim already marks those who incur anger.
positions.reasons: TABRISI: The word maghdūb need not be pluralized because the plural pronoun in ʿalayhim already marks those who incur anger.

positions.position: Al-Jurjani says a speaker may ask to join those favored or be spared the state of the angered without referring to any known group; Antara's beloved is likewise not compared to a third person.
positions.reasons: TABRISI reporting عبد القاهر الجرجاني: Al-Jurjani says a speaker may ask to join those favored or be spared the state of the angered without referring to any known group; Antara's beloved is likewise not compared to a third person.

positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL reporting النبي: A prophetic report distinguishes three kinds of wrongdoing: shirk that is never forgiven, harm between people that is not left unaddressed, and self-wrong that God may forgive; Razi associates them with caprice, anger, and desire.

positions.reasons: BAYDAWI: The sinner's liability to wrath is supported by 4:93, which says God is angry with the deliberate killer. | mentions 4:93

positions.position: “Not those angered nor astray” may be an apposition to “those You favored,” or a qualifying description showing that true favor joins faith with safety from anger and error.
positions.reasons: BAYDAWI-FULL: “Not those angered nor astray” may be an apposition to “those You favored,” or a qualifying description showing that true favor joins faith with safety from anger and error.

positions.reasons: NASAFI-FULL: “Other than those under anger” is an appositive: those favored are the ones spared God's anger and misguidance.

positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN: The passive wording for those angered is tactful in a humble plea: the worshipper attributes favor to the One asked for guidance but avoids confronting Him with the description of vengeance.

positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN: God's anger may mean His intent to requite a sinner, making it an attribute of essence because His knowledge precedes creation and sin; alternatively it is imposing punishment, an attribute of action.

positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN-FULL: The sūra uses fronting and delay in “we worship, we seek help” and in “those angered, those astray.”

positions.position: Al-maghḍūb is genitive by annexation and a passive participle; the prepositional phrase supplies its agent, and the relative al means those who were angered.
positions.reasons: SAMIN-DURR: Al-maghḍūb is genitive by annexation and a passive participle; the prepositional phrase supplies its agent, and the relative al means those who were angered.

positions.position: Al-Khalīl is reported to parse accusative ghayr with an omitted aʿnī, meaning I mean those other than the angered ones.
positions.reasons: SAMIN-DURR reporting الخليل: Al-Khalīl is reported to parse accusative ghayr with an omitted aʿnī, meaning I mean those other than the angered ones.

positions.position: Those subject to anger know the truth but turn away; the astray lack knowledge and wander without reaching the truth.

positions.position: The people under wrath are those whom God treats as an angry person treats the object of his anger.
positions.reasons: BIQAI: The people under wrath are those whom God treats as an angry person treats the object of his anger.

positions.reasons: DURR-FULL reporting النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم: The Prophet rebuked al-Shurayd for sitting with his left hand behind his back, calling it the sitting posture of those under anger.

positions.reasons: ITQAN: The verse explicitly attributes favor to God, but avoids saying “those with whom You were angry,” shifting expression so anger is not verbally attributed to God in direct address.

positions.reasons: ALUSI: The blessing is directly attributed to God as a deferential appeal for guidance to those whose favor is established; anger is put in the passive and left unassigned out of courtesy in a humble request for kindness.

positions.reasons: QUTB-ZILAL: The straight path is that of people granted God's favor, not those who know truth and turn away in anger or those who never find guidance to truth.

positions.reasons: IBNASHUR: The comprehensive reading makes the transition to the following request, for the path excluding those under anger or astray, apt to the context.

positions.reasons: IBNASHUR-FULL: The mention of those angered and astray also alludes to the Qur'an's narratives about misguided peoples.

positions.position: Those granted favor point to the good states of virtuous past nations and individuals; the angered and astray evoke the stories of deviant peoples.
positions.reasons: IBNASHUR-FULL: Those granted favor point to the good states of virtuous past nations and individuals; the angered and astray evoke the stories of deviant peoples.

positions.reasons: SAMARRAI-LAMASAT: Adding lā before the astray makes the exclusion apply to either group separately, rather than only excluding people who combine anger and misguidance.

question: What does divine anger mean here?

positions.position: Divine anger is the will to punish or avenge
positions.reasons: THALABI reporting قوم: One group explains God's anger as His will to take vengeance on sinners. MAWARDI reporting unattributed: Another interpretation takes wrath as the will to exact vengeance, since the linguistic root implies harshness, which cannot be ascribed to God. MAWARDI-FULL: A second account interprets God's anger as a will to punish; anger linguistically means severity, a quality unsuitable for God. WAHIDI-QT: Those under wrath are Jews; God's wrath means His willing punishment. WAHIDI-WAJIZ: Those under divine anger are the Jews; God's anger means His willing punishment. BAGHAWI-FULL: Those under wrath are people whose path incurred God’s anger; divine anger is the will to punish sinners, but does not befall sinful believers, only disbelievers. KASHSHAF: God's anger is His will to avenge sinners and punish them, acting as a king does when angry with a subordinate. KASHSHAF-FULL: God's anger means His will to take vengeance on sinners, punish them, and treat them as a king does those under his authority. TABRISI: Divine anger is God's will to impose deserved punishment, curse the people, and disavow them; its root denotes severity. QURTUBI: Divine anger can mean God's will to punish, an essential attribute, or the punishment itself, an attribute of action; a hadith says charity extinguishes the Lord's anger. QURTUBI-FULL: Alayhim is grammatically understood as “wrath fell upon them”; wrath linguistically means severity, while in God’s attribute it is either His will to punish or punishment itself. NASAFI: God’s anger means His will to take vengeance on liars and punish them, treating them as a king does those under his authority when angry. NASAFI-FULL: The first “upon them” is an object and the second is a subject; God's anger means His will to exact revenge and impose punishment on deniers. ABUHAYYAN: God's anger may mean His intent to requite a sinner, making it an attribute of essence because His knowledge precedes creation and sin; alternatively it is imposing punishment, an attribute of action. ABUHAYYAN-FULL: Divine anger can mean the will to punish, an attribute of essence given God’s prior knowledge, or the act of inflicting punishment, an attribute of action. SAMIN-DURR: Anger is described as the heart's blood surging in intent to take revenge; a prophetic report warns against anger and describes its bodily signs. SAMIN-DURR: Alternative definitions make anger a heart's change toward something disliked, or distinguish divine action-attribute when it means punishment from essential attribute when it means the will to punish. ALUSI reporting السعد: In his commentary on al-Miftāḥ, al-Saʿd defines anger as a movement of the soul whose origin is the will to take revenge. ALUSI reporting السعد: In his commentary on al-Kashshāf, al-Saʿd defines divine anger as the will to take revenge. ALUSI reporting الزمخشري: Al-Zamakhsharī explains God’s anger as His will to punish sinners, bringing punishment upon them as an angry king does to subjects under his authority. ALUSI-FULL: The source gives several technical definitions of anger: a movement arising from desire for vengeance, the will to exact vengeance, or an inward condition producing outward movement; a report likens anger to a glowing ember in the heart. ALUSI-FULL reporting الكشاف: Al-Zamakhshari explains God's anger as His will to exact vengeance and punish sinners, acting as an angry ruler acts toward a subordinate. ELMALILI: When attributed to God, anger means its ultimate end, the will to retaliate or impose punishment, and is compatible with merciful lordship: punishing an oppressor serves mercy to the oppressed.

positions.position: Divine anger is punitive action or its effects
positions.reasons: TAB: The wrathful are identified with those described in the Qur'an as cursed and punished for disobedience; God also shows the community the way to avoid their fate. | mentions 5:60 TAB reporting بعضهم: One view explains God's anger as His imposing punishment on those He is angry with, in this world or the next. | mentions 43:55, 5:60 TAB reporting ابن عباس: In Ibn ʿAbbās's explanation, the prayer asks God to inspire true monotheistic religion, spare the worshippers His anger like the Jews, and keep them from Christian error and punishment. TAB: Recounting punishments for disobedience warns people away from sin and from incurring God's anger, whose consequences lead to destruction. TAB-FULL: Those under anger are the people God describes as cursed and punished in Qur'an 5:60; He informs believers of their fate and shows them the route to salvation out of mercy. | mentions 5:60 TAB-FULL reporting بعضهم: One theological account says God's anger is the imposition of punishment in this life or the next, citing the drowning of Pharaoh's people and the punishment described in Qur'an 5:60. | mentions 43:55, 5:60 TAB-FULL reporting بعضهم: A third account treats anger as a real divine attribute, intelligible by affirmation but unlike human anger, which involves agitation, pain, or harm; it is an attribute like knowledge and power without creaturely limitations. TAB-FULL reporting ابن عباس: Ibn Abbas glosses the astray as Christians whom God led astray through their fabrication about Him; the prayer asks for the true monotheistic faith, protection from Jewish wrath and Christian error, and mercy to prevent their punishment. THALABI reporting قيل: Another explanation calls anger a kind of punishment opposite to divine pleasure. MAWARDI reporting unattributed: A fourth interprets wrath as a kind of punishment named anger, just as God’s blessings are named mercy. MAWARDI-FULL: A fourth account calls a kind of punishment anger, just as God's bounty is called mercy. BAGHAWI: “Not those angered” means a path other than that of those God wills to punish for disobedience. IBNATIYYA: The author says scripture repeatedly describes God’s wrath against Jews, citing their incurring wrath and the punishment of Sabbath-breakers. | mentions 2:61, 3:112, 5:60, 2:65 IBNATIYYA: Here divine wrath means God’s manifesting ordeals, punishments, humiliation, and similar signs that He has emphatically distanced them from His mercy. IBNATIYYA-FULL: God's anger means that he exposes them to trials, punishments, and humiliation, showing their decisive removal from his mercy. RAZI-FULL: Razi poses the problem that divine anger follows knowledge of human sin: if God's knowledge is eternal, why create people destined for endless punishment and why create what He is angry with? RAZI-FULL: Human anger is a bodily change, impossible for God; psychological terms applied to God signify their final effect, so divine anger means willing harm, while divine modesty means leaving an act. QURTUBI: Arabic anger connotes severity: a harsh person is ghadub, a fierce serpent al-ghadub, and a folded camel-hide shield ghadba for its toughness. QURTUBI-FULL reporting النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم: A hadith says charity extinguishes the Lord’s wrath, treating wrath as an attribute of action when it means the punishment. BAYDAWI-FULL: Divine anger denotes its ultimate effect, punishment; عليهم is a passive-subject phrase, unlike the earlier construction, and لا reinforces the negation in غير. ABUHAYYAN: The passive wording for those angered is tactful in a humble plea: the worshipper attributes favor to the One asked for guidance but avoids confronting Him with the description of vengeance. SAMIN-DURR: When attributed to God, anger means retribution; غضبت لفلان is said of a living person and غضبت به of a dead one. BURSEVI: Divine anger cannot mean its human beginning, so it denotes its end or effect, such as punishment, retribution, or painful seizure. BURSEVI: Divine anger perfects the function of the left hand: mercy and severity have distinct effects, and severity completes what cannot be repaired by mercy. | mentions 39:67 ELMALILI: A temporary punishment or pain that prepares future blessings does not make someone one of those under wrath; outcomes determine the judgment, as 2:155 illustrates. | mentions 2:155 IBNASHUR: Because literal anger entails change, which cannot apply to God, the attribution means its consequence—punishment, humiliation, or worldly exclusion—or a representational metaphor. IBNASHUR: Divine anger is God’s treatment of those who oppose guidance, ranging up to the lasting punishment of polytheists and hypocrites; dislike is lesser, and both differ from creative will. | mentions 39:7, 6:112, 10:99 IBNASHUR reporting بعض ملوك الفرس: An unnamed Persian king said his reign endured because he punished according to the offense rather than according to anger. IBNASHUR-FULL: Divine anger means God's treatment of those who leave guidance and disobey, culminating in punishment; anger, dislike, pleasure, and love differ from creative will. | mentions 39:7, 6:112, 10:99 IBNASHUR-FULL: God cannot literally undergo anger or change; the attribution must mean its effects, such as punishment, humiliation, curse, or exclusion, or function as a representational metaphor.

positions.position: Divine anger is condemnation or blame
positions.reasons: TAB reporting بعضهم: Another view takes divine anger as God's blame of people and their deeds, and verbal condemnation of them. TAB: Jews and Christians are both astray and under wrath; God labels each group by a real, recognizable trait, without implying that it lacks the other's blameworthy traits. TAB-FULL reporting بعضهم: A second account understands divine anger as blame for their conduct and verbal reproach or insult. THALABI reporting قيل: A third explanation defines anger as condemnation of sinners for the ugliness of their acts. MAWARDI reporting unattributed: A third interpretation is that God’s wrath means His condemnation of them. MAWARDI-FULL: A third account interprets God's anger as His condemnation of them. IBNKATHIR: Qurʾanic references to Jewish anger and wrongdoing support the identification: Israel's children incur anger for rejecting revelation and are condemned for sin and failure to stop wrongdoing. | mentions 2:90, 5:60, 5:78, 5:79 BIQAI-FULL reporting الحرالي: Al-Harali defines the condemned as those who intentionally oppose guidance and thereby incur divine wrath, or those who turn toward guidance then stray without intending to. | mentions 93:6 ITQAN: The verse explicitly attributes favor to God, but avoids saying “those with whom You were angry,” shifting expression so anger is not verbally attributed to God in direct address. SAMARRAI-ASRAR: The Fātiḥa explicitly attributes favor to God (‘You bestowed favor’) while describing the blameworthy as those under anger and those astray. SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT: The passive المغضوب عليهم leaves the agent open so the condemned face anger from God, angels, people, and even their own skins. SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT: Repeating لا ensures exclusion of either condemned group on its own; without it the wording might exclude only those who combine anger and error, as the two-part prohibition analogy shows. SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT: The angered oppose the favored just as anger opposes grace; the chapter's ending gathers its opening praise, judgment, exclusive worship, reliance, and guidance into the fates of the condemned.

positions.position: Anger is a real divine attribute unlike human agitation

WAHIDI-BASIT reporting عدي بن حاتم: A report from ʿAdī ibn Ḥātim, attributed to the Prophet, identifies those under wrath as Jews and the astray as Christians; no grading is stated. RAZI-FULL reporting أصحابنا: Razi's Ash'arite school reads the sequence as God's anger causing their misguidance; the reverse would make a human attribute affect God, which is impossible. BAYDAWI: When anger is attributed to God, it denotes the final outcome or endpoint, not an emotion in God. IBNKATHIR: The verse attributes favor directly to God, leaves the agent of anger unexpressed although God is its true agent, and assigns misguidance to those who embody it although He misleads by His decree; cited verses affirm His exclusive control of guidance and misguidance. | mentions 58:14, 18:17, 7:186 BURHAN reporting قيل: One explanation says praise uses third person because it ranks below worship, while direct address elevates the worshipper's encounter; similarly, blessing is explicitly attributed to God but anger is phrased obliquely as a matter of etiquette. | mentions 6:101 BURSEVI: A common reading identifies those angered as Jews and those astray as Christians, but neither group's label is exclusive because Scripture attributes both traits to both. ALUSI: Following the early generations, al-Ālūsī affirms anger as an eternal divine attribute fitting God’s majesty without specifying how or claiming to know its reality, like mercy. ALUSI: The blessing is directly attributed to God as a deferential appeal for guidance to those whose favor is established; anger is put in the passive and left unassigned out of courtesy in a humble request for kindness. ALUSI-FULL: Alusi follows the early community: anger is a divine attribute befitting God, whose reality and manner are unknown, like mercy; “My mercy precedes My anger” concerns the greater or earlier manifestation of mercy. ELMALILI: Qur'an also attributes divine wrath to disbelievers generally and describes those who reject God's way as far astray, supporting the comprehensive reading. | mentions 16:106

positions.position: Human anger is bodily or psychological agitation; the divine usage is interpreted accordingly

question: What does the repeated negation before 'the astray' do?

positions.position: Lā is a genuine negation coordinated with ghayr
positions.reasons: MAJAZ: Abū Khirāsh’s verse supplies a further example of lā continuing a negative coordination in ولا البكر. MAJAZ: In wa-lā al-ḍāllīn, lā reinforces the preceding negation; Arabic likewise says ‘without good or blessing’ and ‘no benefit nor defense.’ TAB reporting نحويو الكوفة: The Kufans reject the exception analysis: “nor” is a negative conjunction, and Arabic coordinates a negative with a negative, not a negation with an exception. TAB reporting بعض أهل البصرة: Some Basrans call lā before “the astray” an added particle that completes the expression but contributes no negation, citing poetry and “what prevented you from not prostrating?” | mentions 7:12 TAB: Al-Ṭabarī agrees with the Kufans: lā is a true negation coordinated with the negative sense of ghayr, so the request is for the path of the favored, not the wrathful or astray. TAB-FULL reporting نحويو الكوفيين: Kufan grammarians reject exception: coordinating the negative wa-lā al-ḍāllīn with an exception is unattested, since Arabic coordinates exception with exception and negation with negation. TAB-FULL reporting بعض نحويي الكوفة: A Kufan grammarian rejects ghayr meaning other than because lā cannot coordinate with سوى absent a prior negative; he also rejects starting lā with an omitted-negation sense without previous negation. TAB-FULL reporting نحوي من الكوفة: The Kufan answer reads al-ʿAjjāj's lā as genuine negation and explains the other poems' apparent filler lā by the negative earlier in each sentence, as in the line about Abū Bakr and ʿUmar. TAB-FULL: He prefers the Kufan analysis: lā cannot begin as an omitted negative or coordinate with other than or an exception; since ghayr can mean exception, negation, or other than, the only valid reading here is negation, making the verse ask to avoid both groups. ZAJJAJ: Al-ḍāllīn is coordinated with al-maghḍūb ʿalayhim; lā is allowed because ghayr already carries negation, as in ghayr ḍārib meaning “not striking.” NAHHAS: The Kufan objection is not binding because lā here carries a negative sense. THALABI reporting الزجاج: Al-Zajjāj says lā may coordinate with ghayr because ghayr already carries negation, effectively meaning neither those angered nor those astray; this is not possible when ghayr means ‘other than.’ WAHIDI-BASIT reporting الفراء: Al-Farrāʾ rejects accusative ghayr as an exception, arguing that a positive exception cannot be followed by negative lā in coordination. WAHIDI-BASIT: Those allowing exception say an exception resembles negation, so all came except Zayd can mean all came, not Zayd; lā can coordinate by meaning or be an addition. WAHIDI-BASIT reporting صاحب النظم: The author of al-Naẓm says lā in wa-lā al-ḍāllīn prevents misreading al-ḍāllīn as coordinated with those favored; it marks coordination with ghayr, which implies negation. KASHSHAF: La appears because ghayr already carries negation: neither the angered nor the astray. KASHSHAF-FULL: The negative lā before astray is included because ghayr already carries a negative sense. ABUHAYYAN reporting الأخفش والزجاج: Al-Akhfash and al-Zajjāj allow accusative ghayr as a disconnected exception because the preceding wording does not include those who are astray; some readers reject this analysis because of lā. ABUHAYYAN: Lā reinforces the negation already contained in ghayr and is attached to المغضوب عليهم to avoid suggesting that الضالين is coordinated with الذين. ABUHAYYAN-FULL: The lā before “those astray” reinforces negation; placing it in the coordination prevents “those astray” from being mistaken as part of “those You favored.” SAMIN-DURR: Ghayr can function like illā for exception, as an adjective by analogy with illā, or like lā for negation, permitting its governed object to precede it. SAMIN-DURR: Ghayr is also read in the accusative as a circumstantial from alladhīna or ʿalayhim, or as a disjoint exception; al-Farrāʾ rejects the latter because lā lacks a preceding negation. SAMIN-DURR: Lā reinforces the negation already carried by ghayr and blocks reading al-ḍāllīn as coordinated with those blessed; Kufans instead equate it with ghayr, and ʿUmar reportedly read that way. IBNKATHIR reporting عمر بن الخطاب: ʿUmar read “and other than the astray”; Ibn Kathir says this report has a sound chain and treats it as explanatory, supporting emphatic negation and separation of the two paths. BIQAI: Ghayr conveys negation rather than an exception: the wording excludes those characterized by the trait from the outset and avoids suggesting a merely lesser class. BIQAI-FULL: Removing the object of bestowed favor broadens the wording; the negation excludes the angry and astray as separate failures, one in action and the other in knowledge. ALUSI reporting الأخفش: A report ascribed to al-Akhfash treats the exception as semantically negative, allowing lā to coordinate by meaning and removing al-Farrāʾ’s objection. ALUSI reporting عمر بن الخطاب: A reading with wa-ghayr in place of wa-lā is reported from ʿUmar and ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Zubayr; the muṣḥaf’s mutawātir reading is wa-lā, which reinforces the negation implicit in ghayr. ALUSI-FULL reporting عمر بن الخطاب وعبدالله بن الزبير: A reading attributed to ʿUmar and ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Zubayr adds ghayr before “those astray”; the canonical reading is otherwise, and al-Kufis treat ghayr as negation reinforcing the phrase. ALUSI-FULL reporting الأخفش: Al-Akhfash allows the accusative as a connected or disconnected exception if “favor” is broad; al-Farraʾ forbids joining negative lā to an exceptive phrase meaning “other than.” IBNASHUR-FULL: Ibn ʿĀshūr calls that explanation far-fetched: لا simply reinforces the negation already conveyed by ghayr in a normal negative coordination. | mentions 5:19 SAMARRAI-LAMASAT reporting حاشية الجرجاني على الكشاف: In negation, the added lā after the coordinating conjunction explicitly attaches negation to each item and prevents reading only the combined pair as negated.

positions.position: Lā is added or redundant, reinforcing the expression
positions.reasons: FARRA: Farra rejects the claim that ghayr in al-ḥamd means “other than” and lā is extra; extra lā requires a preceding negation. FARRA: The verse “in a well without ḥawr” does not prove an extra lā: here lā is a true negation, while poetry allows an extra lā after an earlier negation. MAJAZ: In ghayr al-maghḍūbi ʿalayhim wa-lā al-ḍāllīn, the first lā is an extra particle completing the phrase, effectively ‘and the straying.’ MAJAZ: Al-ʿAjjāj’s phrase fī biʾr lā ḥawr has an extra lā; the intended sense is a well of ruin or destruction. MAJAZ: Abū al-Najm’s ألا تسخرا means أن يسخرن, showing an extra lā; al-qafandar means ugly and repulsive. MAJAZ: In the cited line, ‘they reproach me in amusement ألا أحبه’ means ‘that I love it,’ with lā treated as extra. NAHHAS reporting البصريون: Basrans treat lā as extra; the Kufans understand it as ghayr. WAHIDI-BASIT: Before an indefinite, lā may be extra; if not extra, it either joins the noun as one genitive compound or contributes negation without affecting the noun's case. IBNATIYYA reporting الطبري: Al-Ṭabarī calls lā extra, citing a rajaz line where ألا تسخرا is understood as أن تسخر. IBNATIYYA: The author rejects al-Ṭabarī’s reading of al-Aḥwaṣ’s line as proof that lā is extra: it means they reproach him for wanting not to love amusement, so lā is operative. TABRISI reporting البصريون: The Basran grammarians take lā as an emphatic extra particle of negation, eliminating an ambiguity that could otherwise allow separate readings of the coordinated words. TABRISI reporting علي بن عيسى الرماني: Al-Rummani explains lā in the exception reading as an extra particle, like in the line about a pit of destruction and the Qur'anic phrase 'that you should not prostrate'. | mentions 7:12 QURTUBI-FULL reporting الطبري: Al-Tabari treats lā in “and not those astray” as redundant, as in the verse “what prevented you from not prostrating.” | mentions 7:12 BAYDAWI: The lā is an extra particle reinforcing the negation already expressed by ghayr, as in the cited grammatical examples. ABUHAYYAN: Some permit accusative ghayr as an exception by treating lā as extra, since they say lā is extra only after prior negation; they cite Qurʾanic and poetic examples, while other grammarians take lā as genuinely negative. ABUHAYYAN: Abū Ḥayyān says the alleged proof that lā is extra in the verse of the generous man is not decisive: lā itself is the object of أبى, and البخل is its apposition or a causal object. ABUHAYYAN-FULL: ʿAlā can also mean about, with, in, alongside, because of, from, or serve as an extra particle. ABUHAYYAN-FULL reporting القراء: Al-Qurrāʾ allow lā to be extra only after a prior negation, citing poetic usage and 17:61; Abū Ḥayyān discusses competing analyses of the cited poems. | mentions 17:61 IBNKATHIR reporting بعض النحاة: Some grammarians call la before the astray redundant and cite an al-ʿAjjaj line; Ibn Kathir rejects this and treats it as reinforcing the negation. BURHAN: After a conjunction preceded by negation or prohibition, extra لا reinforces the negation; he classifies لا in this verse that way. ALUSI reporting الفراء: Al-Farrāʾ rejects the exception analysis because ghayr then means siwā and the negative lā cannot be coordinated with it unless lā is treated as extra; al-Ālūsī notes the usage after wāw is unattested. | mentions 7:12 IBNASHUR: He takes the extra lā as verbal reinforcement of negation after ghayr, following Arabic coordination under negation, as in 5:19. | mentions 5:19 IBNASHUR reporting السيد: Al-Sayyid says lā prevents the mistaken inference that only the combined group is excluded, allowing one group to remain affirmed; the author distinguishes this from the semantic extra lā in 7:12. | mentions 7:12 IBNASHUR-FULL: This extra لا is only verbal reinforcement and keeps the meaning negative, unlike the particle in the command to Adam not to prostrate. | mentions 7:12

IBNASHUR: Lā coordinates the straying with the objects of ghayr; contrary to the reported view of Makki ibn Abī Ṭālib, it is not needed to prevent attachment to the favored. IBNASHUR-FULL reporting مكي ابن أبي طالب: Makkī b. Abī Ṭālib says the repeated لا prevents readers from connecting those astray to the favored people.

positions.position: Religious misguidance opposes complete faith and can culminate in sealing and veiling; the angered deliberately deviate under worldly desire, while astray groups distort true religions through error.

positions.position: The Qur'an depicts an upward route and a downward route; those struck by wrath fall, while misguidance is associated with shirk, producing three groups: believers, the wrathful, and the wandering astray.; cited verses: 7:40, 20:81, 2:108

positions.position: The blessed are those who have followed the straight path, while those astray are lost from it; the Quran often pairs guidance and misguidance as opposites.; cited verses: 16:93, 2:26

positions.position: Corrupt knowledge produces misguidance and corrupt intention produces anger; these are the two root diseases of the heart.
positions.reasons: SAMARRAI-LAMASAT reporting التفسير القيم: Corrupt knowledge produces misguidance and corrupt intention produces anger; these are the two root diseases of the heart.

positions.position: On a vertical ascent reading, wrath represents descent from God and straying represents horizontal wandering; together they symbolize three spatial dimensions and human possibilities.

positions.position: The Christians, as an identified example or restricted referent
positions.reasons: MUQATIL: The straying people are the polytheists, identified here as the Christians. TAB reporting رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم: In the Wādī al-Qurā report, the Prophet answers that the people asked about are the astray, meaning the Christians. TAB reporting مجاهد: Mujāhid identifies the astray as the Christians. TAB reporting ابن عباس: Ibn ʿAbbās, through al-Ḍaḥḥāk, glosses the phrase as the Christians' way, whom God led astray through their false claim about Him. TAB reporting ابن عباس: Ibn ʿAbbās, in a report through Ibn Jurayj, identifies the astray as the Christians. TAB reporting ابن عباس، ابن مسعود، وناس من أصحاب النبي: The report transmitted by al-Suddī from early authorities identifies the astray as the Christians. TAB reporting الربيع: Al-Rabīʿ identifies the astray as the Christians. TAB reporting عبد الرحمن بن زيد: ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Zayd identifies the astray as the Christians. TAB reporting زيد: Zayd, ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Zayd's father, identifies the astray as the Christians. TAB: In Arabic, anyone who departs from the intended route and follows an unsound way is astray; Christians receive this label for missing the truth and taking a wrong religious path. TAB: Jews and Christians are both astray and under wrath; God labels each group by a real, recognizable trait, without implying that it lacks the other's blameworthy traits. TAB reporting بعض أهل الغباء من القدرية: Some ignorant Qadarites infer from calling Christians astray, without calling them those who mislead, that God has no causal role in their acts of misguidance. TAB-FULL reporting النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم عن عدي بن حاتم: The Prophet identifies those astray as Christians when asked about the verse. TAB-FULL reporting النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم عن عدي بن حاتم: The Prophet tells ʿAdī ibn Ḥātim that those astray are Christians; further routes repeat this identification. TAB-FULL reporting النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم عن عبد الله بن شقيق: Reports from a questioner during the siege at Wādī al-Qurā have the Prophet identify the people asked about as Christians, the astray. TAB-FULL reporting مجاهد: Mujāhid identifies those astray as Christians. TAB-FULL reporting ابن عباس: Ibn Abbas glosses the astray as Christians whom God led astray through their fabrication about Him; the prayer asks for the true monotheistic faith, protection from Jewish wrath and Christian error, and mercy to prevent their punishment. TAB-FULL reporting ابن عباس والسدي عن ابن عباس وابن مسعود وناس من أصحاب النبي وربيع وعبد الرحمن بن زيد وأبوه: The cited authorities—through Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Suddī's report, Rabīʿ, and ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Zayd and his father—identify those astray as Christians. TAB-FULL: In Arabic, anyone deviating from the intended road is astray; Christians are so called because they miss the truth and take a religious route other than the straight one. TAB-FULL: Both Jews and Christians are astray and under wrath, but God labels each by a true, recognizable characteristic, without listing every blameworthy trait of either group. TAB-FULL reporting بعض أهل الغباء من القدرية: Some Qadariyyah wrongly infer from calling Christians astray and Jews objects of wrath that human acts belong only to people and that God does not cause their misguidance; al-Ṭabarī says this betrays ignorance of Arabic attribution and the many verses naming God as guide and misguider. | mentions 10:22, 45:23 IBNABIHATIM reporting رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم: The Prophet identifies those under wrath as Jews and the astray as Christians; the author says exegetes do not disagree on this wording. IBNABIHATIM: The author says he knows no disagreement among exegetes over the identification of those astray as Christians and those under wrath as Jews. IBNABIHATIM reporting رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم: A second report from the Prophet likewise says the Jews incurred wrath and the Christians went astray. THALABI reporting رسول الله: In a report from ʿAdī ibn Ḥātim, the Prophet identifies those angered with the Jews and those astray with the Christians. THALABI reporting رسول الله: At Wādī al-Qurā, the Prophet points to Jews fighting him as those angered and to Christians as the other party, those astray. THALABI: The author links divine anger against Jews to 5:60 and the description of Christians as astray to 5:77. | mentions 5:60, 5:77 MAWARDI reporting عدي بن حاتم: Adi ibn Hatim reports that the Prophet identified those under wrath as Jews and those astray as Christians; al-Mawardi says all exegetes agree. MAWARDI: Al-Mawardi says all exegetes agree that those under wrath are Jews and those astray are Christians. MAWARDI-FULL reporting عدي بن حاتم: He asked the Prophet who the angered and astray groups were; the Prophet identified them as Jews and Christians, respectively, as all exegetes agree. WAHIDI-BASIT reporting عدي بن حاتم: A report from ʿAdī ibn Ḥātim, attributed to the Prophet, identifies those under wrath as Jews and the astray as Christians; no grading is stated. WAHIDI-BASIT reporting النبي: A second report says the Prophet at Wādī al-Qurā was asked by a man from Bali about two groups; he pointed to Jews as those under wrath and Christians as astray; no grading is stated. WAHIDI-QT: Those astray are Christians, and Muslims ask to avoid both their error and the Jews' incurred wrath. WAHIDI-WAJIZ: The people who went astray are the Christians; Muslims ask to avoid their deviation from truth as well as the Jews' incurred anger. BAGHAWI: An unnamed view identifies those angered as the Jews and those astray as the Christians, citing verses on their anger and earlier deviation. | mentions 5:60, 5:77 BAGHAWI-FULL: A reported identification makes the objects of wrath Jews and the straying ones Christians, supported by Quranic descriptions of each group. | mentions 5:60, 5:77 KASHSHAF: Those astray are identified as Christians, with 5:77 cited. | mentions 5:77 IBNATIYYA reporting ابن مسعود وابن عباس ومجاهد والسدي وابن زيد وعدي بن حاتم عن النبي: They identify those under wrath as Jews and the astray as Christians; the same interpretation is reported from ʿAdī ibn Ḥātim from the Prophet. IBNATIYYA-FULL reporting ابن مسعود وابن عباس ومجاهد والسدي وابن زيد: Ibn Masʿud, Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, al-Suddi, and Ibn Zayd identify those angered as Jews and those astray as Christians; ʿAdi ibn Hatim transmits this from the Prophet. IBNATIYYA-FULL: Christians who followed their prior law went astray once Muhammad's law arrived; others had already gone astray through their divided claims about Jesus. IBNATIYYA-FULL: The Qur'an says Christians followed desires of people who had previously strayed and misled many in 5:77. | mentions 5:77 IBNATIYYA-FULL: The author finds this answer insufficient: Jewish aggression, defiance, disbelief despite signs, and killing prophets especially warrant wrath, while Christians strayed from the start without these specific acts. IBNATIYYA-FULL: Calling Christians “astray” does not support Qadarite claims that they made themselves astray: the intransitive phrasing works like “the wall collapsed” or “the tree moved”; God created their error and they acquired it. TABRISI: The astray are identified as Christians, supported by the warning against those who went astray and led many astray. | mentions 5:77 TABRISI reporting الحسن البصري: Hasan says both Jews and Christians are both astray and under anger, though God marks each group by a distinguishing epithet despite their shared traits. TABRISI: This explanation identifies the angered as Jews and the astray as Christians. IBNJAWZI-ZAD reporting عدي بن حاتم عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم: A report from ʿAdī ibn Ḥātim, from the Prophet, identifies the objects of anger as Jews and the astray as Christians. RAZI-FULL reporting المشهور: The commonly reported identification makes those under wrath the Jews and those astray the Christians, citing the Qur'an's descriptions of each. | mentions 5:60, 5:77 QURTUBI reporting جمهور المفسرين: Most commentators identify those under wrath as Jews and the astray as Christians; 2:61, 3:112, and 48:6 concern Jewish wrath, and 5:77 Christian error. | mentions 2:61, 3:112, 48:6, 5:77 QURTUBI-FULL reporting الجمهور: Most interpreters identify those under wrath as Jews and those astray as Christians; the Prophet’s explanation to ʿAdi ibn Hatim supports it, as do verses about their wrath and error. | mentions 3:112, 48:6, 5:77 BAYDAWI: One reported identification makes those astray the Christians, citing 5:77. | mentions 5:77 BAYDAWI-FULL: A reported interpretation identifies those under anger as Jews and those astray as Christians, linking them to 5:60 and 5:77; the identification is also transmitted as a Prophetic report. | mentions 5:60, 5:77 NASAFI reporting قيل: One view identifies those under anger as Jews, citing God’s curse and anger in 5:60, and those astray as Christians, citing their earlier error in 5:77. | mentions 5:60, 5:77 NASAFI-FULL: The reported identification takes the astray as Christians, citing the verse that says they went astray before. | mentions 5:77 QASHANI: The astray are like Christians who stop at inner lights and special mercy, overlooking God’s outward manifestation and losing vision of the beloved’s beauty throughout creation. ABUHAYYAN reporting ابن مسعود وابن عباس ومجاهد والسدي وابن زيد: Ibn Masʿūd, Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, al-Suddī, and Ibn Zayd identify those angered as Jews and those astray as Christians. ABUHAYYAN-FULL reporting ابن مسعود: Ibn Masʿūd, Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, al-Suddī, and Ibn Zayd identify those angered as Jews and those astray as Christians. IBNKATHIR: Jews are characterized by abandoning known truth and thus anger, while Christians seek a goal without knowledge of its way because they do not follow the true Messenger; each group is also both astray and under anger. IBNKATHIR: The Qurʾan calls the Jews recipients of anger and specifically describes Christians as astray, supporting the verse's characteristic labels. | mentions 5:60, 5:77 IBNKATHIR reporting النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم: In the report from ʿAdi ibn Hatim, the Prophet identifies the angered as Jews and the astray as Christians; al-Tirmidhi grades this route hasan gharīb, and Ibn Kathir notes other routes and wordings. IBNKATHIR reporting النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم: At Wadi al-Qura the Prophet points to Jews as the angered and Christians as the astray; other transmitters send the report without naming the eyewitness, while ʿUrwa's route names Ibn ʿUmar. IBNKATHIR reporting السدي: Al-Suddi, transmitting from Ibn ʿAbbas, Ibn Masʿud, and Companions of the Prophet, identifies the Jews as angered and Christians as astray. BURHAN: Putting those under wrath before those astray may convey disparagement: Jews preceded Christians historically and were nearer to the Muslims. DURR reporting الربيع بن أنس: Al-Rabīʿ b. Anas identifies the favored as prophets, those under wrath as Jews, and the astray as Christians. DURR reporting مجاهد: Mujāhid identifies those under wrath as Jews and the astray as Christians. DURR reporting سعيد بن جبير: Saʿīd b. Jubayr identifies the objects of wrath and the astray as Jews and Christians. DURR reporting النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم: At Wādī al-Qurā, the Prophet identified the objects of wrath as Jews and the astray as Christians; ʿAbd Allāh b. Shaqīq reports the exchange. DURR reporting النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم: During the siege of Wādī al-Qurā, the Prophet identified one group as Jews under wrath and the other as astray Christians. DURR reporting أبو ذر: Abū Dharr reports asking the Prophet, who answered that those under wrath are Jews and the astray are Christians. DURR reporting النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم: Ismāʿīl b. DURR reporting ابن مسعود: Ibn Masʿūd identifies those under wrath as Jews and the astray as Christians. DURR reporting ابن أبي حاتم: Ibn Abī Ḥātim knows of no exegetical disagreement identifying those under wrath as Jews and the astray as Christians. DURR-FULL reporting ابن عباس: The people under anger are Jews and the misguided are Christians; the account links their fate to the cited description of apes, swine, and evil destination. | mentions 5:60 DURR-FULL reporting الربيع بن أنس: Al-Rabi ibn Anas identifies the favored as prophets, those under anger as Jews, and the astray as Christians. DURR-FULL reporting مجاهد: Mujahid identifies those under anger as Jews and the astray as Christians. DURR-FULL reporting النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم: Asked at Wadi al-Qura who the people under anger and those astray were, the Prophet answered Jews and Christians respectively. DURR-FULL reporting النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم: Several reports from questions at Wadi al-Qura say the Prophet identified those under anger as Jews and the other group as Christians who are astray. DURR-FULL reporting النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم: A report through a man of Balayn likewise records the Prophet's answer: Jews are under anger and Christians astray. BURSEVI: A common reading identifies those angered as Jews and those astray as Christians, but neither group's label is exclusive because Scripture attributes both traits to both. ALUSI reporting رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم: Aḥmad transmits and Ibn Ḥibbān grades as ḥasan a Prophetic report identifying the objects of anger as Jews and the astray as Christians. ALUSI: Al-Ālūsī also reads the general terms broadly: those erring in outward works, such as sinners, are under anger; those erring in belief are astray. ALUSI reporting بعضهم: Some support the Christian identification from the verse warning against following the desires of a people who went astray. | mentions 5:77 ALUSI: Al-Ālūsī prefers the hadith as evidence: anger and straying are also ascribed generally to unbelievers, and both terms apply specifically to Jews and Christians. | mentions 16:106, 4:167, 5:60, 5:77 ALUSI: He offers several reasons for the order: Jews precede Christians historically; bestowal contrasts with retribution rather than misguidance; and Jews are more obstinate, corrupt, hostile to believers, and abased. ALUSI: Al-Ālūsī says Christians are less culpable and closer to Islam, and a person who is merely astray may still find guidance. positions.position: Those lacking true knowledge or belief
positions.reasons: SULAMI reporting ابن عطاء: Those under anger are abandoned, expelled, and humiliated; the astray have left God's guidance, knowledge, and guardianship. RAZI-FULL: A broader reading takes those under wrath as people who err in outward deeds, including sinners, and those astray as people who err in belief; the wording is general and should not be restricted without cause. RAZI-FULL: The verse divides people into the obedient who are favored, sinners under wrath, and those ignorant of religion or unbelievers who are astray. RAZI-FULL: Those with complete favor unite knowledge of truth for its own sake with doing good for its own sake; lacking practice makes sinners under wrath, while lacking knowledge makes people astray. | mentions 4:93, 10:32 RAZI-FULL: The verse establishes the immunity of prophets and angels from actions or beliefs contrary to the favored path: otherwise they would stray and could not be models or belong among those favored. | mentions 10:32 RAZI-FULL: The favored are complete in knowledge and practice, the condemned neglect righteous deeds, and the astray lack sound belief; asking for the favored path seeks the example of the sound group. BAYDAWI: Bayḍāwī also finds apt a general reading: sinners fail in action and incur wrath, while those ignorant of God fail in understanding and go astray. BAYDAWI-FULL: A further interpretation calls deliberate sinners angered and those ignorant of God astray: failure of action is impiety, while failure of understanding is error. | mentions 4:93 ABUHAYYAN: Ḍalāl can mean ruin, concealment, loss, ignorance of an object's location, waste, neglect, forgetting, departure from the proper route, bewilderment, or hesitation; Qurʾanic usage also includes lack of detailed knowledge and love. ABUHAYYAN-FULL: The root of ḍalāl carries senses including perishing, disappearing, being lost or ignorant, straying, bewilderment, and wavering; Qurʾanic uses can mean lack of detailed knowledge or love. IBNKATHIR: Those subject to anger know the truth but turn away; the astray lack knowledge and wander without reaching the truth. BURSEVI: Misguidance means deliberately or accidentally leaving the sound path; sinners fail in action, while the ignorant fail in knowledge. | mentions 4:93, 10:32 IBNASHUR reporting قالوا: In religious usage, misguidance opposes full faith and ranges from neglecting recommended practice to unbelief; the author defines it as absence of guidance and notes sealing as its extreme form. IBNASHUR-FULL: It also rejects the fate of people who received guidance but failed to preserve their course and became astray through poor understanding of the blessing of knowledge. SAMARRAI-LAMASAT: People are either blessed, or wretched in two ways: knowing truth but violating it, or lacking knowledge of truth and being astray. | mentions 18:103-104 SAMARRAI-LAMASAT reporting البيضاوي: One proposed reading identifies the angry as sinners and the astray as those ignorant of God. SAMARRAI-LAMASAT reporting التفسير القيم: People divide by knowledge and practice: the knowledgeable doer is blessed, the knowledgeable follower of desire is angry upon, and the ignorant is astray; the first is more deserving of anger. STUDYQURAN: The verse prays to follow those whom God elevates in belief, knowledge, and uncorrupted faith, and to avoid disbelievers, some astray and some under wrath. | mentions 6:83, 58:11, 6:82 STUDYQURAN: Another interpretation associates disbelief with wrath and lesser sins with straying. STUDYQURAN: The Quran frequently describes disbelievers, those who exchange belief for disbelief, and caprice-followers without guidance as astray. | mentions 3:90, 2:108, 4:136, 4:167, 28:50

positions.position: Those who leave the Sunnah
positions.reasons: THALABI reporting التستري: Al-Tustarī identifies innovation with those angered and departure from Sunna with those astray. BAGHAWI reporting سهل بن عبد الله: Sahl ibn ʿAbd Allah says those astray are people who have left the Sunna. BAGHAWI-FULL reporting سهل بن عبد الله: Sahl b. Abd Allah interprets those under wrath as innovators and the straying ones as people departing from the Sunnah. QURTUBI-FULL: Another view calls innovators recipients of wrath and those who leave the sunnas astray; the author says this is good, though the Prophet’s interpretation is best. IBNASHUR-FULL: Misguidance is mistakenly taking a path other than the intended one, whether consciously or unknowingly; its religious use is metaphorical and ranges from neglecting sunnahs to disbelief.

positions.position: Polytheists
positions.reasons: QURTUBI reporting قيل: An alternative says those under wrath are polytheists and the astray are hypocrites. QURTUBI-FULL reporting بعضهم: Other interpreters identify those under wrath as polytheists and those astray as hypocrites. positions.position: Hypocrites

question: Why are the angered named before the astray?

positions.position: The order follows historical sequence
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN: Anger precedes misguidance in the wording although it results from it because it contrasts with favor: favor brings good and requital brings harm; the order also suits the sūra's cadence. ABUHAYYAN: The conjunctive wāw does not itself establish temporal priority; if Jews and Christians are intended, the order may reflect chronology or the Jews' greater hostility, as they came earlier. ABUHAYYAN-FULL: Anger precedes misguidance despite resulting from it because it is paired antithetically with favor; the order also suits the verse-ending cadence and the conjunction itself implies no sequence. ABUHAYYAN-FULL: If the groups mean Jews and Christians, Jews come first because they appeared earlier or are more hostile. BURHAN: Putting those under wrath before those astray may convey disparagement: Jews preceded Christians historically and were nearer to the Muslims. ALUSI: He offers several reasons for the order: Jews precede Christians historically; bestowal contrasts with retribution rather than misguidance; and Jews are more obstinate, corrupt, hostile to believers, and abased. ALUSI-FULL: The angry are named before those astray because Jews preceded Christians historically; alternatively, favor contrasts semantically with retribution, or Jews are more hostile and corrupt. | mentions 5:82 SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT: The angered precede the astray because they know truth and reject it, are more culpable than the ignorant, and Jews preceded Christians; an authentic hadith identifies the groups accordingly.

question: What does Āmīn mean after this verse?

positions.position: Āmīn asks God to answer
positions.reasons: MUSNAD-AHMAD reporting أبو موسى الأشعري عن النبي: The Prophet says to follow the imam: say Amin at al-Fatiha's end so God answers, follow his bowing and prostration, and say ‘Our Lord, praise belongs to You’ after he says God hears praise; his movements are offset so followers do not precede him. MUSNAD-AHMAD reporting النبي عن أبي هريرة: The Prophet teaches followers not to anticipate the imam, to say Amin at the end of al-Fatiha, and to answer ‘Our Lord, praise belongs to You’ after the imam says God hears praise; agreement with the angels brings forgiveness for those in the mosque. ZAJJAJ: Amīn and Āmīn mean “O God, answer”; they stand in place of a verbal noun for response, like ṣah standing for silence. SULAMI reporting بعض العراقيين: Amin expresses hope that God will answer the supplications just made. QUSHAYRI: Saying amin after the Fatiha is Sunnah and means “Lord, do and answer”; it seeks enabling for deeds and fulfillment of hopes through humble petition. BAGHAWI: Amin means “O God, hear and answer.” BAGHAWI-FULL: The reciter should say Amin after a separate pause; the word is normally light, though grammarians allow a long or short vowel, and means ‘God, hear and answer.’ KASHSHAF: Amin is a sound-form used as the name of the verb respond, like words meaning wait, hurry, and come. KASHSHAF reporting ابن عباس والنبي: Ibn Abbas asked the Prophet what Amin means, and the Prophet answered, do it. KASHSHAF-FULL: Amin is an indeclinable sound used for the verb respond; it has long and short forms, and a poetic line illustrates it. KASHSHAF-FULL reporting ابن عباس: Ibn Abbas says the Prophet explained Amin as meaning do it or answer. IBNATIYYA reporting النبي: A report says the Prophet heard a man supplicate and said his request was assured if he concluded; when asked how, he answered: with Āmīn. IBNATIYYA-FULL reporting الحسن بن أبي الحسن وثعلب: Most scholars, including al-Hasan and Thaʿlab, interpret amin as “O God, respond” or “Respond, Lord.” IBNJAWZI-ZAD reporting الحسن والزجاج: A second explanation understands āmīn as “O God, answer,” held by al-Ḥasan and al-Zajjāj. BAYDAWI: Āmīn is an imperative-like expression meaning “answer” or “grant the prayer”; it is not part of the Qur'an, by consensus. BAYDAWI-FULL: Āmīn is an imperative noun meaning “answer/accept”; a report from Ibn ʿAbbās says the Prophet explained it as “do so.” It is built on fatḥa to avoid two adjacent still consonants. NASAFI: Amin is a spoken formula meaning ‘answer/respond,’ treated as a noun for the imperative just as ruwayd means ‘wait.’ It has long and short forms; the short vowel length is original, while the long form lengthens the hamza. NASAFI reporting ابن عباس عن رسول الله: Ibn Abbas asked the Messenger about amin’s meaning, and he answered, ‘Do it.’ SAMIN-DURR: Amin is not part of the Quran by consensus; it means respond and is an indeclinable imperative noun. IBNKATHIR: It is recommended to say amin after al-Fatiha, pronounced either with a long or short first vowel; it means “O God, answer.” A report from Waʾil says the Prophet lengthened it, and al-Tirmidhi grades the report hasan. IBNKATHIR reporting أبو موسى: A Prophetic report in Muslim says that when the imam recites “nor the astray,” worshippers should say amin and God will answer them.
