positions.position: Al-Hasan says the imam should not say Amin because the imam is the supplicant.
positions.reasons: KASHSHAF reporting الحسن: Al-Hasan says the imam should not say Amin because the imam is the supplicant.

positions.position: Abu Hanifa is reported to say the imam should not say Amin.
positions.reasons: KASHSHAF reporting أبو حنيفة: Abu Hanifa is reported to say the imam should not say Amin.

positions.position: The well-known position of Abu Hanifa and his followers is to say Amin silently.
positions.reasons: KASHSHAF reporting أبو حنيفة وأصحابه: The well-known position of Abu Hanifa and his followers is to say Amin silently.

positions.position: Ibn Abbas says the Prophet explained Amin as meaning do it or answer.
positions.reasons: KASHSHAF-FULL reporting ابن عباس: Ibn Abbas says the Prophet explained Amin as meaning do it or answer.

positions.position: Hasan says the imam should not say Amin because he is the one supplicating; Abu Hanifa shares this view and is known to recite it quietly.
positions.reasons: KASHSHAF-FULL reporting الحسن وأبو حنيفة: Hasan says the imam should not say Amin because he is the one supplicating; Abu Hanifa shares this view and is known to recite it quietly.

positions.position: The Prophet tells worshippers to say Āmīn when the imam says “nor those who are astray”; the angels in heaven say it, and agreement with them brings forgiveness of past sins.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA reporting أبو هريرة عن النبي: The Prophet tells worshippers to say Āmīn when the imam says “nor those who are astray”; the angels in heaven say it, and agreement with them brings forgiveness of past sins.

positions.position: A report says Gabriel taught the Prophet al-Fātiḥa at its revelation; after the Prophet recited it, Gabriel told him to say Āmīn.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA reporting جبريل: A report says Gabriel taught the Prophet al-Fātiḥa at its revelation; after the Prophet recited it, Gabriel told him to say Āmīn.

positions.position: A report says the Prophet heard a man supplicate and said his request was assured if he concluded; when asked how, he answered: with Āmīn.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA reporting النبي: A report says the Prophet heard a man supplicate and said his request was assured if he concluded; when asked how, he answered: with Āmīn.

positions.position: Another view makes Āmīn one of God’s names; it is reported from Jaʿfar ibn Muḥammad, Mujāhid, and Hilāl ibn Yasāf.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA reporting جعفر بن محمد ومجاهد وهلال بن يساف: Another view makes Āmīn one of God’s names; it is reported from Jaʿfar ibn Muḥammad, Mujāhid, and Hilāl ibn Yasāf.

positions.position: The author infers from these reports that supplicants should say Āmīn at the end of every supplication and after al-Fātiḥa outside prayer, without loud recitation.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA: The author infers from these reports that supplicants should say Āmīn at the end of every supplication and after al-Fātiḥa outside prayer, without loud recitation.

positions.position: One legal view has every worshipper—imam, praying alone, or follower—say Āmīn if they recite or hear al-Fātiḥa.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA reporting بعض العلماء: One legal view has every worshipper—imam, praying alone, or follower—say Āmīn if they recite or hear al-Fātiḥa.

positions.position: In the Mudawwana, Mālik says the imam does not say Āmīn, while followers say it quietly and a person praying alone says it.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA reporting مالك: In the Mudawwana, Mālik says the imam does not say Āmīn, while followers say it quietly and a person praying alone says it.

positions.position: Other reports from Mālik say that the imam says Āmīn either quietly or aloud, or does not say it during audible prayer.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA reporting مالك: Other reports from Mālik say that the imam says Āmīn either quietly or aloud, or does not say it during audible prayer.

positions.position: Ibn Ḥabīb holds that the imam should say Āmīn.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA reporting ابن حبيب: Ibn Ḥabīb holds that the imam should say Āmīn.

positions.position: Ibn Nāfiʿ says a follower says Āmīn only if he hears the imam reach “nor those who are astray”; if too far away to hear, he omits it.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA reporting ابن نافع: Ibn Nāfiʿ says a follower says Āmīn only if he hears the imam reach “nor those who are astray”; if too far away to hear, he omits it.

positions.position: Ibn ʿAbdūs tells a distant follower to estimate the length of the recitation and then say Āmīn.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA reporting ابن عبدوس: Ibn ʿAbdūs tells a distant follower to estimate the length of the recitation and then say Āmīn.

positions.position: Āmīn is built on fatḥa because two sukūns meet; fatḥa is lighter with yāʾ than the other vowel options.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA: Āmīn is built on fatḥa because two sukūns meet; fatḥa is lighter with yāʾ than the other vowel options.

positions.position: Every worshipper—leader, solitary, or follower—says amin after reciting or hearing the closing phrase.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA-FULL: Every worshipper—leader, solitary, or follower—says amin after reciting or hearing the closing phrase.

positions.position: Amin is indeclinable with fatḥa because two vowelless letters meet; fatḥa with yā is the lightest pronunciation.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA-FULL: Amin is indeclinable with fatḥa because two vowelless letters meet; fatḥa with yā is the lightest pronunciation.

positions.position: In the Mudawwana, the imam does not say amin; followers say it quietly, while a solitary worshipper does say it.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA-FULL reporting مالك: In the Mudawwana, the imam does not say amin; followers say it quietly, while a solitary worshipper does say it.

positions.position: A report from Malik allows the imam to say amin either silently or aloud.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA-FULL reporting مالك: A report from Malik allows the imam to say amin either silently or aloud.

positions.position: Another report from Malik says the imam does not say amin during audible recitation.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA-FULL reporting مالك: Another report from Malik says the imam does not say amin during audible recitation.

positions.position: Ibn Habib says the imam says amin.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA-FULL reporting ابن حبيب: Ibn Habib says the imam says amin.

positions.position: A follower says amin only if he hears the imam reach walā al-ḍāllīn; if too far away to hear, he omits it.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA-FULL reporting ابن نافع: A follower says amin only if he hears the imam reach walā al-ḍāllīn; if too far away to hear, he omits it.

positions.position: Ibn Abdus advises estimating the length of the recitation and then saying amin.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA-FULL reporting ابن عبدوس: Ibn Abdus advises estimating the length of the recitation and then saying amin.

positions.position: Abu Hurayra and others report the Prophet instructing worshippers to say amin after the imam recites “those astray”; one who coincides with the angels is forgiven earlier sins.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA-FULL reporting أبو هريرة وغيره: Abu Hurayra and others report the Prophet instructing worshippers to say amin after the imam recites “those astray”; one who coincides with the angels is forgiven earlier sins.

positions.position: A report says Gabriel told the Prophet to say amin after teaching him the opening sura at its revelation.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA-FULL reporting جبريل: A report says Gabriel told the Prophet to say amin after teaching him the opening sura at its revelation.

positions.position: The Prophet says a supplication is assured when sealed, and identifies amin as the seal.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA-FULL reporting رسول الله: The Prophet says a supplication is assured when sealed, and identifies amin as the seal.

positions.position: Jaʿfar ibn Muhammad, Mujahid, and Hilal ibn Yasaf reportedly say Amin is one of God's names.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA-FULL reporting جعفر بن محمد ومجاهد وهلال بن يساف: Jaʿfar ibn Muhammad, Mujahid, and Hilal ibn Yasaf reportedly say Amin is one of God's names.

positions.position: A third view treats āmīn as one of God's names, held by Mujāhid, Hilāl ibn Yasāf, and Jaʿfar ibn Muḥammad.
positions.reasons: IBNJAWZI-ZAD reporting مجاهد وهلال بن يساف وجعفر بن محمد: A third view treats āmīn as one of God's names, held by Mujāhid, Hilāl ibn Yasāf, and Jaʿfar ibn Muḥammad.

positions.position: Abū al-Ḥasan ʿAlī ibn ʿUbayd Allāh says it is Sunnah for a Fātiḥa reader to follow it with āmīn, whether inside or outside prayer.
positions.reasons: IBNJAWZI-ZAD reporting أبو الحسن علي بن عبيد الله: Abū al-Ḥasan ʿAlī ibn ʿUbayd Allāh says it is Sunnah for a Fātiḥa reader to follow it with āmīn, whether inside or outside prayer.

positions.position: A report from Abū Hurayra, from the Prophet, says that when the congregation says āmīn after the imām, matching the angels, prior sins are forgiven.
positions.reasons: IBNJAWZI-ZAD reporting أبو هريرة عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم: A report from Abū Hurayra, from the Prophet, says that when the congregation says āmīn after the imām, matching the angels, prior sins are forgiven.

positions.position: A verse transmitted by Abū al-ʿAbbās from Ibn al-Aʿrābī uses āmīn in a prayer asking rain for a people and protection for a caravan.
positions.reasons: IBNJAWZI-ZAD reporting أبو العباس عن ابن الأعرابي: A verse transmitted by Abū al-ʿAbbās from Ibn al-Aʿrābī uses āmīn in a prayer asking rain for a people and protection for a caravan.

positions.position: Another verse transmitted through Abū al-ʿAbbās has a speaker say āmīn after praying for distance from Faṭḥal and his mother’s son.
positions.reasons: IBNJAWZI-ZAD reporting أبو العباس عن ابن الأعرابي: Another verse transmitted through Abū al-ʿAbbās has a speaker say āmīn after praying for distance from Faṭḥal and his mother’s son.

positions.position: A third poetic citation uses āmīn in a supplication that God never deprive the speaker of his beloved and have mercy on one who says āmīnā.
positions.reasons: IBNJAWZI-ZAD reporting أبو العباس: A third poetic citation uses āmīn in a supplication that God never deprive the speaker of his beloved and have mercy on one who says āmīnā.

positions.position: The imam says āmīn aloud in audible prayers, based on the report that the Prophet raised his voice after al-ḍāllīn.
positions.reasons: BAYDAWI: The imam says āmīn aloud in audible prayers, based on the report that the Prophet raised his voice after al-ḍāllīn.

positions.position: A report from Abū Ḥanīfa says not to say āmīn; his better-known position is to say it quietly, as narrated from ʿAbd Allāh b. Mughaffal and Anas.
positions.reasons: BAYDAWI reporting أبو حنيفة: A report from Abū Ḥanīfa says not to say āmīn; his better-known position is to say it quietly, as narrated from ʿAbd Allāh b. Mughaffal and Anas.

positions.position: The follower says āmīn with the imam; agreement with the angels' āmīn brings forgiveness of prior sins, according to the Prophetic report.
positions.reasons: BAYDAWI reporting رسول الله: The follower says āmīn with the imam; agreement with the angels' āmīn brings forgiveness of prior sins, according to the Prophetic report.

positions.position: Ḥudhayfa b. al-Yamān reports that a child's recitation of al-ḥamdu li-llāh rabbi l-ʿālamīn caused God to lift an otherwise decreed punishment from a people for forty years.
positions.reasons: BAYDAWI reporting رسول الله: Ḥudhayfa b. al-Yamān reports that a child's recitation of al-ḥamdu li-llāh rabbi l-ʿālamīn caused God to lift an otherwise decreed punishment from a people for forty years.

positions.position: Āmīn is an imperative noun meaning “answer/accept”; a report from Ibn ʿAbbās says the Prophet explained it as “do so.” It is built on fatḥa to avoid two adjacent still consonants.
positions.reasons: BAYDAWI-FULL: Āmīn is an imperative noun meaning “answer/accept”; a report from Ibn ʿAbbās says the Prophet explained it as “do so.” It is built on fatḥa to avoid two adjacent still consonants.

positions.position: Āmīn is not Qur'an, but ending the sura with it is recommended because Gabriel taught it to the Prophet as a seal on the book; ʿAlī similarly calls it the seal of the Lord of the worlds.
positions.reasons: BAYDAWI-FULL: Āmīn is not Qur'an, but ending the sura with it is recommended because Gabriel taught it to the Prophet as a seal on the book; ʿAlī similarly calls it the seal of the Lord of the worlds.

positions.position: The Prophet said Gabriel taught him amin after he finished reciting the Fatiha and compared it to a seal on a letter; amin is not Qur’an because it does not appear in the codices.
positions.reasons: NASAFI reporting النبي عليه السلام: The Prophet said Gabriel taught him amin after he finished reciting the Fatiha and compared it to a seal on a letter; amin is not Qur’an because it does not appear in the codices.

positions.position: The poet's evidence shows both long and short forms of Amin, and a Prophetic report says Gabriel taught Amin at the end of al-Fatiha, like a seal on a letter; it is not Qur'an because codices omit…
positions.reasons: NASAFI-FULL: The poet's evidence shows both long and short forms of Amin, and a Prophetic report says Gabriel taught Amin at the end of al-Fatiha, like a seal on a letter; it is not Qur'an because codices omit it.

positions.position: It is recommended to say amin after al-Fatiha, pronounced either with a long or short first vowel; it means “O God, answer.” A report from Waʾil says the Prophet lengthened it, and al-Tirmidhi grades the report hasan.
positions.reasons: IBNKATHIR: It is recommended to say amin after al-Fatiha, pronounced either with a long or short first vowel; it means “O God, answer.” A report from Waʾil says the Prophet lengthened it, and al-Tirmidhi grades the report hasan.

positions.position: Waʾil ibn Hujr reports hearing the Prophet say amin aloud after al-Fatiha; al-Tirmidhi grades the hadith hasan, and reports also come from ʿAli and Ibn Masʿud.
positions.reasons: IBNKATHIR reporting وائل بن حجر: Waʾil ibn Hujr reports hearing the Prophet say amin aloud after al-Fatiha; al-Tirmidhi grades the hadith hasan, and reports also come from ʿAli and Ibn Masʿud.

positions.position: Bilal asked the Prophet not to say amin before him.
positions.reasons: IBNKATHIR reporting بلال: Bilal asked the Prophet not to say amin before him.

positions.position: Saying amin is recommended outside prayer and especially within it, whether alone, imam, or follower; the sound reports promise forgiveness when one's amin coincides with the angels'.
positions.reasons: IBNKATHIR: Saying amin is recommended outside prayer and especially within it, whether alone, imam, or follower; the sound reports promise forgiveness when one's amin coincides with the angels'.

positions.position: In the two Ṣaḥīḥ collections, the Prophet says that when the imam says amin, worshippers should say it; agreement with the angels' amin brings forgiveness of prior sins.
positions.reasons: IBNKATHIR reporting أبو هريرة: In the two Ṣaḥīḥ collections, the Prophet says that when the imam says amin, worshippers should say it; agreement with the angels' amin brings forgiveness of prior sins.

positions.position: The matching between a worshipper's amin and the angels' may mean matching in time, in the response received, or in sincerity.
positions.reasons: IBNKATHIR: The matching between a worshipper's amin and the angels' may mean matching in time, in the response received, or in sincerity.

positions.position: A Prophetic report in Muslim says that when the imam recites “nor the astray,” worshippers should say amin and God will answer them.
positions.reasons: IBNKATHIR reporting أبو موسى: A Prophetic report in Muslim says that when the imam recites “nor the astray,” worshippers should say amin and God will answer them.

positions.position: A report through Juwaybir and al-Dahhak explains amin as “Lord, do”; al-Jawhari says “so let it be,” al-Tirmidhi says it means do not disappoint our hope, and most interpreters say “O God, answer us.”
positions.reasons: IBNKATHIR reporting ابن عباس: A report through Juwaybir and al-Dahhak explains amin as “Lord, do”; al-Jawhari says “so let it be,” al-Tirmidhi says it means do not disappoint our hope, and most interpreters say “O God, answer us.”

positions.position: Mujahid, Jaʿfar al-Sadiq, and Hilal ibn Kaysan are reported to call amin one of God's names, but Ibn al-ʿArabi says the Prophetic report from Ibn ʿAbbas for this is unsound.
positions.reasons: IBNKATHIR reporting مجاهد: Mujahid, Jaʿfar al-Sadiq, and Hilal ibn Kaysan are reported to call amin one of God's names, but Ibn al-ʿArabi says the Prophetic report from Ibn ʿAbbas for this is unsound.

positions.position: Malik's companions say the imam does not say amin but the follower does, citing Abu Hurayra's report that followers should say it when the imam reaches “nor the astray”; Ibn Kathir counters with reports that the Prophet…
positions.reasons: IBNKATHIR reporting أصحاب مالك: Malik's companions say the imam does not say amin but the follower does, citing Abu Hurayra's report that followers should say it when the imam reaches “nor the astray”; Ibn Kathir counters with reports that the Prophet himself said amin.

positions.position: The new Shafiʿi position, also held by Abu Hanifa and one Maliki report, is that a follower does not say amin aloud when the imam does; it is a remembrance like other prayer remembrances.
positions.reasons: IBNKATHIR reporting القول الجديد: The new Shafiʿi position, also held by Abu Hanifa and one Maliki report, is that a follower does not say amin aloud when the imam does; it is a remembrance like other prayer remembrances.

positions.position: The old Shafiʿi position, held by Ahmad and another Maliki report, is that the follower says amin aloud, based on the report that the mosque echoed with it.
positions.reasons: IBNKATHIR reporting القول القديم: The old Shafiʿi position, held by Ahmad and another Maliki report, is that the follower says amin aloud, based on the report that the mosque echoed with it.

positions.position: A third position has the follower say amin quietly in a small mosque, where the imam can be heard, and aloud in a large mosque so it reaches its far sides.
positions.reasons: IBNKATHIR: A third position has the follower say amin quietly in a small mosque, where the imam can be heard, and aloud in a large mosque so it reaches its far sides.

positions.position: A report from ʿAisha says Jews envy Muslims for Friday, the qibla, and saying amin behind the imam; Ibn Majah's wording adds greeting and amin.
positions.reasons: IBNKATHIR reporting عائشة: A report from ʿAisha says Jews envy Muslims for Friday, the qibla, and saying amin behind the imam; Ibn Majah's wording adds greeting and amin.

positions.position: Anas reports that the Prophet was given amin in prayer and supplication; only Moses had it earlier, with Harun saying amin to Moses' prayer, so supplications should end with amin for acceptance.
positions.reasons: IBNKATHIR reporting أنس: Anas reports that the Prophet was given amin in prayer and supplication; only Moses had it earlier, with Harun saying amin to Moses' prayer, so supplications should end with amin for acceptance.

positions.position: The account of Moses' prayer and the dual reply that “your two prayers” were answered implies that Harun said amin; this makes the person who says amin to a prayer like one who prayed it.; cited verses:…
positions.reasons: IBNKATHIR: The account of Moses' prayer and the dual reply that “your two prayers” were answered implies that Harun said amin; this makes the person who says amin to a prayer like one who prayed it. | mentions 10:88, 10:89

positions.position: Some use this reasoning to argue that the follower need not recite aloud behind the imam because amin after al-Fatiha counts as recitation; they cite “whoever has an imam, the imam's recitation is his recitation” and Bilal's…
positions.reasons: IBNKATHIR: Some use this reasoning to argue that the follower need not recite aloud behind the imam because amin after al-Fatiha counts as recitation; they cite “whoever has an imam, the imam's recitation is his recitation” and Bilal's request not to be preceded in amin.

positions.position: A report through Kaʿb says that when the imam says amin and the amins of earth and heaven coincide, God forgives the worshipper; one who omits amin is compared to a warrior whose lot was not drawn.
positions.reasons: IBNKATHIR reporting أبو هريرة: A report through Kaʿb says that when the imam says amin and the amins of earth and heaven coincide, God forgives the worshipper; one who omits amin is compared to a warrior whose lot was not drawn.

positions.position: Stopping after these phrases is good because their sense is understood, but starting with attached phrases such as rabb al-ʿālamīn, ṣirāṭ alladhīna, or ghayr al-maghḍūb ʿalayhim is poor, except at verse ends per the Sunnah.
positions.reasons: NASHR: Stopping after these phrases is good because their sense is understood, but starting with attached phrases such as rabb al-ʿālamīn, ṣirāṭ alladhīna, or ghayr al-maghḍūb ʿalayhim is poor, except at verse ends per the Sunnah.

positions.position: Al-Harali analyzes amīn as a word of resolve rooted in security, expressing confidence that the one invoked will not reject the caller.
positions.reasons: BIQAI reporting الحرالي: Al-Harali analyzes amīn as a word of resolve rooted in security, expressing confidence that the one invoked will not reject the caller.

positions.position: Al-Harali says the condemned intentionally show defiance, while the astray turn toward guidance and deviate without intending it; Amin expresses a decisive plea for a response.
positions.reasons: BIQAI-FULL reporting الحرالي: Al-Harali says the condemned intentionally show defiance, while the astray turn toward guidance and deviate without intending it; Amin expresses a decisive plea for a response.

positions.position: The Prophet says congregants should say amin when the imam says wa-la al-dallin, and God will love them.
positions.reasons: DURR reporting النبي: The Prophet says congregants should say amin when the imam says wa-la al-dallin, and God will love them.

positions.position: Abū Maysara reports that Gabriel instructed the Prophet to say Āmīn at al-Fātiḥa’s final phrase, and the Prophet did.
positions.reasons: DURR reporting النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم: Abū Maysara reports that Gabriel instructed the Prophet to say Āmīn at al-Fātiḥa’s final phrase, and the Prophet did.

positions.position: Wāʾil b. Ḥujr heard the Prophet say Āmīn after al-Fātiḥa’s ending, prolonging his voice.
positions.reasons: DURR reporting وائل بن حجر: Wāʾil b. Ḥujr heard the Prophet say Āmīn after al-Fātiḥa’s ending, prolonging his voice.

positions.position: Wāʾil b. Ḥujr also heard the Prophet say “Lord, forgive me” and Āmīn after al-Fātiḥa.
positions.reasons: DURR reporting النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم: Wāʾil b. Ḥujr also heard the Prophet say “Lord, forgive me” and Āmīn after al-Fātiḥa.

positions.position: Wāʾil b. Ḥujr reports seeing the Prophet say Āmīn three times after al-Fātiḥa in prayer.
positions.reasons: DURR reporting وائل بن حجر: Wāʾil b. Ḥujr reports seeing the Prophet say Āmīn three times after al-Fātiḥa in prayer.

positions.position: ʿAlī reports hearing the Prophet say Āmīn after al-Fātiḥa’s final phrase.
positions.reasons: DURR reporting النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم: ʿAlī reports hearing the Prophet say Āmīn after al-Fātiḥa’s final phrase.

positions.position: Abū Mūsā reports the Prophet instructing congregants to say Āmīn at the imam’s ending, promising God’s response.
positions.reasons: DURR reporting أبو موسى الأشعري: Abū Mūsā reports the Prophet instructing congregants to say Āmīn at the imam’s ending, promising God’s response.

positions.position: Abū Hurayra reports that agreement with the angels’ Āmīn after the imam brings forgiveness of past sins.
positions.reasons: DURR reporting أبو هريرة: Abū Hurayra reports that agreement with the angels’ Āmīn after the imam brings forgiveness of past sins.

positions.position: A good-chain report says congregants’ Āmīn meets that of heaven and earth; the one omitting it is like a soldier whose share is missed.
positions.reasons: DURR reporting أبو هريرة: A good-chain report says congregants’ Āmīn meets that of heaven and earth; the one omitting it is like a soldier whose share is missed.

positions.position: ʿĀʾisha reports the Jews envied Muslims for nothing as much as saying Āmīn.
positions.reasons: DURR reporting عائشة: ʿĀʾisha reports the Jews envied Muslims for nothing as much as saying Āmīn.

positions.position: A weak report says Jews envied Muslims for Āmīn and urges saying it often.
positions.reasons: DURR reporting ابن عباس: A weak report says Jews envied Muslims for Āmīn and urges saying it often.

positions.position: Muʿādh b. Jabal reports that Jews envy returning greetings, prayer rows, and Āmīn behind the imam in obligatory prayer.
positions.reasons: DURR reporting معاذ بن جبل: Muʿādh b. Jabal reports that Jews envy returning greetings, prayer rows, and Āmīn behind the imam in obligatory prayer.

positions.position: Through al-Ḍaḥḥāk, Ibn ʿAbbās says Āmīn means “Lord, do it.”
positions.reasons: DURR reporting ابن عباس: Through al-Ḍaḥḥāk, Ibn ʿAbbās says Āmīn means “Lord, do it.”

positions.position: Hilāl b. Yasāf and Mujāhid say Āmīn is one of God’s names.
positions.reasons: DURR reporting هلال بن يساف ومجاهد: Hilāl b. Yasāf and Mujāhid say Āmīn is one of God’s names.

positions.position: Ḥakīm b. Jubayr likewise says Āmīn is one of God’s names.
positions.reasons: DURR reporting حكيم بن جبير: Ḥakīm b. Jubayr likewise says Āmīn is one of God’s names.

positions.position: Ibrāhīm al-Nakhaʿī recommended saying “O God, forgive me” and Āmīn at al-Fātiḥa’s end.

question: Is Āmīn said aloud or quietly?

positions.position: Say Āmīn quietly
positions.reasons: MUSNAD-AHMAD reporting وائل بن حجر عن النبي: Wa'il reports that the Prophet said Amin quietly after al-Fatiha, placed his right hand over his left in prayer, and gave salutation to both sides. KASHSHAF reporting أبو حنيفة وأصحابه: The well-known position of Abu Hanifa and his followers is to say Amin silently. KASHSHAF-FULL reporting الحسن وأبو حنيفة: Hasan says the imam should not say Amin because he is the one supplicating; Abu Hanifa shares this view and is known to recite it quietly. IBNATIYYA reporting مالك: In the Mudawwana, Mālik says the imam does not say Āmīn, while followers say it quietly and a person praying alone says it. IBNATIYYA reporting مالك: Other reports from Mālik say that the imam says Āmīn either quietly or aloud, or does not say it during audible prayer. IBNATIYYA-FULL reporting مالك: In the Mudawwana, the imam does not say amin; followers say it quietly, while a solitary worshipper does say it. IBNATIYYA-FULL reporting مالك: A report from Malik allows the imam to say amin either silently or aloud. BAYDAWI reporting أبو حنيفة: A report from Abū Ḥanīfa says not to say āmīn; his better-known position is to say it quietly, as narrated from ʿAbd Allāh b. Mughaffal and Anas. IBNKATHIR: A third position has the follower say amin quietly in a small mosque, where the imam can be heard, and aloud in a large mosque so it reaches its far sides. ALUSI reporting الحسن: Al-Ḥasan says the imam should not say Āmīn because he is the supplicant; this is also found in a less famous report from Abū Ḥanīfa, whereas the famous view is that he says it silently. ALUSI-FULL reporting رسول الله: The Prophet instructed congregants to say amin after the imam recites the ending of al-Fatiha, saying God will love them; Hanafis say it quietly, while Shafiʿis say it aloud. ALUSI-FULL reporting علي وعبدالله بن مسعود: Quiet amin is attributed to ʿAli and Ibn Masʿud and is the Hanafi position; Shafiʿis vocalize it, Hasan says the imam should omit it, and one uncommon report from Abu Hanifa also favors concealment. ELMALILI: Amin is established by Sunna and should be said quietly by the imam, congregation, and a person praying alone. KURANYOLU-TEFSIR: Because sound hadiths support saying amin aloud after audible Fatiha, most legal schools adopt that practice; Hanafis always say it silently in prayer. STUDYQURAN: Sunnis customarily say Āmīn after the Fātiḥah; it is recommended, not obligatory, and scholars differ whether it should be said aloud or quietly.

positions.position: Say Āmīn aloud
positions.reasons: MUSNAD-AHMAD reporting وائل بن حجر: Wa'il saw the Prophet place his right hand over his left and raise his hands to his ears at the prayer's opening; the Prophet said Amin aloud after al-Fatiha. SULAMI reporting بعضهم: Anger follows innovations, while error is abandoning guidance and Sunnah, including the Sunnah of saying Amin aloud after the chapter in prayer. KASHSHAF reporting الشافعي: Al-Shafii holds Amin is said aloud. KASHSHAF reporting وائل بن حجر والنبي: Waʾil ibn Hujr reports that the Prophet said Amin aloud after wa-la al-dallin. KASHSHAF-FULL reporting رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم: Wail ibn Hujr reports that the Prophet said Amin aloud after reciting wa-la al-dallin. IBNATIYYA: The author infers from these reports that supplicants should say Āmīn at the end of every supplication and after al-Fātiḥa outside prayer, without loud recitation. IBNATIYYA-FULL: Given these reports, anyone praying or reciting al-Fatiha outside prayer should end the supplication with amin, but outside prayer it is not said aloud in the manner of formal recitation. BAYDAWI: The imam says āmīn aloud in audible prayers, based on the report that the Prophet raised his voice after al-ḍāllīn. IBNKATHIR reporting وائل بن حجر: Waʾil ibn Hujr reports hearing the Prophet say amin aloud after al-Fatiha; al-Tirmidhi grades the hadith hasan, and reports also come from ʿAli and Ibn Masʿud. IBNKATHIR reporting أبو هريرة: Abu Hurayra reports that the Prophet said amin loudly enough for the first row to hear; Abu Dawud and Ibn Majah add that the mosque resounded, and al-Daraqutni calls the chain hasan. IBNKATHIR reporting القول الجديد: The new Shafiʿi position, also held by Abu Hanifa and one Maliki report, is that a follower does not say amin aloud when the imam does; it is a remembrance like other prayer remembrances. IBNKATHIR reporting القول القديم: The old Shafiʿi position, held by Ahmad and another Maliki report, is that the follower says amin aloud, based on the report that the mosque echoed with it. IBNKATHIR: Some use this reasoning to argue that the follower need not recite aloud behind the imam because amin after al-Fatiha counts as recitation; they cite “whoever has an imam, the imam's recitation is his recitation” and Bilal's request not to be preceded in amin. ALUSI reporting الحنفية: The Ḥanafīs conceal Āmīn, following ʿAlī and Ibn Masʿūd; the Shāfiʿīs say it aloud. The report of the majority’s loud recitation is interpreted as instruction or discussion. ABUDAWUD reporting أبو هريرة عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم: Abu Hurayra reports that when the Prophet recited al-Fatiha’s closing words, he said Amin loudly enough for the first row to hear. positions.reasons: MUSNAD-AHMAD reporting النبي عن أبي هريرة: When the imam finishes al-Fatiha, worshippers should say Amin; if their response coincides with the angels' and imam's, their past sins are forgiven.

positions.position: The Prophet instructs worshippers to say amin when the imam reaches the verse's ending; the imam and angels say it too, and agreement with the angels brings forgiveness of past sins.

question: Where may reciters pause in or after this verse?

positions.position: Both are normally paused sounds rather than verb-derived forms; nūn is opened to resolve adjacent quiescent letters, since kasra is heavy after yāʾ, as in ayna and kayfa.
positions.reasons: ZAJJAJ: Both are normally paused sounds rather than verb-derived forms; nūn is opened to resolve adjacent quiescent letters, since kasra is heavy after yāʾ, as in ayna and kayfa.

positions.position: Final alif is retained in pauses and rhyme while yāʾ may be deleted; exceptional deletion of alif is poetic necessity, so it does not refute the rule.

positions.position: The shared deletion in pause follows naturally because plural glide deletion already occurs in liaison, and pause permits still more changes.

positions.position: Ṭayyiʾ uses yāʾ where other dialects use final alif in both pause and liaison, as in afʿay for afʿā; this supports treating yāʾ in ʿalayhim like alif.
positions.reasons: FARISI-HUJJA reporting أبو علي: Ṭayyiʾ uses yāʾ where other dialects use final alif in both pause and liaison, as in afʿay for afʿā; this supports treating yāʾ in ʿalayhim like alif.

positions.position: Yāʾ and wāw do not assimilate into alif because alif is long and always still; sibilants likewise resist stops because their extra hiss is absent from stops.

positions.position: He treats lafẓ, literally throwing, as metaphorical for spoken sounds: breath is expelled, and the letters produced by that breath are as if thrown outward.

positions.position: An optional pause is preferable and is classified by how the two parts of the statement depend on each other.

question: How is this verse counted within al-Fātiḥa?

positions.position: Count the basmala and combine the closing words as one verse
positions.reasons: BAGHAWI-FULL: All agree the Fatiha has seven verses, but those counting the basmala begin the final verse at ‘those You favored’; others begin it at ‘not those under wrath.’ BAGHAWI-FULL: Those counting the basmala cite its Quranic-script placement and a report from Ibn Abbas through Saʿid b. Jubayr: it is the seventh of the seven oft-repeated verses. | mentions 15:87 IBNATIYYA: Consensus counts al-Fātiḥa as seven verses, ending them respectively at العالمين, الرحيم, الدين, نستعين, المستقيم, أنعمت عليهم, and ولا الضالين; he says the weak dispute over the basmala was discussed earlier. TABRISI reporting النبي: The Prophet says God bestowed the Opening of the Book from a treasure of Paradise, including the basmala and the verse about people turning away when God alone is mentioned. | mentions 17:46 RAZI-FULL reporting أم سلمة عن النبي: Umm Salama reports that the Prophet recited al-Fatiha while counting the basmala as its first verse, followed by the rest of its verses. RAZI-FULL: The seven-verse count supports al-Shafi'i's division, with the basmala as one verse and the final phrase as one; Abu Hanifa denies the basmala verse and splits that final phrase, a weak view for Razi. ABUHAYYAN: Abū Ḥayyān concludes that the sūra is seven verses by consensus apart from disregarded dissent; Meccan and Kufan counters differ over whether the basmala or صراط الذين is an āya, while ʿAmr b. ʿUbayd counts eight and Ḥusayn al-Juʿfī six. ABUHAYYAN: Reports about the sūra's letter count, supposed occasions of revelation, basmala's merit, and many titles are not necessarily causes of revelation or core tafsīr; only sound Prophetic clarification, occasions, and abrogation are indispensable to tafsīr. ABUHAYYAN-FULL reporting الجمهور المكيون والكوفيون: The Meccan and Kufan majority count the basmala as a verse and do not count “whom You favored” separately; other counters reverse those choices. BURHAN: Al-Shafiʿi counts the basmala and makes the rest of 1:7 one verse; Abu Hanifa omits the basmala and divides its two phrases. Both count seven verses, but al-Shafiʿi's division better preserves the endings because anʿamta ʿalayhim does not match prior endings. DURR-FULL reporting أم سلمة: Umm Salama reports that the Prophet recited the Fātiḥa including the basmala and called it seven verses. ITQAN reporting أبو ميسرة عمرو بن شرحبيل: A mursal report with trustworthy narrators recounts Muhammad telling Khadija he feared the voice he heard; Waraqa advised him to listen, then taught him the opening of al-Fatiha from the basmala through “those astray.” | mentions 1:1, 1:7 ITQAN reporting الإمام فخر الدين وغيره: Qur'anic verse endings fall into only two kinds, identical or near-sounding; their similarity supports counting al-Fatiha as seven verses with the basmala and treating the final phrase as one verse. IBNASHUR-FULL: The verse division differs by region: Medinans exclude the basmala and count “those You favored” as a verse; Meccans and Kufans include the basmala and combine that phrase with its verse; Hasan counts both separately.

positions.position: Seven verses
positions.reasons: TAB reporting أهل الإلحاد الطاعنون في القرآن: Critics ask why al-Fātiḥa has seven verses when, they argue, the meaning of its remaining verses is already contained in “Master of Judgment Day” and “You alone we worship and ask for help.” TAB-FULL: Answering why al-Fātiḥa has seven verses if two contain its meanings: earlier scriptures each included only some meanings, while the Qur'an gathers all of them for Muhammad's community and adds many more. IBNATIYYA-FULL: There is agreement that al-Fatiha has seven verses, counted as al-ʿalamin, al-Rahim, al-Din, nastaʿin, al-mustaqim, anʿamta ʿalayhim, and wa-la al-dallin; the earlier discussion noted anomalous contrary reports. RAZI-FULL: Al-Fatiha has seven verses to counter these seven vices; its opening three names answer the three basic vices, and the Qur'an and moral traits branch from these foundations. QUTB-ZILAL: Al-Fatiha is Meccan and has seven verses; Muslims recite it at least seventeen times daily, more with voluntary prayers, and may repeat it without limit.

question: What does the divine report say about the servant's closing request?

positions.position: God answers the recitation and grants the servant's closing petition
positions.reasons: MUQATIL reporting أبو هريرة عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم: A report from Abū Hurayra says the Prophet related that God divided this sūra between Himself and the servant: praise is thanks, the two mercy names are praise, the King verse is glorification, and the rest belongs to the servant; seeking help is God's special acknowledgment of the servant's plea. TAB reporting رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم: Abū Hurayra reports that the Prophet said God answers the worshipper's recitation: He calls al-ḥamdu praise, al-Raḥmān al-Raḥīm commendation, Mālik Yawm al-Dīn glorification, and the rest of the surah the servant's share. BAGHAWI reporting النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم: In a qudsi report, God divides prayer between Himself and His servant and answers each part of al-Fatiha; Baghawi grades it sahih. | mentions 1:4 RAZI-FULL reporting أبو هريرة عن النبي: In the divided-prayer report, God calls the basmala glorification, al-Hamd praise, the two mercy names extolling, the Master of Judgment entrustment, and the remaining response a sharing and a request granted. RAZI-FULL: A divine report says God remembers a servant in a gathering better than the servant's; the angels then long to visit, and the worshipper greets them on both sides. NASAFI reporting أبو هريرة عن النبي: Abu Hurayra reports God’s dialogue dividing the Fatiha between Himself and the servant: praise, glorification, and exaltation belong to God; the worshipper’s request for guidance and the response to it belong to the servant, while worship and aid are shared. IBNKATHIR reporting الله تعالى: In a divine report, God divides the prayer between Himself and His servant, responds to each recited section, calls 1:5 shared between them, and grants the servant's request. BIQAI-FULL reporting الحرالي: Al-Harali explains the sound report that God divided prayer between Himself and His servant: the first three verses are God's praise, which He accepts from the reciting servant as praise and glorification. BIQAI-FULL reporting أبو هريرة: In the authentic report in Muslim and the four Sunan, God says the Fatiha is divided between Himself and His servant: He answers praise, glorification and worship, and grants the servant's final requests. DURR-FULL reporting الله عز وجل: In Abū Hurayra's report, God says the prayer is divided between Him and His servant: the opening praise is His, the middle is shared, and the servant receives what he asks in the remainder. ITQAN reporting الطيبي: Al-Tibi divides the Fatiha’s religious knowledge into foundations (God and attributes, prophethood, resurrection), branches (worship), ethical perfection and seeking the path, and accounts of earlier peoples with promise and threat. | mentions 1:2, 1:4, 1:6, 1:7 QUTB-ZILAL reporting رسول الله: Abu Hurayra reports in Sahih Muslim that God calls al-Fatiha a prayer divided between Himself and His servant: praise, mercy, and glorification are the Lord's; worship and aid are shared; guidance and the servant's request belong to the servant, who receives what he asks. IBNASHUR-FULL reporting النبيء صلى الله عليه وسلم: A hadith in both Sahihs from Abu Hurayra has God divide prayer between Himself and the servant, answering each portion of al-Fatiha and granting the servant's request. | mentions 1:2, 1:3, 1:4, 1:5, 1:6, 1:7 TABATABAI reporting النبي: The Prophet transmits God's division of al-Fatiha between Himself and the servant: each phrase receives divine acknowledgement and a tailored promise of blessing, mercy, ease of judgment, reward, help, and fulfillment of the servant's requests. ABUDAWUD reporting الله تعالى: In a hadith qudsi transmitted by Abu Hurayra, God divides al-Fatiha between Himself and the servant: praise and glorification receive divine responses, worship is mutual, and the guidance petition belongs to the servant. MALIK reporting الله تبارك وتعالى: The qudsi report assigns the final plea for guidance to the servant and says the servant receives what he asks. MUSLIM reporting الله تعالى: When the servant asks for the guided path and names those favored rather than those under anger or astray, Allah says this request is for the servant and grants what was asked. NASAI reporting رسول الله: The same report assigns the servant’s request for the favored path, away from those under wrath and those astray, to the servant; God grants what the servant asks. TIRMIDHI reporting الله تعالى: In the divine report the Opening is divided into halves: praise belongs to God, the central pledge of worship and seeking help is shared, and its closing requests belong to the worshipper, who receives what he asks.

positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: When thought rises to the highest names and angelic praises, the worshipper should recite the declaration that God is above what they describe. | mentions 37:180

positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: A report attributed to Ali says God created intellect from a hidden light, endowed it with virtues, and had it first speak praise; God said no creature was dearer to Him.

positions.position: Another report says Adam's first words after sneezing were praise of God.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: Another report says Adam's first words after sneezing were praise of God.

positions.position: Because praise is the first speech of both the first and last created beings, God made it the opening of Muhammad's revealed Book and named the Prophet Ahmad and Muhammad.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: Because praise is the first speech of both the first and last created beings, God made it the opening of Muhammad's revealed Book and named the Prophet Ahmad and Muhammad.

positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: The Prophet is called Ahmad in heaven and Muhammad on earth: heavenly beings praise God and the Prophet, while God praises earthly believers. | mentions 17:19

positions.position: The Fatiha is a treasure, cure, sufficiency, fulfillment, protection and incantation; it gathers praise, gratitude and supplication, with prayer as their greatest assembly.
positions.reasons: BIQAI-FULL: The Fatiha is a treasure, cure, sufficiency, fulfillment, protection and incantation; it gathers praise, gratitude and supplication, with prayer as their greatest assembly.

positions.reasons: IBNJAWZI-NUZHA reporting بعض المفسرين: An eighth sense is ample livelihood, illustrated by God's abundant outward and inward blessings. | mentions 31:20

positions.position: Ibn Qutayba defines ḍalāl as bewilderment and turning away from what is true.
positions.reasons: IBNJAWZI-ZAD reporting ابن قتيبة: Ibn Qutayba defines ḍalāl as bewilderment and turning away from what is true.

positions.position: The sūra contains inexhaustible discussions and secrets; the claim that it contains ten thousand questions suits the audience's understanding of its vast implications.
positions.reasons: RAZI: The sūra contains inexhaustible discussions and secrets; the claim that it contains ten thousand questions suits the audience's understanding of its vast implications.

positions.position: Those who affirm inner speech say the inward meaning is itself called kalām and qawl; they cite the hypocrites' false claim to be witnesses and Umar's recollection of an inwardly prepared speech.; cited verses: 63:1
positions.reasons: RAZI reporting مثبتو كلام النفس: Those who affirm inner speech say the inward meaning is itself called kalām and qawl; they cite the hypocrites' false claim to be witnesses and Umar's recollection of an inwardly prepared speech. | mentions 63:1

positions.position: Some of Razi's school hold that qawl and kalām are equivocal terms for both the inward meaning and the spoken expression.
positions.reasons: RAZI reporting بعض أصحابنا: Some of Razi's school hold that qawl and kalām are equivocal terms for both the inward meaning and the spoken expression.

positions.position: The inquiry can descend from words into speech and phonetics, respiratory and vocal anatomy, sensory qualities, philosophical categories, substances, accidents, existence, and knowledge.
positions.reasons: RAZI: The inquiry can descend from words into speech and phonetics, respiratory and vocal anatomy, sensory qualities, philosophical categories, substances, accidents, existence, and knowledge.

positions.position: Razi's school distinguishes inward request from will and mental judgment from belief; God's command that an unbeliever believe is not evidence that He wills that belief.
positions.reasons: RAZI reporting أصحابنا: Razi's school distinguishes inward request from will and mental judgment from belief; God's command that an unbeliever believe is not evidence that He wills that belief.

positions.position: A single soul is weaker than many united souls; joining the purified spirits seeking spiritual disclosures strengthens readiness to attain the path of those favored.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: A single soul is weaker than many united souls; joining the purified spirits seeking spiritual disclosures strengthens readiness to attain the path of those favored.

positions.position: Connection with purified spirits increases strength, while connection with evil spirits brings failure and deprivation; Razi identifies those under wrath as immoral people and the astray as unbelievers.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: Connection with purified spirits increases strength, while connection with evil spirits brings failure and deprivation; Razi identifies those under wrath as immoral people and the astray as unbelievers.

positions.position: The sūra contains limitless discussions and secrets; saying it contains ten thousand problems is an expression suited to its audience's understanding.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: The sūra contains limitless discussions and secrets; saying it contains ten thousand problems is an expression suited to its audience's understanding.

positions.position: Every benefit or removal of harm reaching creatures is ultimately from God, and blessings fall into three categories.; cited verses: 16:53
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: Every benefit or removal of harm reaching creatures is ultimately from God, and blessings fall into three categories. | mentions 16:53

positions.position: The spiritual realm has ranks and one supreme being obeyed by the others; correspondingly, the human realm has one supreme person, with the former as source and the latter as manifestation.; cited verses: 81:21
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: The spiritual realm has ranks and one supreme being obeyed by the others; correspondingly, the human realm has one supreme person, with the former as source and the latter as manifestation. | mentions 81:21

positions.position: The spiritual messenger and human messenger meet and correspond, and together complete happiness in the afterlife and this world.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: The spiritual messenger and human messenger meet and correspond, and together complete happiness in the afterlife and this world.

positions.position: The seven ranks at the end of al-Baqara were revealed to Muhammad in the spiritual realm during the ascent and expressed as al-Fatiha when he descended.; cited verses: 2:285, 2:286
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: The seven ranks at the end of al-Baqara were revealed to Muhammad in the spiritual realm during the ascent and expressed as al-Fatiha when he descended. | mentions 2:285, 2:286

positions.position: The three original satanic entrances are desire, anger, and caprice: animalistic, predatory, and satanic respectively; anger is worse than desire, and caprice worse than anger.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: The three original satanic entrances are desire, anger, and caprice: animalistic, predatory, and satanic respectively; anger is worse than desire, and caprice worse than anger.

positions.position: Envy closes the catalogue of human evils as satanic whispering closes satanic evils; Razi repeats a story in which Iblis tells Pharaoh that the envious are worse than either of them.; cited verses: 113:5, 114:6
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: Envy closes the catalogue of human evils as satanic whispering closes satanic evils; Razi repeats a story in which Iblis tells Pharaoh that the envious are worse than either of them. | mentions 113:5, 114:6

positions.position: The seven Fatiha verses correspond to the seven bodily prayer acts—standing, bowing, rising, first prostration, rising between prostrations, second prostration, and sitting—as soul to body.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: The seven Fatiha verses correspond to the seven bodily prayer acts—standing, bowing, rising, first prostration, rising between prostrations, second prostration, and sitting—as soul to body.

positions.position: The seven Fatiha verses are the soul of the seven prayer acts, themselves the soul of seven stages of human formation; God is the soul of souls and light of lights.; cited verses: 23:12, 23:13, 23:14, 53:42
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: The seven Fatiha verses are the soul of the seven prayer acts, themselves the soul of seven stages of human formation; God is the soul of souls and light of lights. | mentions 23:12, 23:13, 23:14, 53:42

positions.position: Prayer was given to Muhammad as a gift for his community because it joins bodily ascent through actions with spiritual ascent through remembrances.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: Prayer was given to Muhammad as a gift for his community because it joins bodily ascent through actions with spiritual ascent through remembrances.

positions.position: “Blessed is Your name” unveils pre-eternity and eternity, since blessing here indicates abiding beyond extinction and nonexistence.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: “Blessed is Your name” unveils pre-eternity and eternity, since blessing here indicates abiding beyond extinction and nonexistence.

positions.position: Muhammad's ascent has a bodily journey from Mecca to Jerusalem and then the high kingdom, and a spiritual journey from the visible to the unseen and from the unseen to the unseen of the unseen.; cited verses:…
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: Muhammad's ascent has a bodily journey from Mecca to Jerusalem and then the high kingdom, and a spiritual journey from the visible to the unseen and from the unseen to the unseen of the unseen. | mentions 53:9

positions.position: The spiritual ascent rises through human spirits, the spirits of the heavens, angels, throne-bearers, and pure spirits detached from bodies, whose worship and love of God exceed human comprehension.; cited verses: 39:75, 69:17, 21:20, 12:76
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: The spiritual ascent rises through human spirits, the spirits of the heavens, angels, throne-bearers, and pure spirits detached from bodies, whose worship and love of God exceed human comprehension. | mentions 39:75, 69:17, 21:20, 12:76

positions.position: The ascent continues through ever-higher spiritual ranks until God, the source of all good and mercy; thus the spirit-world is the unseen and God's presence the unseen of the unseen.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: The ascent continues through ever-higher spiritual ranks until God, the source of all good and mercy; thus the spirit-world is the unseen and God's presence the unseen of the unseen.

positions.position: The soul is softened by awe like wood before fire; bend it in bowing, then let it straighten and practice religion gently.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: The soul is softened by awe like wood before fire; bend it in bowing, then let it straighten and practice religion gently.

positions.position: The worshipper's spirit meets Muhammad's spirit in this station, prompting a greeting to the Prophet.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: The worshipper's spirit meets Muhammad's spirit in this station, prompting a greeting to the Prophet.

positions.position: The final clause is the gate of following and being guided by pure spirits.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: The final clause is the gate of following and being guided by pure spirits.

positions.position: Reciting the surah with insight opens eight gates of paradise, identified with the doors of Eden and spiritual knowledge.; cited verses: 38:50
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: Reciting the surah with insight opens eight gates of paradise, identified with the doors of Eden and spiritual knowledge. | mentions 38:50

positions.position: Before the opening takbir, the worshipper should mentally survey all bodily and natural creation, then the heavens and the Throne, and finally the earthly and celestial spirits.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: Before the opening takbir, the worshipper should mentally survey all bodily and natural creation, then the heavens and the Throne, and finally the earthly and celestial spirits.

positions.position: A third interpretation sees the first prostration as the annihilation of all things and the second as their continued existence through God's sustaining act.; cited verses: 28:88
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: A third interpretation sees the first prostration as the annihilation of all things and the second as their continued existence through God's sustaining act. | mentions 28:88

positions.position: A fourth interpretation assigns the first prostration to the submission of the visible world and the second to the submission of the spiritual world.; cited verses: 7:54
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: A fourth interpretation assigns the first prostration to the submission of the visible world and the second to the submission of the spiritual world. | mentions 7:54

positions.position: The worshipper uses Fatiha as a mirror of creation, afterlife, divine mercy and majesty, law, spiritual way, truth, and the ranks of the blessed and damned.; cited verses: 10:10
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: The worshipper uses Fatiha as a mirror of creation, afterlife, divine mercy and majesty, law, spiritual way, truth, and the ranks of the blessed and damned. | mentions 10:10

positions.position: After spiritual insight into these stations, the worshipper must return to acknowledging God's grandeur and personal lowliness with another takbir.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: After spiritual insight into these stations, the worshipper must return to acknowledging God's grandeur and personal lowliness with another takbir.

positions.position: The five names address five human constituents: the rational spirit, satanic soul, irascible soul, appetitive soul, and body, restraining each by a fitting divine name.; cited verses: 13:28, 25:26, 5:4
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: The five names address five human constituents: the rational spirit, satanic soul, irascible soul, appetitive soul, and body, restraining each by a fitting divine name. | mentions 13:28, 25:26, 5:4

positions.position: These constituents answer in reverse order through Fatiha, from the body's worship to the purified spirits asking to join the spiritually blessed.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: These constituents answer in reverse order through Fatiha, from the body's worship to the purified spirits asking to join the spiritually blessed.

positions.position: The final plea seeks protection from two veils separating people from God: the fiery veil of the material world and the luminous veil of the spirit world.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: The final plea seeks protection from two veils separating people from God: the fiery veil of the material world and the luminous veil of the spirit world.

positions.position: Divine self-disclosure has three levels: through acts and signs to ordinary people, through attributes to God's friends, and through the essence to eminent prophets and angels.; cited verses: 42:32, 3:190, 3:191, 6:91
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: Divine self-disclosure has three levels: through acts and signs to ordinary people, through attributes to God's friends, and through the essence to eminent prophets and angels. | mentions 42:32, 3:190, 3:191, 6:91

positions.position: The name Allah most powerfully indicates disclosure of the essence: its wording is evident, yet its meaning escapes minds and its secrets remain inaccessible.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: The name Allah most powerfully indicates disclosure of the essence: its wording is evident, yet its meaning escapes minds and its secrets remain inaccessible.

positions.position: Al-Rahman signifies disclosure through God's exalted attributes, whereas al-Rahim signifies disclosure through His acts and signs.; cited verses: 17:110, 40:7
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: Al-Rahman signifies disclosure through God's exalted attributes, whereas al-Rahim signifies disclosure through His acts and signs. | mentions 17:110, 40:7

positions.position: Acquired blessings include purifying the soul, gaining noble character, adorning the body, and attaining status and wealth.
positions.reasons: BAYDAWI: Acquired blessings include purifying the soul, gaining noble character, adorning the body, and attaining status and wealth.

positions.position: Unacquired spiritual blessings include the spirit, intellect, understanding, thought, speech, and their associated faculties.
positions.reasons: BAYDAWI: Unacquired spiritual blessings include the spirit, intellect, understanding, thought, speech, and their associated faculties.

positions.position: Divine favors fall into worldly and afterlife kinds; worldly favors are bestowed or acquired, with spiritual and bodily branches, while acquired favors include virtue, good character, adornment, status, and wealth.; cited verses: 16:18
positions.reasons: BAYDAWI-FULL: Divine favors fall into worldly and afterlife kinds; worldly favors are bestowed or acquired, with spiritual and bodily branches, while acquired favors include virtue, good character, adornment, status, and wealth. | mentions 16:18

positions.position: Those under wrath are like Jews who stop at outward forms and bodily pleasures, veiling themselves from spiritual truths and intellectual delight; wrath entails expulsion, distance, and darkness of appearances.
positions.reasons: QASHANI: Those under wrath are like Jews who stop at outward forms and bodily pleasures, veiling themselves from spiritual truths and intellectual delight; wrath entails expulsion, distance, and darkness of appearances.

positions.position: One Sufi reading asks for guidance through becoming absent from the path, so that one is not bound to the path; Abū Ḥayyān says such readings do not follow the wording, while acknowledging their experiential insight.
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN reporting بعضهم: One Sufi reading asks for guidance through becoming absent from the path, so that one is not bound to the path; Abū Ḥayyān says such readings do not follow the wording, while acknowledging their experiential insight.

positions.position: Al-Junayd says asking for guidance amid bewilderment is among the clearest pre-eternal attributes; the request seeks the qualities of servanthood to avoid absorption in those attributes.
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN reporting الجنيد: Al-Junayd says asking for guidance amid bewilderment is among the clearest pre-eternal attributes; the request seeks the qualities of servanthood to avoid absorption in those attributes.

positions.position: Other explanations identify the path as observing the obligations and following the Sunan, or as inward agreement with outward practice in the completion of blessing.
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN: Other explanations identify the path as observing the obligations and following the Sunan, or as inward agreement with outward practice in the completion of blessing.

positions.position: The explanation of inward and outward blessing is linked to 31:20, which says God has poured out both manifest and hidden blessings upon you.; cited verses: 31:20
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN: The explanation of inward and outward blessing is linked to 31:20, which says God has poured out both manifest and hidden blessings upon you. | mentions 31:20

positions.position: The wording leaves the blessing unrestricted, so it can encompass every kind of blessing through a general use of the category.
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN: The wording leaves the blessing unrestricted, so it can encompass every kind of blessing through a general use of the category.

positions.position: Ḍalāl can mean ruin, concealment, loss, ignorance of an object's location, waste, neglect, forgetting, departure from the proper route, bewilderment, or hesitation; Qurʾanic usage also includes lack of detailed knowledge and love.
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN: Ḍalāl can mean ruin, concealment, loss, ignorance of an object's location, waste, neglect, forgetting, departure from the proper route, bewilderment, or hesitation; Qurʾanic usage also includes lack of detailed knowledge and love.

positions.position: The blessing intended is religious; those angered and those astray are general categories covering everyone who incurs anger or goes astray.
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN: The blessing intended is religious; those angered and those astray are general categories covering everyone who incurs anger or goes astray.

positions.position: A Sufi restriction interprets those angered as people who neglect proper courtesy while serving God, and the astray as those who perceive that conduct; Abū Ḥayyān says the wording does not support such restrictions.
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN reporting بعضهم: A Sufi restriction interprets those angered as people who neglect proper courtesy while serving God, and the astray as those who perceive that conduct; Abū Ḥayyān says the wording does not support such restrictions.

positions.position: Another interpretation makes the path harmony between inward and outward states in the fullness of divine favor.; cited verses: 31:20
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN-FULL reporting قيل: Another interpretation makes the path harmony between inward and outward states in the fullness of divine favor. | mentions 31:20

positions.position: Sufi writers add many restrictions, but the wording does not support assigning the favor one particular restriction.
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN-FULL: Sufi writers add many restrictions, but the wording does not support assigning the favor one particular restriction.

positions.position: The root of ḍalāl carries senses including perishing, disappearing, being lost or ignorant, straying, bewilderment, and wavering; Qurʾanic uses can mean lack of detailed knowledge or love.
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN-FULL: The root of ḍalāl carries senses including perishing, disappearing, being lost or ignorant, straying, bewilderment, and wavering; Qurʾanic uses can mean lack of detailed knowledge or love.

positions.position: The intended favor is religious; “those angered” and “those astray” are general categories of everyone who incurs anger and goes astray.
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN-FULL: The intended favor is religious; “those angered” and “those astray” are general categories of everyone who incurs anger and goes astray.

positions.position: Other identifications say the angered are Jews and polytheists; Sufi restrictions also circulate but are not supported by the verse’s wording.
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN-FULL reporting قيل: Other identifications say the angered are Jews and polytheists; Sufi restrictions also circulate but are not supported by the verse’s wording.

positions.position: Al-Sakkākī’s account places all six kinds in the final category of iltifāt, the shift by implication.
positions.reasons: BURHAN reporting السكاكي: Al-Sakkākī’s account places all six kinds in the final category of iltifāt, the shift by implication.

positions.position: The ending loops back to the opening invocation of God's name: the first group gains mercy, while the two deviant groups join Satan's party and incur punishment.
positions.reasons: BIQAI: The ending loops back to the opening invocation of God's name: the first group gains mercy, while the two deviant groups join Satan's party and incur punishment.

positions.position: Al-Harali sees the Fātiḥa as God's disclosure from the beginning of dominion to praise, and the servants' progress from disavowing error to the straight path; the Qur'an gathers their relation.; cited verses: 93:7
positions.reasons: BIQAI reporting الحرالي: Al-Harali sees the Fātiḥa as God's disclosure from the beginning of dominion to praise, and the servants' progress from disavowing error to the straight path; the Qur'an gathers their relation. | mentions 93:7

positions.position: The spiritual seeker passes through awe of God's attributes, recognizes many perilous paths and the lack of guidance or safety apart from God, then asks for the straight path, its blessed companions and protection from both condemned…
positions.reasons: BIQAI-FULL: The spiritual seeker passes through awe of God's attributes, recognizes many perilous paths and the lack of guidance or safety apart from God, then asks for the straight path, its blessed companions and protection from both condemned groups.

positions.position: Alternatively, the surah's purpose is solely to describe the Book; it establishes the truth of its meaning, exposes disbelief and hypocrisy to show that inward faith matters, then proves its inimitable form and authority for teaching law.;…
positions.reasons: BIQAI-FULL: Alternatively, the surah's purpose is solely to describe the Book; it establishes the truth of its meaning, exposes disbelief and hypocrisy to show that inward faith matters, then proves its inimitable form and authority for teaching law. | mentions 2:21

positions.position: Calling the path that of people God favored, rather than people killed or punished, softens the demand and invites believers toward prophetic and saintly states.
positions.reasons: BURSEVI: Calling the path that of people God favored, rather than people killed or punished, softens the demand and invites believers toward prophetic and saintly states.

positions.position: Steadfastness means moderation between excess and neglect across natural and spiritual traits; the law sets this balance in action, speech, money, and character.; cited verses: 17:29, 25:67, 53:17
positions.reasons: BURSEVI: Steadfastness means moderation between excess and neglect across natural and spiritual traits; the law sets this balance in action, speech, money, and character. | mentions 17:29, 25:67, 53:17

positions.position: When Umar recited loudly to wake sleepers and repel Satan, the Prophet told him to lower his voice slightly; he told Abu Bakr, who prayed softly, to raise his slightly.
positions.reasons: BURSEVI: When Umar recited loudly to wake sleepers and repel Satan, the Prophet told him to lower his voice slightly; he told Abu Bakr, who prayed softly, to raise his slightly.

positions.position: The author grades spiritual integrity by combinations of heart, action, and speech: complete inward and outward integrity is highest, while integrity in only one or two can harm its holder.
positions.reasons: BURSEVI: The author grades spiritual integrity by combinations of heart, action, and speech: complete inward and outward integrity is highest, while integrity in only one or two can harm its holder.

positions.position: Ibn Ata assigns knowledge to knowers, truthfulness, contentment, certainty and purity to saints, patience and compassion to the righteous, obedience's sweetness to seekers, and steadfastness to believers.
positions.reasons: BURSEVI reporting أبو العباس بن عطاء: Ibn Ata assigns knowledge to knowers, truthfulness, contentment, certainty and purity to saints, patience and compassion to the righteous, obedience's sweetness to seekers, and steadfastness to believers.

positions.position: Attributing the path to God cuts off the servant's vanity; attributing it to the servant comforts and honors him, and removes Satan's hope of stripping believers of dignity.; cited verses: 63:8, 35:10
positions.reasons: BURSEVI: Attributing the path to God cuts off the servant's vanity; attributing it to the servant comforts and honors him, and removes Satan's hope of stripping believers of dignity. | mentions 63:8, 35:10

positions.reasons: BURSEVI: Bewilderment has blameworthy and praiseworthy forms; a beginner resolves confusion by identifying the goal, sound path, guide, helpful practices, and obstacles.

positions.position: The bewilderment of advanced knowers is not a defect but appears after perfected knowledge, witnessing, and insight into the secret of existence.
positions.reasons: BURSEVI: The bewilderment of advanced knowers is not a defect but appears after perfected knowledge, witnessing, and insight into the secret of existence.

positions.position: In his commentary on al-Miftāḥ, al-Saʿd defines anger as a movement of the soul whose origin is the will to take revenge.
positions.reasons: ALUSI reporting السعد: In his commentary on al-Miftāḥ, al-Saʿd defines anger as a movement of the soul whose origin is the will to take revenge.

positions.position: A definition in Sharḥ al-Maqāṣid describes anger as a state of the soul followed by the spirit’s outward motion seeking revenge; another account calls it a change when the heart’s blood boils.
positions.reasons: ALUSI: A definition in Sharḥ al-Maqāṣid describes anger as a state of the soul followed by the spirit’s outward motion seeking revenge; another account calls it a change when the heart’s blood boils.

positions.position: Another interpretation is conformity between inward and outward life in the full bestowal of blessing.
positions.reasons: ALUSI reporting قيل: Another interpretation is conformity between inward and outward life in the full bestowal of blessing.

positions.position: Al-Ālūsī calls the sūra the Mother of the Book and a treasure of gnosis; he says some spiritual masters derive cosmic events, Muslim rulers’ names, their histories, and their fates from it, likening it to the Preserved…

positions.position: Al-Ālūsī closes by praying for the sūra’s lights to shine upon him and for access to its hidden secrets, declaring God the source of success and guide to verified truth.
positions.reasons: ALUSI: Al-Ālūsī closes by praying for the sūra’s lights to shine upon him and for access to its hidden secrets, declaring God the source of success and guide to verified truth.

positions.position: Other reported interpretations make it inward agreement with outward gratitude, or observance of religious duties and sunnas; Alusi dismisses the latter as a departure from the straight path.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL reporting قيل: Other reported interpretations make it inward agreement with outward gratitude, or observance of religious duties and sunnas; Alusi dismisses the latter as a departure from the straight path.

positions.position: Ibn Abi Hatim says he knows no disagreement among exegetes that the angry are Jews and the astray are Christians; Alusi rejects replacing this with generic categories of sinners and doctrinally mistaken people.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL reporting إبن أبي حاتم: Ibn Abi Hatim says he knows no disagreement among exegetes that the angry are Jews and the astray are Christians; Alusi rejects replacing this with generic categories of sinners and doctrinally mistaken people.

positions.position: The source gives several technical definitions of anger: a movement arising from desire for vengeance, the will to exact vengeance, or an inward condition producing outward movement; a report likens anger to a glowing ember in the…
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL: The source gives several technical definitions of anger: a movement arising from desire for vengeance, the will to exact vengeance, or an inward condition producing outward movement; a report likens anger to a glowing ember in the heart.

positions.position: Alusi calls al-Fatiha the Mother of the Book and a treasury of hidden knowledge and says some spiritual masters derive cosmic events and rulers' histories from it.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL: Alusi calls al-Fatiha the Mother of the Book and a treasury of hidden knowledge and says some spiritual masters derive cosmic events and rulers' histories from it.

positions.position: Al-Baqara follows al-Fatiha's sequence: knowledge of the Lord, worship, and requests for worldly and spiritual needs; al-Fatiha's request for guidance is echoed by “guidance for the God-conscious” at its opening.; cited verses: 2:2
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL: Al-Baqara follows al-Fatiha's sequence: knowledge of the Lord, worship, and requests for worldly and spiritual needs; al-Fatiha's request for guidance is echoed by “guidance for the God-conscious” at its opening. | mentions 2:2

positions.position: Umar's humble patched garment amid conquests and justice exemplifies the companions' spiritual joy and stature above imperial luxury.
positions.reasons: ELMALILI: Umar's humble patched garment amid conquests and justice exemplifies the companions' spiritual joy and stature above imperial luxury.

positions.position: Anger is the soul's agitation toward retaliation at something disliked, opposed to satisfaction; Turkish equivalents include anger, indignation, and wrath.
positions.reasons: ELMALILI: Anger is the soul's agitation toward retaliation at something disliked, opposed to satisfaction; Turkish equivalents include anger, indignation, and wrath.

positions.position: Dalaal means straying from the right path, intentionally or accidentally, opposite guidance; it can progress from heedlessness or bewilderment to loss and ruin.
positions.reasons: ELMALILI: Dalaal means straying from the right path, intentionally or accidentally, opposite guidance; it can progress from heedlessness or bewilderment to loss and ruin.

positions.position: The term first concerns departure from a physical route and extends to mental and spiritual matters; Turkish usage distinguishes religious dalalet from intellectual or verbal sapıklık.
positions.reasons: ELMALILI: The term first concerns departure from a physical route and extends to mental and spiritual matters; Turkish usage distinguishes religious dalalet from intellectual or verbal sapıklık.

positions.position: The definite articles in the wrath and deviation phrases most naturally mark generic, comprehensive categories, excluding every unbelieving path from the fully safe blessing.
positions.reasons: ELMALILI: The definite articles in the wrath and deviation phrases most naturally mark generic, comprehensive categories, excluding every unbelieving path from the fully safe blessing.

positions.position: The Qur'an explicitly says that those who disbelieve and obstruct God's way have gone far astray, extending the category beyond specific communities.; cited verses: 4:167
positions.reasons: ELMALILI: The Qur'an explicitly says that those who disbelieve and obstruct God's way have gone far astray, extending the category beyond specific communities. | mentions 4:167

positions.position: Its doctrine made God both one and three through the union of three persons, violating the law of noncontradiction and stunting intellectual development.
positions.reasons: ELMALILI: Its doctrine made God both one and three through the union of three persons, violating the law of noncontradiction and stunting intellectual development.

positions.position: The Fatiha substantiates Islam through observation, experience, and historical testimony after its rational and spiritual guidance, requiring no further proof.
positions.reasons: ELMALILI: The Fatiha substantiates Islam through observation, experience, and historical testimony after its rational and spiritual guidance, requiring no further proof.

positions.position: These favors include worldly gifts and achievements, bodily and spiritual goods, and afterlife rewards; their central substance is guidance, including wise use of gifted goods.
positions.reasons: IBNASHUR: These favors include worldly gifts and achievements, bodily and spiritual goods, and afterlife rewards; their central substance is guidance, including wise use of gifted goods.

positions.position: Important guidance requires preparing listeners, stirring their attention, and removing stubbornness, false assumptions, and satanic impulses that block learning.
positions.reasons: IBNASHUR-FULL: Important guidance requires preparing listeners, stirring their attention, and removing stubbornness, false assumptions, and satanic impulses that block learning.

positions.position: The definite phrase identifies the mentally understood unique straight path; truth is one while misguidance has many forms, and Satan's speech confirms this usage.; cited verses: 7:16, 10:32, 5:100

positions.position: Niʿma derives from ease and pleasant living; the feminine noun denotes a good state, first bodily pleasure and later beneficial intellectual or spiritual goods.
positions.reasons: IBNASHUR-FULL: Niʿma derives from ease and pleasant living; the feminine noun denotes a good state, first bodily pleasure and later beneficial intellectual or spiritual goods.

positions.position: The requested favor is complete good with no damaging aftermath: worldly and afterlife benefits, acquired or bestowed, spiritual or bodily, with the afterlife foremost.

positions.position: The blessed are those who obey God and the Messenger: prophets, truthful ones, martyrs, and righteous people, described by complete outward and inward submission.; cited verses: 4:69, 4:65, 4:66
positions.reasons: TABATABAI: The blessed are those who obey God and the Messenger: prophets, truthful ones, martyrs, and righteous people, described by complete outward and inward submission. | mentions 4:69, 4:65, 4:66

positions.position: The straight path is the spirit shared by the many ways, like one soul persisting through the changing stages of a body; individual ways can suffer flaws that do not characterize the path itself.; cited verses: 36:61,…

positions.position: A follower of the final, fullest law may still be below Noah or Abraham in realized divine knowledge and spiritual station; asking for the latter's rank is therefore coherent.
