positions.position: All creatures travel toward God and meet Him; the Qur'an distinguishes the straight way of worship from the opposing way of following Satan.; cited verses: 84:6, 64:3, 42:53, 36:60, 36:61
positions.reasons: TABATABAI: All creatures travel toward God and meet Him; the Qur'an distinguishes the straight way of worship from the opposing way of following Satan. | mentions 84:6, 64:3, 42:53, 36:60, 36:61

positions.position: The category may inherit a preexisting topos stripped of political targeting; since Jewish opponents were not yet in view, hearers fill in its referent.

positions.position: Living out worship and seeking aid in knowledge, action, and inward state cures corruption of the heart and intention.

positions.position: The title The Cure reflects its reputed healing power for body and soul.
positions.reasons: STUDYQURAN: The title The Cure reflects its reputed healing power for body and soul.

question: What discussions of language and speech does this commentary derive from the sūra?

positions.position: Kalima can denote one word or extended connected speech; the latter is metaphorical, by part-for-whole naming or because connected speech resembles a single unit.
positions.reasons: RAZI: Kalima can denote one word or extended connected speech; the latter is metaphorical, by part-for-whole naming or because connected speech resembles a single unit.

positions.position: The Qurʾānic uses of kalima include Jesus, created by God's command or in a short time, and God's acts, called His words; both uses are explained by the preceding metaphorical grounds.; cited verses: 3:45, 18:109
positions.reasons: RAZI: The Qurʾānic uses of kalima include Jesus, created by God's command or in a short time, and God's acts, called His words; both uses are explained by the preceding metaphorical grounds. | mentions 3:45, 18:109

positions.position: Razi reads the six permutations of ق و ل as expressing movement or lightness, explaining qawl as easy on the tongue and adducing examples such as the swift bird and animal.; cited verses: 24:15
positions.reasons: RAZI: Razi reads the six permutations of ق و ل as expressing movement or lightness, explaining qawl as easy on the tongue and adducing examples such as the swift bird and animal. | mentions 24:15

positions.position: Ibn Jinnī derives lugha from laghawtu, meaning I spoke, and proposes an original form ending in wāw, supported by related forms such as kurra and qulla.; cited verses: 25:72
positions.reasons: RAZI reporting ابن جني: Ibn Jinnī derives lugha from laghawtu, meaning I spoke, and proposes an original form ending in wāw, supported by related forms such as kurra and qulla. | mentions 25:72

positions.position: He treats lafẓ, literally throwing, as metaphorical for spoken sounds: breath is expelled, and the letters produced by that breath are as if thrown outward.
positions.reasons: RAZI: He treats lafẓ, literally throwing, as metaphorical for spoken sounds: breath is expelled, and the letters produced by that breath are as if thrown outward.

positions.position: The permutations of ʿ-b-r share crossing or transition: speech moves between letters and transfers meaning to a hearer, with related examples including tears, crossing, and interpretation.
positions.reasons: RAZI: The permutations of ʿ-b-r share crossing or transition: speech moves between letters and transfers meaning to a hearer, with related examples including tears, crossing, and interpretation.

positions.position: Most grammarians define kalima as a single word and kalām as a meaningful sentence; Ibn Jinnī sides with them, though Razi finds his evidence weak.
positions.reasons: RAZI reporting النحويون: Most grammarians define kalima as a single word and kalām as a meaningful sentence; Ibn Jinnī sides with them, though Razi finds his evidence weak.

positions.position: Most legal theorists see no difference between kalima and kalām: either term may cover a single utterance or a compound expression.
positions.reasons: RAZI reporting الأصوليون: Most legal theorists see no difference between kalima and kalām: either term may cover a single utterance or a compound expression.

positions.position: Legal theorists argue that a single word counts as speech because it opposes silence, affects a listener through meaning, and can naturally be described as something a person said.
positions.reasons: RAZI reporting الأصوليون: Legal theorists argue that a single word counts as speech because it opposes silence, affects a listener through meaning, and can naturally be described as something a person said.

positions.position: In an unconsummated marriage, Zufar says that repeating the conditional phrase إن كلمتك completes the condition before the divorce clause, so the ensuing divorce does not take effect.
positions.reasons: RAZI reporting زفر: In an unconsummated marriage, Zufar says that repeating the conditional phrase إن كلمتك completes the condition before the divorce clause, so the ensuing divorce does not take effect.

positions.position: Abū Ḥanīfa and his two companions treat the condition as incomplete until the whole sentence is finished, so one divorce takes effect when the sentence is complete.
positions.reasons: RAZI reporting أبو حنيفة: Abū Ḥanīfa and his two companions treat the condition as incomplete until the whole sentence is finished, so one divorce takes effect when the sentence is complete.

positions.position: Scholars disagree whether kalima and kalām include meaningless speech: some say yes because it can be called unused or unintelligible speech, while others require meaningful expression.
positions.reasons: RAZI: Scholars disagree whether kalima and kalām include meaningless speech: some say yes because it can be called unused or unintelligible speech, while others require meaningful expression.

positions.position: Scholars also dispute whether naturally meaningful sounds, such as pain cries, coughs, or bird calls, count as words; the issue affects whether hearing one triggers an oath.
positions.reasons: RAZI: Scholars also dispute whether naturally meaningful sounds, such as pain cries, coughs, or bird calls, count as words; the issue affects whether hearing one triggers an oath.

positions.position: Ibn Jinnī says qawl literally applies to a sentence or a single word, kalām only to a complete sentence, and kalima only to an isolated word; a poem treating qāf as a qawl supports the first distinction.
positions.reasons: RAZI reporting ابن جني: Ibn Jinnī says qawl literally applies to a sentence or a single word, kalām only to a complete sentence, and kalima only to an isolated word; a poem treating qāf as a qawl supports the first distinction.

positions.position: Ibn Jinnī says qawl can metaphorically mean a belief or opinion, as in attributing a doctrine to Abū Ḥanīfa or Mālik, because belief is apprehended through its expression.
positions.reasons: RAZI reporting ابن جني: Ibn Jinnī says qawl can metaphorically mean a belief or opinion, as in attributing a doctrine to Abū Ḥanīfa or Mālik, because belief is apprehended through its expression.

positions.position: Qāla can be used for nonverbal events, as when birds, eyes, or a full basin are said to speak; Razi also cites two Qurʾānic examples of such speech.; cited verses: 16:40, 41:11
positions.reasons: RAZI: Qāla can be used for nonverbal events, as when birds, eyes, or a full basin are said to speak; Razi also cites two Qurʾānic examples of such speech. | mentions 16:40, 41:11

positions.position: Those who affirm inner speech say the inward meaning is itself called kalām and qawl; they cite the hypocrites' false claim to be witnesses and Umar's recollection of an inwardly prepared speech.; cited verses: 63:1
positions.reasons: RAZI reporting مثبتو كلام النفس: Those who affirm inner speech say the inward meaning is itself called kalām and qawl; they cite the hypocrites' false claim to be witnesses and Umar's recollection of an inwardly prepared speech. | mentions 63:1

positions.position: Razi illustrates how analyzing Aʿūdhu billāh requires definitions and subdivisions of nouns, verbs, particles, and the possible derivations of the name Allah.
positions.reasons: RAZI: Razi illustrates how analyzing Aʿūdhu billāh requires definitions and subdivisions of nouns, verbs, particles, and the possible derivations of the name Allah.

positions.position: A report from ʿUmar says that at the Saqīfa he had composed words within himself, but Abū Bakr spoke first; Razi gives no grading.
positions.reasons: RAZI reporting عمر: A report from ʿUmar says that at the Saqīfa he had composed words within himself, but Abū Bakr spoke first; Razi gives no grading.

positions.position: The poet al-Akhṭal is cited for the claim that speech resides in the heart and the tongue serves as its guide; Razi gives no grading.
positions.reasons: RAZI reporting الأخطل: The poet al-Akhṭal is cited for the claim that speech resides in the heart and the tongue serves as its guide; Razi gives no grading.

positions.position: Those denying inner speech argue that someone who neither speaks nor pronounces letters is described as not having spoken, and that oaths attach to uttered words.
positions.reasons: RAZI reporting من أنكر كلام النفس: Those denying inner speech argue that someone who neither speaks nor pronounces letters is described as not having spoken, and that oaths attach to uttered words.

positions.position: Some of Razi's school hold that qawl and kalām are equivocal terms for both the inward meaning and the spoken expression.
positions.reasons: RAZI reporting بعض أصحابنا: Some of Razi's school hold that qawl and kalām are equivocal terms for both the inward meaning and the spoken expression.

positions.position: Utterances are called aḥādīth because their successive letters occur one after another, or because hearing them brings knowledge and meanings into hearts.; cited verses: 52:34
positions.reasons: RAZI: Utterances are called aḥādīth because their successive letters occur one after another, or because hearing them brings knowledge and meanings into hearts. | mentions 52:34

positions.position: Razi lists kalima, kalām, qawl, lafẓ, ʿibāra, ḥadīth, and nuṭq as terms needing comparison, leaving the derivation and precise relation of nuṭq for inquiry.
positions.reasons: RAZI: Razi lists kalima, kalām, qawl, lafẓ, ʿibāra, ḥadīth, and nuṭq as terms needing comparison, leaving the derivation and precise relation of nuṭq for inquiry.

positions.position: Meaningful sound has four form-meaning combinations: both simple, both compound, simple form with compound meaning, or compound form with compound meaning; compound form with simple meaning is impossible.
positions.reasons: RAZI: Meaningful sound has four form-meaning combinations: both simple, both compound, simple form with compound meaning, or compound form with compound meaning; compound form with simple meaning is impossible.

positions.position: Razi defines kalima as a single conventional utterance signifying a meaning; the definition excludes non-words and compounds through its four restrictions.
positions.reasons: RAZI: Razi defines kalima as a single conventional utterance signifying a meaning; the definition excludes non-words and compounds through its four restrictions.

positions.position: The inquiry can descend from words into speech and phonetics, respiratory and vocal anatomy, sensory qualities, philosophical categories, substances, accidents, existence, and knowledge.
positions.reasons: RAZI: The inquiry can descend from words into speech and phonetics, respiratory and vocal anatomy, sensory qualities, philosophical categories, substances, accidents, existence, and knowledge.

positions.position: The Muʿtazila require an informative word to contain at least two letters; they explain one-letter particles as shortened forms, but Razi notes that many useful particles remain counterexamples.
positions.reasons: RAZI reporting المعتزلة: The Muʿtazila require an informative word to contain at least two letters; they explain one-letter particles as shortened forms, but Razi notes that many useful particles remain counterexamples.

positions.position: Razi's preferred definition is anything spoken that conveys something by convention; it includes simple and compound forms while excluding writing and gesture.
positions.reasons: RAZI: Razi's preferred definition is anything spoken that conveys something by convention; it includes simple and compound forms while excluding writing and gesture.

positions.position: ʿAbbād holds that words naturally signify their meanings; Razi rejects this because natural properties do not vary across places and times, and answers that conventional assignments need not be unmotivated.
positions.reasons: RAZI reporting عباد: ʿAbbād holds that words naturally signify their meanings; Razi rejects this because natural properties do not vary across places and times, and answers that conventional assignments need not be unmotivated.

positions.position: Some words imitate their referents' sounds: qaṭā and laqlaq echo birds, while khaḍm and qaḍm distinguish eating moist and dry foods; Ibn Jinnī gives further examples.
positions.reasons: RAZI: Some words imitate their referents' sounds: qaṭā and laqlaq echo birds, while khaḍm and qaḍm distinguish eating moist and dry foods; Ibn Jinnī gives further examples.

positions.position: Razi says one cannot decide whether language was divinely instituted: the regress argument for divine origin and the appeal to God's teaching Adam both admit alternatives.; cited verses: 2:31
positions.reasons: RAZI: Razi says one cannot decide whether language was divinely instituted: the regress argument for divine origin and the appeal to God's teaching Adam both admit alternatives. | mentions 2:31

positions.position: The Muʿtazila argue that conventional language must be created by humans, since necessary knowledge that God assigned words would entail necessary knowledge of God and undermine moral responsibility.
positions.reasons: RAZI reporting المعتزلة: The Muʿtazila argue that conventional language must be created by humans, since necessary knowledge that God assigned words would entail necessary knowledge of God and undermine moral responsibility.

positions.position: Razi answers that God could create necessary knowledge that a human assigner fixed a word's meaning without revealing that the assigner was God.
positions.reasons: RAZI: Razi answers that God could create necessary knowledge that a human assigner fixed a word's meaning without revealing that the assigner was God.

positions.position: Because the proofs are inconclusive, Razi allows that all languages are divinely instituted, all conventional, or partly each.
positions.reasons: RAZI: Because the proofs are inconclusive, Razi allows that all languages are divinely instituted, all conventional, or partly each.

positions.position: A simple word cannot explain its own meaning from scratch without circularity, since recognizing its convention requires prior awareness of the word and meaning; learned association resolves the problem.
positions.reasons: RAZI: A simple word cannot explain its own meaning from scratch without circularity, since recognizing its convention requires prior awareness of the word and meaning; learned association resolves the problem.

positions.position: The circularity problem does not apply to compounds: convention supplies the simple meanings, and reason combines them to understand the compound.
positions.reasons: RAZI: The circularity problem does not apply to compounds: convention supplies the simple meanings, and reason combines them to understand the compound.

positions.position: Words signify mental conceptions rather than external objects: changing one's perception of a distant object changes the name used, and contradictory propositions do not make the world both old and originated.
positions.reasons: RAZI: Words signify mental conceptions rather than external objects: changing one's perception of a distant object changes the name used, and contradictory propositions do not make the world both old and originated.

positions.position: Concepts most necessary to communicate, such as commands, prohibitions, generality, and specification, are likeliest to receive words because need supplies strong motivation.
positions.reasons: RAZI: Concepts most necessary to communicate, such as commands, prohibitions, generality, and specification, are likeliest to receive words because need supplies strong motivation.

positions.position: A familiar word cannot name a hidden concept unknown to the public: motion names observable transition, not a subtle cause; likewise knowledge and power name the evident state, not its hidden ground.
positions.reasons: RAZI: A familiar word cannot name a hidden concept unknown to the public: motion names observable transition, not a subtle cause; likewise knowledge and power name the evident state, not its hidden ground.

positions.position: Maʿnā denotes the mental conception intended by a speaker; an external thing is called a meaning only derivatively, as what the conception concerns.
positions.reasons: RAZI: Maʿnā denotes the mental conception intended by a speaker; an external thing is called a meaning only derivatively, as what the conception concerns.

positions.position: Some distinctions cannot be defined verbally because language lacks a dedicated term, as with kinds of sweetness; private experiences are also indefinable to listeners who have never conceived them.
positions.reasons: RAZI: Some distinctions cannot be defined verbally because language lacks a dedicated term, as with kinds of sweetness; private experiences are also indefinable to listeners who have never conceived them.

positions.position: Language serves humans' need to communicate what is in their minds to obtain help; compared with writing, gestures, or clapping, speech is easy to produce, temporary, and combinatorially abundant.
positions.reasons: RAZI: Language serves humans' need to communicate what is in their minds to obtain help; compared with writing, gestures, or clapping, speech is easy to produce, temporary, and combinatorially abundant.

positions.position: Human perfection is knowledge of truth and action upon good; the body, heart, and respiratory system serve that end, with breathing cooling the heart and expelled air becoming the material of sound.
positions.reasons: RAZI: Human perfection is knowledge of truth and action upon good; the body, heart, and respiratory system serve that end, with breathing cooling the heart and expelled air becoming the material of sound.

positions.position: The Creator formed articulatory passages in the throat, tongue, teeth, and lips so breath produces distinct letters and limitless words containing wisdom beyond human grasp.
positions.reasons: RAZI: The Creator formed articulatory passages in the throat, tongue, teeth, and lips so breath produces distinct letters and limitless words containing wisdom beyond human grasp.

positions.position: Spoken kalām is a conventional act by which a living agent reveals inner intentions and beliefs; inner speech, by contrast, is a real attribute like knowledge, power, and will.
positions.reasons: RAZI: Spoken kalām is a conventional act by which a living agent reveals inner intentions and beliefs; inner speech, by contrast, is a real attribute like knowledge, power, and will.

positions.position: A word's referent may itself be another word: technical terms such as noun, verb, particle, general, and specific name linguistic expressions.
positions.reasons: RAZI: A word's referent may itself be another word: technical terms such as noun, verb, particle, general, and specific name linguistic expressions.

positions.position: Language is known through transmission, either mass-transmitted or solitary, and through a mix of transmission and reasoning; the majority's combined inference from exception and its effect is weak because it assumes the language-maker accepts the inference.
positions.reasons: RAZI: Language is known through transmission, either mass-transmitted or solitary, and through a mix of transmission and reasoning; the majority's combined inference from exception and its effect is weak because it assumes the language-maker accepts the inference.

positions.position: Although some question whether language is mass-transmitted because even Allah, faith, disbelief, and grammatical forms are disputed, Razi says the underlying transmitted usage is certainly mass-transmitted.
positions.reasons: RAZI: Although some question whether language is mass-transmitted because even Allah, faith, disbelief, and grammatical forms are disputed, Razi says the underlying transmitted usage is certainly mass-transmitted.

positions.position: Razi distinguishes ordinary derivation from greater derivation, which studies permutations of a word's consonants; he gives 2, 6, 24, and 120 permutations for words of two through five letters.
positions.reasons: RAZI: Razi distinguishes ordinary derivation from greater derivation, which studies permutations of a word's consonants; he gives 2, 6, 24, and 120 permutations for words of two through five letters.

positions.position: Greater derivation is difficult beyond triliteral roots because quadriliteral and quinqueliteral permutations proliferate and are mostly unused; even triliteral roots often have unused permutations.
positions.reasons: RAZI: Greater derivation is difficult beyond triliteral roots because quadriliteral and quinqueliteral permutations proliferate and are mostly unused; even triliteral roots often have unused permutations.

positions.position: Razi says five permutations of ك ل م are attested and share force or intensity: speech affects hearing and mind, a wound, rough ground, striking, kneading, and power.
positions.reasons: RAZI: Razi says five permutations of ك ل م are attested and share force or intensity: speech affects hearing and mind, a wound, rough ground, striking, kneading, and power.

positions.position: Razi judges Ibn Jinnī's case for distinguishing kalima from kalām weak, resting chiefly on an implication he draws from a statement by Sībawayh.
positions.reasons: RAZI: Razi judges Ibn Jinnī's case for distinguishing kalima from kalām weak, resting chiefly on an implication he draws from a statement by Sībawayh.

positions.position: Razi rejects al-Zamakhsharī's definition of kalima as an utterance denoting one simple meaning by convention: past-tense forms and imperative particles convey more than one element.
positions.reasons: RAZI: Razi rejects al-Zamakhsharī's definition of kalima as an utterance denoting one simple meaning by convention: past-tense forms and imperative particles convey more than one element.

positions.position: Razi rejects Avicenna's definition of kalima as a single meaningful sound: sound is a remote genus, whereas lafẓ is the more suitable proximate genus.
positions.reasons: RAZI: Razi rejects Avicenna's definition of kalima as a single meaningful sound: sound is a remote genus, whereas lafẓ is the more suitable proximate genus.

positions.reasons: TAB-FULL reporting ابن عباس: Ibn Abbas glosses the astray as Christians whom God led astray through their fabrication about Him; the prayer asks for the true monotheistic faith, protection from Jewish wrath and Christian error, and mercy to prevent their punishment.

positions.position: An unnamed poet uses Amīn in a prayer that God increase the distance between the speaker and Fataḥl.
positions.reasons: ZAJJAJ: An unnamed poet uses Amīn in a prayer that God increase the distance between the speaker and Fataḥl.

positions.position: He associates being under anger with leaving this chapter's recitation in prayer and being astray with not reciting it; the wording is awkward in the source.
positions.reasons: SULAMI reporting أبو عثمان: He associates being under anger with leaving this chapter's recitation in prayer and being astray with not reciting it; the wording is awkward in the source.

positions.position: Abu Hurayra reports the Prophet saying a prayer without Umm al-Qur'an is incomplete; Baghawi grades the report sahih.
positions.reasons: BAGHAWI reporting النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم: Abu Hurayra reports the Prophet saying a prayer without Umm al-Qur'an is incomplete; Baghawi grades the report sahih.

positions.position: When a Persian worshipper asks about praying behind the imam, Abu Hurayra tells him to recite al-Fatiha silently to himself.
positions.reasons: BAGHAWI reporting أبو هريرة: When a Persian worshipper asks about praying behind the imam, Abu Hurayra tells him to recite al-Fatiha silently to himself.

positions.position: In a qudsi report, God divides prayer between Himself and His servant and answers each part of al-Fatiha; Baghawi grades it sahih.; cited verses: 1:4
positions.reasons: BAGHAWI reporting النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم: In a qudsi report, God divides prayer between Himself and His servant and answers each part of al-Fatiha; Baghawi grades it sahih. | mentions 1:4

positions.position: Ibn Bukayr says the imam may choose whether to say it.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA reporting ابن بكير: Ibn Bukayr says the imam may choose whether to say it.

positions.position: The disagreement concerns the imam; no disagreement applies to the person praying alone or the follower except for Ibn Nāfiʿ’s position.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA: The disagreement concerns the imam; no disagreement applies to the person praying alone or the follower except for Ibn Nāfiʿ’s position.

positions.position: One unnamed explanation takes agreeing with the angels to mean agreement in the response to prayer.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA: One unnamed explanation takes agreeing with the angels to mean agreement in the response to prayer.

positions.position: Ibn Bukayr says the imam has a choice.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA-FULL reporting ابن بكير: Ibn Bukayr says the imam has a choice.

positions.position: The disagreement concerns the imam; solitary worshippers and followers are agreed upon apart from Ibn Nafi.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA-FULL: The disagreement concerns the imam; solitary worshippers and followers are agreed upon apart from Ibn Nafi.

positions.position: Al-Rummani explains lā in the exception reading as an extra particle, like in the line about a pit of destruction and the Qur'anic phrase 'that you should not prostrate'.; cited verses: 7:12
positions.reasons: TABRISI reporting علي بن عيسى الرماني: Al-Rummani explains lā in the exception reading as an extra particle, like in the line about a pit of destruction and the Qur'anic phrase 'that you should not prostrate'. | mentions 7:12

positions.position: Al-Jurjani instead reads the language generically as a prayer to avoid a state like that of the angered, not a reference to a particular people.
positions.reasons: TABRISI reporting عبد القاهر الجرجاني: Al-Jurjani instead reads the language generically as a prayer to avoid a state like that of the angered, not a reference to a particular people.

positions.position: Having reached knowledge of truth, the worshiper asks for lasting guidance and protection from error because he lacks infallibility; the request includes knowledge of rulings, Islamic practice, and following the divinely appointed Imams.
positions.reasons: TABRISI: Having reached knowledge of truth, the worshiper asks for lasting guidance and protection from error because he lacks infallibility; the request includes knowledge of rulings, Islamic practice, and following the divinely appointed Imams.

positions.position: Ibn Qutayba explains it as “O trustworthy one, answer our prayer,” with the vocative yāʾ omitted as in “Yūsuf, turn away from this” (12:29).; cited verses: 12:29
positions.reasons: IBNJAWZI-ZAD reporting ابن قتيبة: Ibn Qutayba explains it as “O trustworthy one, answer our prayer,” with the vocative yāʾ omitted as in “Yūsuf, turn away from this” (12:29). | mentions 12:29

positions.position: Most transmit from Aḥmad that al-Fātiḥa is required for a valid prayer, so one able to recite it who omits it has no valid prayer; this is Mālik's and al-Shāfiʿī's position.
positions.reasons: IBNJAWZI-ZAD reporting الأكثرون عن أحمد: Most transmit from Aḥmad that al-Fātiḥa is required for a valid prayer, so one able to recite it who omits it has no valid prayer; this is Mālik's and al-Shāfiʿī's position.

positions.position: The first position is supported by the Ṣaḥīḥayn report from ʿUbāda ibn al-Ṣāmit: the Prophet said there is no prayer for one who does not recite the Opening of the Book.
positions.reasons: IBNJAWZI-ZAD: The first position is supported by the Ṣaḥīḥayn report from ʿUbāda ibn al-Ṣāmit: the Prophet said there is no prayer for one who does not recite the Opening of the Book.

positions.position: In the divided-prayer report, God calls the basmala glorification, al-Hamd praise, the two mercy names extolling, the Master of Judgment entrustment, and the remaining response a sharing and a request granted.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL reporting أبو هريرة عن النبي: In the divided-prayer report, God calls the basmala glorification, al-Hamd praise, the two mercy names extolling, the Master of Judgment entrustment, and the remaining response a sharing and a request granted.

positions.position: The verse means asking for the path of those favored; 4:69 identifies them as prophets and the truthful, whose chief is Abu Bakr, so it supports his imamate and the propriety of following him.; cited verses: 4:69
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: The verse means asking for the path of those favored; 4:69 identifies them as prophets and the truthful, whose chief is Abu Bakr, so it supports his imamate and the propriety of following him. | mentions 4:69

positions.position: Reciting al-Fatiha in prayer sends the lights from manifestation back to their source, mirroring their descent to Muhammad; hence prayer is the believer's ascent.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: Reciting al-Fatiha in prayer sends the lights from manifestation back to their source, mirroring their descent to Muhammad; hence prayer is the believer's ascent.

positions.position: The prayer's prohibition of indecency, wrongdoing, and aggression addresses the effects of desire, anger, and caprice respectively.; cited verses: 29:45
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: The prayer's prohibition of indecency, wrongdoing, and aggression addresses the effects of desire, anger, and caprice respectively. | mentions 29:45

positions.position: The seven Fatiha verses correspond to the seven bodily prayer acts—standing, bowing, rising, first prostration, rising between prostrations, second prostration, and sitting—as soul to body.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: The seven Fatiha verses correspond to the seven bodily prayer acts—standing, bowing, rising, first prostration, rising between prostrations, second prostration, and sitting—as soul to body.

positions.position: The seven Fatiha verses are the soul of the seven prayer acts, themselves the soul of seven stages of human formation; God is the soul of souls and light of lights.; cited verses: 23:12, 23:13, 23:14, 53:42
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: The seven Fatiha verses are the soul of the seven prayer acts, themselves the soul of seven stages of human formation; God is the soul of souls and light of lights. | mentions 23:12, 23:13, 23:14, 53:42

positions.position: Prayer was given to Muhammad as a gift for his community because it joins bodily ascent through actions with spiritual ascent through remembrances.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: Prayer was given to Muhammad as a gift for his community because it joins bodily ascent through actions with spiritual ascent through remembrances.

positions.position: Before beginning the ascent, the worshipper purifies body and clothing for the holy presence and chooses which of opposing companions—angel or devil, reason or desire, truth or falsehood, and so forth—to follow, since settled companionship is hard…
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: Before beginning the ascent, the worshipper purifies body and clothing for the holy presence and chooses which of opposing companions—angel or devil, reason or desire, truth or falsehood, and so forth—to follow, since settled companionship is hard to break. | mentions 9:119

positions.position: The opening glorification links the worshipper's prayer to the ascent of the angels and Muhammad, while Abraham's formula supplies another prophetic ascent.; cited verses: 2:30
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: The opening glorification links the worshipper's prayer to the ascent of the angels and Muhammad, while Abraham's formula supplies another prophetic ascent. | mentions 2:30

positions.position: The worshipper should view worship from God's perspective and so regard it as inadequate, never suppose that personal worship gives one a claim on God.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: The worshipper should view worship from God's perspective and so regard it as inadequate, never suppose that personal worship gives one a claim on God.

positions.position: The soul is softened by awe like wood before fire; bend it in bowing, then let it straighten and practice religion gently.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: The soul is softened by awe like wood before fire; bend it in bowing, then let it straighten and practice religion gently.

positions.position: The bow and two prostrations overcome three ruinous obstacles: desire, anger, and caprice.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: The bow and two prostrations overcome three ruinous obstacles: desire, anger, and caprice.

positions.position: In the closing sitting, greetings are offered by the tongue, prayers by the limbs, and good words by the heart and faith.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: In the closing sitting, greetings are offered by the tongue, prayers by the limbs, and good words by the heart and faith.

positions.position: The worshipper's spirit meets Muhammad's spirit in this station, prompting a greeting to the Prophet.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: The worshipper's spirit meets Muhammad's spirit in this station, prompting a greeting to the Prophet.

positions.position: Seeking refuge after these praises guards the worshipper against self-admiration.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: Seeking refuge after these praises guards the worshipper against self-admiration.

positions.position: The prayer opens a gate of knowledge, followed by remembrance in the basmala and gratitude in the praise of God.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: The prayer opens a gate of knowledge, followed by remembrance in the basmala and gratitude in the praise of God.

positions.position: Bodily prayer begins with standing like the Companions of the Cave and the people at resurrection, then the prescribed invocations and Fatiha.; cited verses: 18:14, 83:6
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: Bodily prayer begins with standing like the Companions of the Cave and the people at resurrection, then the prescribed invocations and Fatiha. | mentions 18:14, 83:6

positions.position: The exchange of greetings prompts the worshipper to testify that all blessings come from God, while honoring Muhammad as guide and Abraham for asking that a messenger be sent.; cited verses: 2:129
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: The exchange of greetings prompts the worshipper to testify that all blessings come from God, while honoring Muhammad as guide and Abraham for asking that a messenger be sent. | mentions 2:129

positions.position: After the testimony, the worshipper asks God to bless Muhammad and Abraham, then declares that every blessing ultimately comes from the Praiseworthy and Glorious God.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: After the testimony, the worshipper asks God to bless Muhammad and Abraham, then declares that every blessing ultimately comes from the Praiseworthy and Glorious God.

positions.position: A divine report says God remembers a servant in a gathering better than the servant's; the angels then long to visit, and the worshipper greets them on both sides.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: A divine report says God remembers a servant in a gathering better than the servant's; the angels then long to visit, and the worshipper greets them on both sides.

positions.position: The Prophet's invocation to call on God as possessor of majesty and honor frames prayer as seeking God's face.; cited verses: 55:27, 55:78, 18:28
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: The Prophet's invocation to call on God as possessor of majesty and honor frames prayer as seeking God's face. | mentions 55:27, 55:78, 18:28

positions.position: Entering prayer requires purification at several levels: repentance from sins, renunciation of worldly things, and progressively leaving attachment to one's works, good deeds, and everything besides God.; cited verses: 66:8, 30:30, 18:28
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: Entering prayer requires purification at several levels: repentance from sins, renunciation of worldly things, and progressively leaving attachment to one's works, good deeds, and everything besides God. | mentions 66:8, 30:30, 18:28

positions.position: Before the opening takbir, the worshipper should mentally survey all bodily and natural creation, then the heavens and the Throne, and finally the earthly and celestial spirits.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: Before the opening takbir, the worshipper should mentally survey all bodily and natural creation, then the heavens and the Throne, and finally the earthly and celestial spirits.

positions.position: Another meaning is that God is too great to fail to see or hear the worshipper, as described in the hadith of ihsan.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: Another meaning is that God is too great to fail to see or hear the worshipper, as described in the hadith of ihsan.

positions.position: The formula 'God hears whoever praises Him' is a station of intercession, so it has no takbir associated with it; takbir instead expresses awe and fear.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: The formula 'God hears whoever praises Him' is a station of intercession, so it has no takbir associated with it; takbir instead expresses awe and fear.

positions.position: When thought rises to the highest names and angelic praises, the worshipper should recite the declaration that God is above what they describe.; cited verses: 37:180
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: When thought rises to the highest names and angelic praises, the worshipper should recite the declaration that God is above what they describe. | mentions 37:180

positions.position: Prostration expresses more humility than bowing, so its wording uses the superlative 'highest' while bowing uses the ordinary 'great.'
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: Prostration expresses more humility than bowing, so its wording uses the superlative 'highest' while bowing uses the ordinary 'great.'

positions.position: One interpretation makes the first prostration for eternity past and the second for eternity future, with worldly life between them.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: One interpretation makes the first prostration for eternity past and the second for eternity future, with worldly life between them.

positions.position: Another interpretation says the first prostration recognizes worldly life ending in the afterlife, while the second recognizes the afterlife's passing when God's majesty appears.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: Another interpretation says the first prostration recognizes worldly life ending in the afterlife, while the second recognizes the afterlife's passing when God's majesty appears.

positions.position: A third interpretation sees the first prostration as the annihilation of all things and the second as their continued existence through God's sustaining act.; cited verses: 28:88
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: A third interpretation sees the first prostration as the annihilation of all things and the second as their continued existence through God's sustaining act. | mentions 28:88

positions.position: A fourth interpretation assigns the first prostration to the submission of the visible world and the second to the submission of the spiritual world.; cited verses: 7:54
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: A fourth interpretation assigns the first prostration to the submission of the visible world and the second to the submission of the spiritual world. | mentions 7:54

positions.position: A fifth interpretation makes the first prostration gratitude for knowledge of God and His attributes and the second an admission of inability to fulfill His rights.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: A fifth interpretation makes the first prostration gratitude for knowledge of God and His attributes and the second an admission of inability to fulfill His rights.

positions.position: The worshipper uses Fatiha as a mirror of creation, afterlife, divine mercy and majesty, law, spiritual way, truth, and the ranks of the blessed and damned.; cited verses: 10:10
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: The worshipper uses Fatiha as a mirror of creation, afterlife, divine mercy and majesty, law, spiritual way, truth, and the ranks of the blessed and damned. | mentions 10:10

positions.position: After spiritual insight into these stations, the worshipper must return to acknowledging God's grandeur and personal lowliness with another takbir.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: After spiritual insight into these stations, the worshipper must return to acknowledging God's grandeur and personal lowliness with another takbir.

positions.position: The difference between 'great' in bowing and 'highest' in prostration has subtle meanings the author declines to disclose.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: The difference between 'great' in bowing and 'highest' in prostration has subtle meanings the author declines to disclose.

positions.position: After bowing, pray for those sharing one's standing; God's help to the worshipper follows from helping another Muslim.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: After bowing, pray for those sharing one's standing; God's help to the worshipper follows from helping another Muslim.

positions.position: The five pillars correspond to the five names: testimony to God, prayer to Lord, almsgiving to the Merciful, fasting to the Compassionate, and pilgrimage to Master of Judgment.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: The five pillars correspond to the five names: testimony to God, prayer to Lord, almsgiving to the Merciful, fasting to the Compassionate, and pilgrimage to Master of Judgment.

positions.position: Five kinds of qibla—Jerusalem, the Kaaba, the Frequented House, the Throne, and God's presence—are assigned to the five names.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: Five kinds of qibla—Jerusalem, the Kaaba, the Frequented House, the Throne, and God's presence—are assigned to the five names.

positions.position: Al-Sulami and al-Mawardi report that those under wrath neglect the sura in prayer and the astray miss its blessing.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI reporting السلمي والماوردي: Al-Sulami and al-Mawardi report that those under wrath neglect the sura in prayer and the astray miss its blessing.

positions.position: The verse refutes Qadariyya, Mu'tazila, and Imamiya claims that human will suffices and humans create their acts: repeated requests for guidance and protection from deviation show dependence on God, as does 3:8.; cited verses: 3:8
positions.reasons: QURTUBI: The verse refutes Qadariyya, Mu'tazila, and Imamiya claims that human will suffices and humans create their acts: repeated requests for guidance and protection from deviation show dependence on God, as does 3:8. | mentions 3:8

positions.position: Al-Tabari treats lā in “and not those astray” as redundant, as in the verse “what prevented you from not prostrating.”; cited verses: 7:12
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL reporting الطبري: Al-Tabari treats lā in “and not those astray” as redundant, as in the verse “what prevented you from not prostrating.” | mentions 7:12

positions.position: The verse refutes Qadariyya, Muʿtazila, and Imamiyya claims that humans create their acts: repeated requests for guidance and protection from deviation show dependence on God.; cited verses: 3:8
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL: The verse refutes Qadariyya, Muʿtazila, and Imamiyya claims that humans create their acts: repeated requests for guidance and protection from deviation show dependence on God. | mentions 3:8

positions.position: The Prophet said آمين aloud after ولا الضالين; al-Bayḍāwī cites this for an imam's audible response in audible prayers.
positions.reasons: BAYDAWI-FULL reporting وائل بن حجر: The Prophet said آمين aloud after ولا الضالين; al-Bayḍāwī cites this for an imam's audible response in audible prayers.

positions.position: Abū Ḥanīfa is reported not to say آمين, though the better-known report says he says it quietly; a congregant says it with the imam.
positions.reasons: BAYDAWI-FULL reporting أبو حنيفة: Abū Ḥanīfa is reported not to say آمين, though the better-known report says he says it quietly; a congregant says it with the imam.

positions.position: Abu Hurayra reports God’s dialogue dividing the Fatiha between Himself and the servant: praise, glorification, and exaltation belong to God; the worshipper’s request for guidance and the response to it belong to the servant, while worship and…
positions.reasons: NASAFI reporting أبو هريرة عن النبي: Abu Hurayra reports God’s dialogue dividing the Fatiha between Himself and the servant: praise, glorification, and exaltation belong to God; the worshipper’s request for guidance and the response to it belong to the servant, while worship and aid are shared.

positions.position: The unified path joins hope and fear, prayer for complete light, steadfastness, gardens, reward and light, seeing God’s face wherever one turns, and the best reward with increase.; cited verses: 17:57, 66:8, 41:30, 98:8, 57:19, 2:115, 10:26
positions.reasons: QASHANI: The unified path joins hope and fear, prayer for complete light, steadfastness, gardens, reward and light, seeing God’s face wherever one turns, and the best reward with increase. | mentions 17:57, 66:8, 41:30, 98:8, 57:19, 2:115, 10:26

positions.position: The prayer asks that guidance to the path of the favored continue: those who praise God and declare worship and reliance already possess guidance, but ask for its permanence.
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN: The prayer asks that guidance to the path of the favored continue: those who praise God and declare worship and reliance already possess guidance, but ask for its permanence.

positions.position: The passive wording for those angered is tactful in a humble plea: the worshipper attributes favor to the One asked for guidance but avoids confronting Him with the description of vengeance.
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN: The passive wording for those angered is tactful in a humble plea: the worshipper attributes favor to the One asked for guidance but avoids confronting Him with the description of vengeance.

positions.position: Grammarians enumerate seven kinds of apposition; the first three are undisputed, while some assert apposition of clarification and cite a prayer report, which does not apply to Qur'anic wording.
positions.reasons: SAMIN-DURR: Grammarians enumerate seven kinds of apposition; the first three are undisputed, while some assert apposition of clarification and cite a prayer report, which does not apply to Qur'anic wording.

positions.position: In a divine report, God divides the prayer between Himself and His servant, responds to each recited section, calls 1:5 shared between them, and grants the servant's request.
positions.reasons: IBNKATHIR reporting الله تعالى: In a divine report, God divides the prayer between Himself and His servant, responds to each recited section, calls 1:5 shared between them, and grants the servant's request.

positions.position: Some imams say al-Fatiha affirms lordship, seeks guidance in Islam, and asks protection from Judaism and Christianity.
positions.reasons: BURHAN reporting بعض الأئمة: Some imams say al-Fatiha affirms lordship, seeks guidance in Islam, and asks protection from Judaism and Christianity.

positions.position: One explanation says praise uses third person because it ranks below worship, while direct address elevates the worshipper's encounter; similarly, blessing is explicitly attributed to God but anger is phrased obliquely as a matter of etiquette.; cited…
positions.reasons: BURHAN reporting قيل: One explanation says praise uses third person because it ranks below worship, while direct address elevates the worshipper's encounter; similarly, blessing is explicitly attributed to God but anger is phrased obliquely as a matter of etiquette. | mentions 6:101

positions.position: Maki deems these noncanonical-imam readings permissible when reliably transmitted, since each has a sound Arabic analysis and agrees with the codex spelling; Ibn al-Jazari says others also share some forms.
positions.reasons: NASHR: Maki deems these noncanonical-imam readings permissible when reliably transmitted, since each has a sound Arabic analysis and agrees with the codex spelling; Ibn al-Jazari says others also share some forms.

positions.position: Because the Fātiḥa's order is obligatory, reversing its parts or inserting material not belonging to it invalidates prayer by disrupting the arrangement.
positions.reasons: BIQAI: Because the Fātiḥa's order is obligatory, reversing its parts or inserting material not belonging to it invalidates prayer by disrupting the arrangement.

positions.position: Having requested the noblest way, the worshipper asks for its best companions; because blessing may be worldly, he seeks protection from confused or unjust wanderers.
positions.reasons: BIQAI: Having requested the noblest way, the worshipper asks for its best companions; because blessing may be worldly, he seeks protection from confused or unjust wanderers.

positions.position: The Fatiha's many titles converge on مراقبة: it is the Mother of the Book, foundation, oft-repeated, treasure, healing, sufficing, complete, protecting, incantation, praise, thanks, supplication and prayer.
positions.reasons: BIQAI-FULL: The Fatiha's many titles converge on مراقبة: it is the Mother of the Book, foundation, oft-repeated, treasure, healing, sufficing, complete, protecting, incantation, praise, thanks, supplication and prayer.

positions.position: The Fatiha is a treasure, cure, sufficiency, fulfillment, protection and incantation; it gathers praise, gratitude and supplication, with prayer as their greatest assembly.
positions.reasons: BIQAI-FULL: The Fatiha is a treasure, cure, sufficiency, fulfillment, protection and incantation; it gathers praise, gratitude and supplication, with prayer as their greatest assembly.

positions.position: Al-Harali explains the sound report that God divided prayer between Himself and His servant: the first three verses are God's praise, which He accepts from the reciting servant as praise and glorification.
positions.reasons: BIQAI-FULL reporting الحرالي: Al-Harali explains the sound report that God divided prayer between Himself and His servant: the first three verses are God's praise, which He accepts from the reciting servant as praise and glorification.

positions.position: The Qur'an's arrangement is miraculous, so the Fatiha must retain its required order in prayer; rearrangement or insertion of foreign material invalidates it. Al-Isfahani locates its clearest inimitability in order.
positions.reasons: BIQAI-FULL: The Qur'an's arrangement is miraculous, so the Fatiha must retain its required order in prayer; rearrangement or insertion of foreign material invalidates it. Al-Isfahani locates its clearest inimitability in order.

positions.position: Baqara answers the Fatiha's plea for guidance by directing worshippers to the Book, describing the guided and denied groups as patterns to follow or avoid; its pious are the straight path and its others the path of…
positions.reasons: BIQAI-FULL: Baqara answers the Fatiha's plea for guidance by directing worshippers to the Book, describing the guided and denied groups as patterns to follow or avoid; its pious are the straight path and its others the path of ruin.

positions.position: In Qatada's sequential gloss, the Day of Recompense is when creatures are repaid; the worship-prayer is what people should say and directs them to God; the straight path is named, the favored are prophets, the objects of…
positions.reasons: DURR reporting قتادة: In Qatada's sequential gloss, the Day of Recompense is when creatures are repaid; the worship-prayer is what people should say and directs them to God; the straight path is named, the favored are prophets, the objects of anger are Jews, and the astray are Christians.

positions.position: Ibn al-Zubayr used the same reading in prayer.
positions.reasons: DURR reporting عبد الله بن الزبير: Ibn al-Zubayr used the same reading in prayer.

positions.position: Ibn ʿAbbās identifies the favored path as that of obedient worshippers among angels, prophets, the truthful, martyrs, and righteous.
positions.reasons: DURR reporting ابن عباس: Ibn ʿAbbās identifies the favored path as that of obedient worshippers among angels, prophets, the truthful, martyrs, and righteous.

positions.position: In Abū Hurayra's report, God says the prayer is divided between Him and His servant: the opening praise is His, the middle is shared, and the servant receives what he asks in the remainder.
positions.reasons: DURR-FULL reporting الله عز وجل: In Abū Hurayra's report, God says the prayer is divided between Him and His servant: the opening praise is His, the middle is shared, and the servant receives what he asks in the remainder.

positions.position: Ibn al-Zubayr used the same variant in prayer, with “min” and repeated “ghayr.”
positions.reasons: DURR-FULL reporting عبد الله بن الزبير: Ibn al-Zubayr used the same variant in prayer, with “min” and repeated “ghayr.”

positions.position: Mujahid recommends asking for Paradise and refuge from the Fire after the imam's recitation.
positions.reasons: DURR-FULL reporting مجاهد: Mujahid recommends asking for Paradise and refuge from the Fire after the imam's recitation.

positions.position: Al-Fatiha's final prayer details the highest request: faith protected from sin and its resulting wrath and error; “those You favored” means believers, and the favor is unrestricted because faith entails every blessing.
positions.reasons: ITQAN: Al-Fatiha's final prayer details the highest request: faith protected from sin and its resulting wrath and error; “those You favored” means believers, and the favor is unrestricted because faith entails every blessing.

positions.position: The Sunna explains commands left general in the Qur'an, including how to perform prayer and pilgrimage and the taxable thresholds for kinds of zakat.; cited verses: 2:43, 3:97
positions.reasons: ITQAN: The Sunna explains commands left general in the Qur'an, including how to perform prayer and pilgrimage and the taxable thresholds for kinds of zakat. | mentions 2:43, 3:97

positions.position: Using the active second-person verb is an appeal: since God has already bestowed favor, the worshipper asks Him to grant guidance too; the cited verse of poetry illustrates that God taught people to ask in order to…
