positions.reasons: ZAJJAJ: The phrase is an adjective for al-ṣirāṭ al-mustaqīm. | mentions 1:6

positions.position: Sībawayh says the wāw added after masculine hāʾ parallels the added alif in feminine hāʾ forms.
positions.reasons: ZAJJAJ reporting سِيبَوَيْهِ: Sībawayh says the wāw added after masculine hāʾ parallels the added alif in feminine hāʾ forms.

positions.position: Sībawayh's and al-Khalīl's associates explain the added wāw as clarifying the faint hāʾ; it disappears in pause and is not retained as an original letter.
positions.reasons: ZAJJAJ reporting أصحاب سيبويه والخليل: Sībawayh's and al-Khalīl's associates explain the added wāw as clarifying the faint hāʾ; it disappears in pause and is not retained as an original letter.

positions.position: With a preceding kasra the wāw may change to yāʾ; the Hijazi readings of 28:81 include both hī and hū forms.; cited verses: 28:81
positions.reasons: ZAJJAJ: With a preceding kasra the wāw may change to yāʾ; the Hijazi readings of 28:81 include both hī and hū forms. | mentions 28:81

positions.position: Some Arabs are reported to use a kasra with the second-person kāf in ʿalaykum and bikum, but he rejects this as an anomalous dialect; the correct poetic wording is faḍl aḥlāmikum.
positions.reasons: ZAJJAJ: Some Arabs are reported to use a kasra with the second-person kāf in ʿalaykum and bikum, but he rejects this as an anomalous dialect; the correct poetic wording is faḍl aḥlāmikum.

positions.position: Sībawayh quotes the poem with the anomalous form, though its sound transmission is faḍl aḥlāmikum.
positions.reasons: ZAJJAJ: Sībawayh quotes the poem with the anomalous form, though its sound transmission is faḍl aḥlāmikum.

positions.position: Plural hāʾ forms originally had a wāw, but speakers omit it because mīm suffices and the wāw is heavy; Arabic names do not end in wāw preceded by a vowel.
positions.reasons: ZAJJAJ: Plural hāʾ forms originally had a wāw, but speakers omit it because mīm suffices and the wāw is heavy; Arabic names do not end in wāw preceded by a vowel.

positions.position: The reading with the wāw in ʿalayhumū is rare; he says the widespread form without it should be read.
positions.reasons: ZAJJAJ: The reading with the wāw in ʿalayhumū is rare; he says the widespread form without it should be read.

positions.position: One cannot say mithla ḍārib in the parallel construction, because Zayd depends on ḍārib and cannot precede it.
positions.reasons: ZAJJAJ: One cannot say mithla ḍārib in the parallel construction, because Zayd depends on ḍārib and cannot precede it.

positions.position: The sīn reading of الصراط is transmitted from Ibn Kathīr and Abū ʿAmr through named reciters, while Ibn Kathīr also has transmissions with ṣād; Abū ʿAmr is reported with all three sibilant realizations.
positions.reasons: IBNMUJAHID reporting ابن كثير وأبو عمرو: The sīn reading of الصراط is transmitted from Ibn Kathīr and Abū ʿAmr through named reciters, while Ibn Kathīr also has transmissions with ṣād; Abū ʿAmr is reported with all three sibilant realizations.

positions.position: One transmission from Abū ʿAmr places the sound between ṣād and zāy; the ordinary reading preserves clear ṣād, while Ḥamza’s imāla approaches zāy and cannot be represented precisely in writing.
positions.reasons: IBNMUJAHID reporting عريان بن أبي سفيان عن أبي عمرو: One transmission from Abū ʿAmr places the sound between ṣād and zāy; the ordinary reading preserves clear ṣād, while Ḥamza’s imāla approaches zāy and cannot be represented precisely in writing.

positions.position: Reports differ on whether Ḥamza shades only quiescent ṣād toward zāy or also moving ṣād; some say he gives the zāy outright only when ṣād is quiescent.
positions.reasons: IBNMUJAHID reporting الكسائي عن حمزة: Reports differ on whether Ḥamza shades only quiescent ṣād toward zāy or also moving ṣād; some say he gives the zāy outright only when ṣād is quiescent.

positions.position: Al-Kisāʾī follows Ḥamza in ṣād before dāl in قصد and related forms; he says sīn is more common in Arabic but reads ṣād to follow the written Qurʾānic text.; cited verses: 16:9, 28:23, 6:46, 52:37, 88:22
positions.reasons: IBNMUJAHID reporting الكسائي: Al-Kisāʾī follows Ḥamza in ṣād before dāl in قصد and related forms; he says sīn is more common in Arabic but reads ṣād to follow the written Qurʾānic text. | mentions 16:9, 28:23, 6:46, 52:37, 88:22

positions.position: Sīn is etymologically original, but scribes and readers use ṣād to ease articulation beside emphatic ṭāʾ: both sounds can be made with the tongue raised, unlike sīn and ṭāʾ together.
positions.reasons: IBNMUJAHID: Sīn is etymologically original, but scribes and readers use ṣād to ease articulation beside emphatic ṭāʾ: both sounds can be made with the tongue raised, unlike sīn and ṭāʾ together.

positions.position: Nafiʿ has reports allowing raised or quiescent mīm; the author’s own recitation uses sukūn. Warsh keeps hāʾ kasra and joins mīm to wāw before an initial vowel.; cited verses: 2:6
positions.reasons: IBNMUJAHID reporting نافع: Nafiʿ has reports allowing raised or quiescent mīm; the author’s own recitation uses sukūn. Warsh keeps hāʾ kasra and joins mīm to wāw before an initial vowel. | mentions 2:6

positions.position: With a following consonant, these readers keep hāʾ kasra and raise mīm; Abū ʿAmr raises neither, while Ḥamza and al-Kisāʾī raise both.; cited verses: 2:61, 28:23
positions.reasons: IBNMUJAHID reporting عاصم ونافع وابن كثير وابن عامر: With a following consonant, these readers keep hāʾ kasra and raise mīm; Abū ʿAmr raises neither, while Ḥamza and al-Kisāʾī raise both. | mentions 2:61, 28:23

positions.position: Kasra on hāʾ follows a preceding kasra or yāʾ because hāʾ is close to yāʾ; plural wāw is retained as the original plural marker, parallel to dual alif in عليهما.
positions.reasons: IBNMUJAHID: Kasra on hāʾ follows a preceding kasra or yāʾ because hāʾ is close to yāʾ; plural wāw is retained as the original plural marker, parallel to dual alif in عليهما.

positions.position: Shading ṣād toward voiced zāy matches the voicing of ṭāʾ while retaining a sibilant; the same voicing rationale applies to the cited ṣād+dāl words.; cited verses: 16:9, 28:23, 6:46
positions.reasons: IBNMUJAHID: Shading ṣād toward voiced zāy matches the voicing of ṭāʾ while retaining a sibilant; the same voicing rationale applies to the cited ṣād+dāl words. | mentions 16:9, 28:23, 6:46

positions.position: Ḥamza pronounces hāʾ with ḍamma and mīm quiescent in عليهم, إليهم, and لديهم; other readers use kasra on hāʾ.
positions.reasons: IBNMUJAHID reporting حمزة: Ḥamza pronounces hāʾ with ḍamma and mīm quiescent in عليهم, إليهم, and لديهم; other readers use kasra on hāʾ.

positions.position: Ḥamza’s ḍamma on hāʾ reflects its underlying form, since the pronoun begins with ḍamma in هم.
positions.reasons: IBNMUJAHID reporting حمزة: Ḥamza’s ḍamma on hāʾ reflects its underlying form, since the pronoun begins with ḍamma in هم.

positions.position: When mīm meets a following consonant it must move; some restore its original ḍamma while leaving hāʾ kasra, others match kasras to avoid a heavy ḍamma after kasra.
positions.reasons: IBNMUJAHID: When mīm meets a following consonant it must move; some restore its original ḍamma while leaving hāʾ kasra, others match kasras to avoid a heavy ḍamma after kasra.

positions.position: Al-Kisāʾī restores both mīm and hāʾ to ḍamma before a following consonant, avoiding the transition from kasra to ḍamma.
positions.reasons: IBNMUJAHID reporting الكسائي: Al-Kisāʾī restores both mīm and hāʾ to ḍamma before a following consonant, avoiding the transition from kasra to ḍamma.

positions.position: Ḥamza limits hāʾ-ḍamma to عليهم, إليهم, and لديهم: when followed by an overt noun, their yāʾ becomes alif, which cannot follow a kasra, so the pronoun follows the overt form.; cited verses: 8:16, 6:1, 2:142
positions.reasons: IBNMUJAHID reporting حمزة: Ḥamza limits hāʾ-ḍamma to عليهم, إليهم, and لديهم: when followed by an overt noun, their yāʾ becomes alif, which cannot follow a kasra, so the pronoun follows the overt form. | mentions 8:16, 6:1, 2:142

positions.position: The author again says he knows no exegetical disagreement over this wording.
positions.reasons: IBNABIHATIM: The author again says he knows no exegetical disagreement over this wording.

positions.position: Ḥamza and the Kufans read ʿalayhum with ḍamma on hāʾ and still mīm, dropping the heavy wāw.
positions.reasons: NAHHAS reporting حمزة وأهل الكوفة: Ḥamza and the Kufans read ʿalayhum with ḍamma on hāʾ and still mīm, dropping the heavy wāw.

positions.position: Muḥammad ibn Yazīd rejects as impermissible two irregular forms with hāʾ and mīm both ḍamma or both kasra without wāw or yāʾ.
positions.reasons: NAHHAS reporting محمد بن يزيد: Muḥammad ibn Yazīd rejects as impermissible two irregular forms with hāʾ and mīm both ḍamma or both kasra without wāw or yāʾ.

positions.position: Abū al-ʿAbbās says the kasra in minhu is possible because the nūn is still; Banū Bakr also use kasra in ʿalaykum, but he rejects the analogy as a grave error.
positions.reasons: NAHHAS reporting أبو العباس: Abū al-ʿAbbās says the kasra in minhu is possible because the nūn is still; Banū Bakr also use kasra in ʿalaykum, but he rejects the analogy as a grave error.

positions.position: Al-Akhfash parses the accusative as a circumstantial accusative or an exception.
positions.reasons: NAHHAS reporting الأخفش: Al-Akhfash parses the accusative as a circumstantial accusative or an exception.

positions.position: Abū al-ʿAbbās calls it a detached exception rather than an exception from the preceding expression.
positions.reasons: NAHHAS reporting أبو العباس: Abū al-ʿAbbās calls it a detached exception rather than an exception from the preceding expression.

positions.position: The Kufans deny an exception parse because lā follows and, they say, lā is not superfluous in exceptions.
positions.reasons: NAHHAS reporting الكوفيون: The Kufans deny an exception parse because lā follows and, they say, lā is not superfluous in exceptions.

positions.position: Al-ḍāllīn is coordinated with al-maghḍūb ʿalayhim; the Kufans call this coordination, while Sībawayh calls it sharing.
positions.reasons: NAHHAS: Al-ḍāllīn is coordinated with al-maghḍūb ʿalayhim; the Kufans call this coordination, while Sībawayh calls it sharing.

positions.position: The sīn form preserves the word’s original consonant; ṣād replaces sīn to harmonize its hissing quality with ṭāʾ’s emphatic articulation.
positions.reasons: IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA: The sīn form preserves the word’s original consonant; ṣād replaces sīn to harmonize its hissing quality with ṭāʾ’s emphatic articulation.

positions.position: Some Nāfiʿ transmitters allow either a damma or still mim after kasra hāʾ; Aḥmad b. Qālūn infers Nāfiʿ read with still mim, as did Aḥmad b. Mūsā.
positions.reasons: FARISI-HUJJA reporting إسماعيل بن جعفر وابن جماز وقالون والمسيبي: Some Nāfiʿ transmitters allow either a damma or still mim after kasra hāʾ; Aḥmad b. Qālūn infers Nāfiʿ read with still mim, as did Aḥmad b. Mūsā.

positions.position: Warsh keeps hāʾ kasra and mim still, but inserts a wāw when an original alif follows, as in sawāʾ ʿalayhumu.
positions.reasons: FARISI-HUJJA reporting ورش: Warsh keeps hāʾ kasra and mim still, but inserts a wāw when an original alif follows, as in sawāʾ ʿalayhumu.

positions.position: Abū ʿAmr, ʿĀṣim, Ibn ʿĀmir, and al-Kisāʾī generally use kasra hāʾ and still mim; before a following sukūn, readers differ over mim and sometimes hāʾ.
positions.reasons: FARISI-HUJJA: Abū ʿAmr, ʿĀṣim, Ibn ʿĀmir, and al-Kisāʾī generally use kasra hāʾ and still mim; before a following sukūn, readers differ over mim and sometimes hāʾ.

positions.position: Aḥmad b. Mūsā says the variation of hāʾ depends on whether it follows kasra or silent yāʾ; elsewhere it is damma, while mim is damma or still.
positions.reasons: FARISI-HUJJA reporting أحمد بن موسى: Aḥmad b. Mūsā says the variation of hāʾ depends on whether it follows kasra or silent yāʾ; elsewhere it is damma, while mim is damma or still.

positions.position: Sibawayh reports that some say ʿalayhumu by assimilating to the preceding yāʾ; Abū Ḥātim identifies it as al-Aʿraj’s reading.
positions.reasons: FARISI-HUJJA reporting سيبويه: Sibawayh reports that some say ʿalayhumu by assimilating to the preceding yāʾ; Abū Ḥātim identifies it as al-Aʿraj’s reading.

positions.position: One defense says hāʾ shares yāʾ’s articulation, so the hāʾ should follow the yāʾ; another treats hāʾ as related to yāʾ by its articulation.
positions.reasons: FARISI-HUJJA: One defense says hāʾ shares yāʾ’s articulation, so the hāʾ should follow the yāʾ; another treats hāʾ as related to yāʾ by its articulation.

positions.position: Ḥamza treats damma hāʾ as original, like hum when independent; the waw reading is described as old and Qurayshī, Ḥijāzī, and Yemeni eloquent usage.
positions.reasons: FARISI-HUJJA reporting حمزة: Ḥamza treats damma hāʾ as original, like hum when independent; the waw reading is described as old and Qurayshī, Ḥijāzī, and Yemeni eloquent usage.

positions.position: Damma on a mim before a following sukūn restores its original vowel after movement becomes necessary; this is common in the two Holy Cities.
positions.reasons: FARISI-HUJJA reporting أبو حاتم: Damma on a mim before a following sukūn restores its original vowel after movement becomes necessary; this is common in the two Holy Cities.

positions.position: Kasra mim before a following sukūn assimilates kasra to kasra, avoiding the heaviness of damma after kasra.
positions.reasons: FARISI-HUJJA: Kasra mim before a following sukūn assimilates kasra to kasra, avoiding the heaviness of damma after kasra.

positions.position: Al-Kisāʾī keeps hāʾ kasra unless the mim meets a following sukūn, then restores both hāʾ and mim to damma to avoid switching from kasra to damma.
positions.reasons: FARISI-HUJJA reporting الكسائي: Al-Kisāʾī keeps hāʾ kasra unless the mim meets a following sukūn, then restores both hāʾ and mim to damma to avoid switching from kasra to damma.

positions.position: The author prefers kasra on hāʾ because it is easier to pronounce and is the majority reading.
positions.reasons: FARISI-HUJJA: The author prefers kasra on hāʾ because it is easier to pronounce and is the majority reading.

positions.position: Sibawayh explains kasra hāʾ after yāʾ or kasra by its hidden quality and closeness to yāʾ and alif; adjacent kasra also changes wāw to yāʾ.
positions.reasons: FARISI-HUJJA reporting سيبويه: Sibawayh explains kasra hāʾ after yāʾ or kasra by its hidden quality and closeness to yāʾ and alif; adjacent kasra also changes wāw to yāʾ.

positions.position: Abū ʿAlī argues that hāʾ resembles alif in articulation and hiddenness, so a preceding kasra or yāʾ draws its damma toward kasra as imāla draws alif toward yāʾ.
positions.reasons: FARISI-HUJJA reporting أبو علي: Abū ʿAlī argues that hāʾ resembles alif in articulation and hiddenness, so a preceding kasra or yāʾ draws its damma toward kasra as imāla draws alif toward yāʾ.

positions.position: The pronunciation ḍarabtu ḍarbih shows hāʾ can trigger imāla even without a preceding kasra or yāʾ, like imāla in some proper names.
positions.reasons: FARISI-HUJJA reporting أبو علي: The pronunciation ḍarabtu ḍarbih shows hāʾ can trigger imāla even without a preceding kasra or yāʾ, like imāla in some proper names.

positions.position: Hāʾ and alif both clarify a preceding vowel in pause; al-Khalīl permits either hāʾ or alif after a consonant, supporting their parallel treatment in ʿalayhim.
positions.reasons: FARISI-HUJJA reporting أبو علي: Hāʾ and alif both clarify a preceding vowel in pause; al-Khalīl permits either hāʾ or alif after a consonant, supporting their parallel treatment in ʿalayhim.

positions.position: The optional hāʾ or alif suffix is allowed because each resembles and can stand for the other; alif also occurs in the same pause pattern after bāʾ, tāʾ, and thāʾ.
positions.reasons: FARISI-HUJJA reporting أبو علي: The optional hāʾ or alif suffix is allowed because each resembles and can stand for the other; alif also occurs in the same pause pattern after bāʾ, tāʾ, and thāʾ.

positions.position: Although hāʾ lacks the sustained sound of alif, their shared hiddenness, weakness, and articulation allow one to be brought near the other.
positions.reasons: FARISI-HUJJA reporting أبو علي: Although hāʾ lacks the sustained sound of alif, their shared hiddenness, weakness, and articulation allow one to be brought near the other.

positions.position: Hāʾ can replace other letters in pause just as alif can, another sign of their similarity.
positions.reasons: FARISI-HUJJA reporting أبو علي: Hāʾ can replace other letters in pause just as alif can, another sign of their similarity.

positions.position: The reported phrase lam aḍribihimā is treated as liaison pronounced like pause, not as a general rule for inflectional sukūn; inflectional endings do not assimilate freely.
positions.reasons: FARISI-HUJJA reporting أبو علي: The reported phrase lam aḍribihimā is treated as liaison pronounced like pause, not as a general rule for inflectional sukūn; inflectional endings do not assimilate freely.

positions.position: A jussive consonant may move to avoid a following sukūn, as in the cited yattaqihi form, unlike a freely altered inflectional ending.
positions.reasons: FARISI-HUJJA reporting أبو علي: A jussive consonant may move to avoid a following sukūn, as in the cited yattaqihi form, unlike a freely altered inflectional ending.

positions.position: Hāʾ behaves like weak letters: it can be deleted word-finally, as in shāh, shafah, and sanah, and shared rules strengthen the analogy.
positions.reasons: FARISI-HUJJA reporting أبو علي: Hāʾ behaves like weak letters: it can be deleted word-finally, as in shāh, shafah, and sanah, and shared rules strengthen the analogy.

positions.position: Hāʾ substitutes for yāʾ in ذه/هذه; Ḥijāzī and Tamīmī dialects differ in whether it drops or becomes yāʾ in pause and liaison.
positions.reasons: FARISI-HUJJA reporting أبو علي: Hāʾ substitutes for yāʾ in ذه/هذه; Ḥijāzī and Tamīmī dialects differ in whether it drops or becomes yāʾ in pause and liaison.

positions.position: Hāʾ also alternates with yāʾ under doubling, as in dahdayt for dahdaht and related forms.
positions.reasons: FARISI-HUJJA reporting أبو علي: Hāʾ also alternates with yāʾ under doubling, as in dahdayt for dahdaht and related forms.

positions.position: Abū Zayd records the forms māhat and tamūhu/tamīhu, and a poetic line using māh as a word for a heart softened by tears.
positions.reasons: FARISI-HUJJA reporting أبو زيد: Abū Zayd records the forms māhat and tamūhu/tamīhu, and a poetic line using māh as a word for a heart softened by tears.

positions.position: Some speakers kasra hāʾ despite an intervening consonant, as in minhum; this weaker analogy still supports kasra when yāʾ is adjacent.
positions.reasons: FARISI-HUJJA reporting أبو علي: Some speakers kasra hāʾ despite an intervening consonant, as in minhum; this weaker analogy still supports kasra when yāʾ is adjacent.

positions.position: Abū Zayd reports a Bakrī speaker saying minhu, minhuma, and minhumī, breaking the pronoun in both connected and paused speech.
positions.reasons: FARISI-HUJJA reporting أبو زيد: Abū Zayd reports a Bakrī speaker saying minhu, minhuma, and minhumī, breaking the pronoun in both connected and paused speech.

positions.position: Other Bakrī speakers say bikum and faḍlu aḥlāmikum with kasra on kāf, since kāf shares hāʾ’s whispering and pronoun function.
positions.reasons: FARISI-HUJJA reporting أبو علي: Other Bakrī speakers say bikum and faḍlu aḥlāmikum with kasra on kāf, since kāf shares hāʾ’s whispering and pronoun function.

positions.position: The author replies that proximity can override a default vowel; Arabic regularly abandons original sounds for harmony or ease, including ṣād in ṣirāṭ and several broken forms.
positions.reasons: FARISI-HUJJA reporting أبو علي: The author replies that proximity can override a default vowel; Arabic regularly abandons original sounds for harmony or ease, including ṣād in ṣirāṭ and several broken forms.

positions.position: Numerous forms depart from their expected morphology: ʿīd has plural aʿyād, dunya’s pattern is otherwise abandoned, and Adam/Akhir form plurals with wāw despite an expected hamza.
positions.reasons: FARISI-HUJJA reporting أبو علي: Numerous forms depart from their expected morphology: ʿīd has plural aʿyād, dunya’s pattern is otherwise abandoned, and Adam/Akhir form plurals with wāw despite an expected hamza.

positions.position: The expected form of qasī is abandoned in three respects, illustrating that a linguistic default need not prevail when analogy or ease favors another form.
positions.reasons: FARISI-HUJJA reporting أبو علي: The expected form of qasī is abandoned in three respects, illustrating that a linguistic default need not prevail when analogy or ease favors another form.

positions.position: Hamza’s reading in buyūt shows that kasra can replace a default damma because of nearby yāʾ; Sibawayh’s diminutive bayyit supports the same allowance.
positions.reasons: FARISI-HUJJA reporting أبو علي: Hamza’s reading in buyūt shows that kasra can replace a default damma because of nearby yāʾ; Sibawayh’s diminutive bayyit supports the same allowance.

positions.position: The hāʾ in bihi and ʿalayhi can therefore follow kasra or yāʾ just as alif does, despite being pronounced with a movement.
positions.reasons: FARISI-HUJJA reporting أبو علي: The hāʾ in bihi and ʿalayhi can therefore follow kasra or yāʾ just as alif does, despite being pronounced with a movement.

positions.position: A moving hāʾ is often ignored as a separator: imāla occurs before it in yadribahā, yanziʿahā, and baynī wa-baynahā, as before alif.
positions.reasons: FARISI-HUJJA reporting أبو علي: A moving hāʾ is often ignored as a separator: imāla occurs before it in yadribahā, yanziʿahā, and baynī wa-baynahā, as before alif.

positions.position: The shared opening of the doubled dāl in raddahā and raddā likewise shows that hāʾ does not block the alif-like pattern.
positions.reasons: FARISI-HUJJA reporting أبو علي: The shared opening of the doubled dāl in raddahā and raddā likewise shows that hāʾ does not block the alif-like pattern.

positions.position: When moving hāʾ is not counted, retaining its following yāʾ or wāw would leave two adjacent sukūns; deletion is therefore favored in fīhi hudan and khudhūhu.
positions.reasons: FARISI-HUJJA reporting أبو علي: When moving hāʾ is not counted, retaining its following yāʾ or wāw would leave two adjacent sukūns; deletion is therefore favored in fīhi hudan and khudhūhu.

positions.position: Weak letters are deleted in many settings where other letters remain, including suffixes, possessive forms, pauses, and rhyme, so deleting the glide after mim is ordinary.
positions.reasons: FARISI-HUJJA reporting أبو علي: Weak letters are deleted in many settings where other letters remain, including suffixes, possessive forms, pauses, and rhyme, so deleting the glide after mim is ordinary.

positions.position: Poetic examples demonstrate deletion of weak endings in verse and rhyme; the text also reports a variant wording for the line with sawāfa.
positions.reasons: FARISI-HUJJA reporting أبو علي: Poetic examples demonstrate deletion of weak endings in verse and rhyme; the text also reports a variant wording for the line with sawāfa.

positions.position: Repeated deletion of weak endings makes it legitimate to apply the same deletion to nouns as well as other forms.
positions.reasons: FARISI-HUJJA reporting أبو علي: Repeated deletion of weak endings makes it legitimate to apply the same deletion to nouns as well as other forms.

positions.position: Both lexical and grammatical weak endings are deleted elsewhere, even without a surviving marker; that makes deletion from ʿalayhim especially fitting.
positions.reasons: FARISI-HUJJA reporting أبو علي: Both lexical and grammatical weak endings are deleted elsewhere, even without a surviving marker; that makes deletion from ʿalayhim especially fitting.

positions.position: Retaining the mim vowel could restore the missing glide through vowel lengthening, so a still mim best realizes the intended lightening.
positions.reasons: FARISI-HUJJA reporting أبو علي: Retaining the mim vowel could restore the missing glide through vowel lengthening, so a still mim best realizes the intended lightening.

positions.position: A kasra or damma may be lengthened into the very yāʾ or wāw that was deleted; still mim prevents that reversal and preserves the lighter form.
positions.reasons: FARISI-HUJJA reporting أبو علي: A kasra or damma may be lengthened into the very yāʾ or wāw that was deleted; still mim prevents that reversal and preserves the lighter form.

positions.position: A vowelled mim would create four or five consecutive moving syllables, a sequence avoided in Arabic word patterns and poetic meters; deleting its vowel prevents that sequence.
positions.reasons: FARISI-HUJJA reporting أبو علي: A vowelled mim would create four or five consecutive moving syllables, a sequence avoided in Arabic word patterns and poetic meters; deleting its vowel prevents that sequence.

positions.position: Arabic meter alternates deletions in mustafʿilun to avoid five consecutive movements, an analogy for removing mim’s vowel.
positions.reasons: FARISI-HUJJA reporting أبو علي: Arabic meter alternates deletions in mustafʿilun to avoid five consecutive movements, an analogy for removing mim’s vowel.

positions.position: Arabic alternations such as ḥāḥayt, ṭāʾī, and ḥārī support the close relation of yāʾ and alif; alif from wāw is comparatively rare.
positions.reasons: FARISI-HUJJA reporting أبو علي: Arabic alternations such as ḥāḥayt, ṭāʾī, and ḥārī support the close relation of yāʾ and alif; alif from wāw is comparatively rare.

positions.position: Against the claim that dāwiya has an alif derived from wāw, Abū ʿAlī suggests it may derive from daw with a nisba ending, supported by a cited poetic use.
positions.reasons: FARISI-HUJJA reporting أبو علي: Against the claim that dāwiya has an alif derived from wāw, Abū ʿAlī suggests it may derive from daw with a nisba ending, supported by a cited poetic use.

positions.position: The common analogy should prevail over a rare alternative unless evidence forces the exception; poetic shortening of nisba yāʾ does not do so.
positions.reasons: FARISI-HUJJA reporting أبو علي: The common analogy should prevail over a rare alternative unless evidence forces the exception; poetic shortening of nisba yāʾ does not do so.

positions.position: Abū Zayd reports an eloquent Arab saying ḍarabat yadāh and waḍaʿtuhu ʿalāh; al-Khalīl used such speech to explain forms with alif-like treatment.
positions.reasons: FARISI-HUJJA reporting أبو زيد: Abū Zayd reports an eloquent Arab saying ḍarabat yadāh and waḍaʿtuhu ʿalāh; al-Khalīl used such speech to explain forms with alif-like treatment.

positions.position: Ḥijāz and Qays use final hāʾ in both pause and liaison, paralleling Ṭayyiʾ’s yāʾ substitution and strengthening the analogy.
positions.reasons: FARISI-HUJJA reporting أبو علي: Ḥijāz and Qays use final hāʾ in both pause and liaison, paralleling Ṭayyiʾ’s yāʾ substitution and strengthening the analogy.

positions.position: The attested dialect and the analogous Ḥijāzī/Tamīmī alternations establish the language and make its use for Ḥamza’s reading legitimate.
positions.reasons: FARISI-HUJJA reporting أبو علي: The attested dialect and the analogous Ḥijāzī/Tamīmī alternations establish the language and make its use for Ḥamza’s reading legitimate.

positions.position: Poetic meter balances duration, so the longer alif cannot share the rhyme position of yāʾ and wāw.
positions.reasons: FARISI-HUJJA reporting أبو علي: Poetic meter balances duration, so the longer alif cannot share the rhyme position of yāʾ and wāw.

positions.position: Unlike long alif, short fatha can precede a rhyme with damma or kasra; examples from Abū al-Ḥasan show the distinction.
positions.reasons: FARISI-HUJJA reporting أبو علي: Unlike long alif, short fatha can precede a rhyme with damma or kasra; examples from Abū al-Ḥasan show the distinction.

positions.position: Alif’s greater duration appears in how hamza is softened after alif but not after yāʾ or wāw, strengthening its distinct treatment.
positions.reasons: FARISI-HUJJA reporting أبو علي: Alif’s greater duration appears in how hamza is softened after alif but not after yāʾ or wāw, strengthening its distinct treatment.

positions.position: Examples such as ruwiya, ruwiyya, and nuwwi show that a replacement wāw can inherit the behavior of its source; bīs similarly keeps its original kasra after hamza is dropped.
positions.reasons: FARISI-HUJJA reporting أبو علي: Examples such as ruwiya, ruwiyya, and nuwwi show that a replacement wāw can inherit the behavior of its source; bīs similarly keeps its original kasra after hamza is dropped.

positions.position: Yāʾ can also be fixed across case positions like alif, preserving one surface form; he cites ayādī sabā, bādī badā, qālī qalā, and maʿdīkarib.
positions.reasons: FARISI-HUJJA reporting أبو علي: Yāʾ can also be fixed across case positions like alif, preserving one surface form; he cites ayādī sabā, bādī badā, qālī qalā, and maʿdīkarib.

positions.position: These fixed-yāʾ forms occur in accusative position, whether analyzed as one of the cited nominal patterns or as an attached ending.
positions.reasons: FARISI-HUJJA reporting أبو علي: These fixed-yāʾ forms occur in accusative position, whether analyzed as one of the cited nominal patterns or as an attached ending.

positions.position: Abū Bakr counts seven transmitted vocalizations of the pronoun in عليهم; al-Akhfash adds three, yielding ten forms, five with hāʾ ḍamma and five with kasra.
positions.reasons: IBNJINNI-MUHTASAB reporting أبو بكر أحمد بن موسى: Abū Bakr counts seven transmitted vocalizations of the pronoun in عليهم; al-Akhfash adds three, yielding ten forms, five with hāʾ ḍamma and five with kasra.

positions.position: These readers transmit عليهمو; al-Ḥasan and ʿAmr b. Fāʾid transmit عليهمي, while al-Aʿraj is also reported with two unextended forms.
positions.reasons: IBNJINNI-MUHTASAB reporting ابن أبي إسحاق ومسلم بن جندب والأعرج وعيسى الثقفي وعبد الله بن يزيد: These readers transmit عليهمو; al-Ḥasan and ʿAmr b. Fāʾid transmit عليهمي, while al-Aʿraj is also reported with two unextended forms.

positions.position: Ibn Jinnī regards the plural wāw as original: mīm marks more than one, including the dual, while wāw specifically marks the plural.
positions.reasons: IBNJINNI-MUHTASAB: Ibn Jinnī regards the plural wāw as original: mīm marks more than one, including the dual, while wāw specifically marks the plural.

positions.position: He derives عليهمي from kasra spreading from the preceding yāʾ to the weak, nearby hāʾ, then to mīm; the wāw becomes yāʾ after a kasra.
positions.reasons: IBNJINNI-MUHTASAB: He derives عليهمي from kasra spreading from the preceding yāʾ to the weak, nearby hāʾ, then to mīm; the wāw becomes yāʾ after a kasra.

positions.position: The blessed relinquish personal interests and stand with God in good etiquette.
positions.reasons: SULAMI reporting بعض البغداديين: The blessed relinquish personal interests and stand with God in good etiquette.

positions.position: The blessed witness the Benefactor rather than the gift itself.
positions.reasons: SULAMI reporting بعضهم: The blessed witness the Benefactor rather than the gift itself.

positions.position: God's favor restrains their limbs through awe while they serve Him.
positions.reasons: SULAMI reporting محمد بن علي: God's favor restrains their limbs through awe while they serve Him.

positions.position: The blessed path is acceptance of the obligations God imposed.
positions.reasons: SULAMI reporting محمد بن الفضل: The blessed path is acceptance of the obligations God imposed.

positions.position: Divine care keeps the blessed steadfast on the path of intimate conversation with God.
positions.reasons: SULAMI reporting أبو الحسن الوراق: Divine care keeps the blessed steadfast on the path of intimate conversation with God.

positions.position: The blessed path means following the Prophet.
positions.reasons: SULAMI reporting مالك بن أنس: The blessed path means following the Prophet.

positions.position: The path is worshipping God as though one sees Him, as in the Prophetic definition of excellence.
positions.reasons: SULAMI: The path is worshipping God as though one sees Him, as in the Prophetic definition of excellence.

positions.position: The blessed path means following the Sunnah.
positions.reasons: SULAMI reporting سهل بن عبد الله: The blessed path means following the Sunnah.

positions.position: The supplicant asks God to act accordingly and not leave him to himself for even an instant.
positions.reasons: SULAMI reporting ابن عطاء: The supplicant asks God to act accordingly and not leave him to himself for even an instant.

positions.position: The condemned follow the path of the doomed, while the astray follow desire away from guidance.
positions.reasons: SULAMI reporting بعضهم: The condemned follow the path of the doomed, while the astray follow desire away from guidance.

positions.position: Anger is associated with seeing one's own acts or seeking compensation for deeds; error is failing to see favors or thank God for enabled service.
positions.reasons: SULAMI reporting بعضهم: Anger is associated with seeing one's own acts or seeking compensation for deeds; error is failing to see favors or thank God for enabled service.

positions.position: Anger follows bad etiquette in service; the contrasting phrase refers to turning back in repentance, though its wording is broken in this segment.
positions.reasons: SULAMI reporting بعضهم: Anger follows bad etiquette in service; the contrasting phrase refers to turning back in repentance, though its wording is broken in this segment.

positions.position: Al-Aʿmash and Ḥamza read ʿalayhum with ḍamma on hāʾ and a still mīm; a report attributes it to the Prophet and ʿUmar as well.
positions.reasons: THALABI reporting الأعمش: Al-Aʿmash and Ḥamza read ʿalayhum with ḍamma on hāʾ and a still mīm; a report attributes it to the Prophet and ʿUmar as well.

positions.position: ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar and Ibn Abī Isḥāq read with ḍamma on both hāʾ and mīm and an added wāw.
positions.reasons: THALABI reporting عيسى بن عمر: ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar and Ibn Abī Isḥāq read with ḍamma on both hāʾ and mīm and an added wāw.

positions.position: Ibn Kathīr and al-Aʿraj read with kasra on hāʾ, ḍamma on mīm, and an appended wāw.
positions.reasons: THALABI reporting ابن كثير: Ibn Kathīr and al-Aʿraj read with kasra on hāʾ, ḍamma on mīm, and an appended wāw.

positions.position: Al-Ḥasan reads with kasra on both hāʾ and mīm and an appended yāʾ.
positions.reasons: THALABI reporting الحسن: Al-Ḥasan reads with kasra on both hāʾ and mīm and an appended yāʾ.

positions.position: Ibn ʿAbbās identifies them as the people of Moses and Jesus before they changed God's favors upon them.
positions.reasons: THALABI reporting ابن عباس: Ibn ʿAbbās identifies them as the people of Moses and Jesus before they changed God's favors upon them.

positions.position: Shahr ibn Ḥawshab identifies them as the Prophet's companions and his household.
positions.reasons: THALABI reporting شهر بن حوشب: Shahr ibn Ḥawshab identifies them as the Prophet's companions and his household.

positions.position: ʿIkrima says they were granted steadfastness in faith and uprightness.
positions.reasons: THALABI reporting عكرمة: ʿIkrima says they were granted steadfastness in faith and uprightness.

positions.position: ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥusayn ibn Dāwūd says they give thanks in ease and patience in hardship.
positions.reasons: THALABI reporting علي بن الحسين بن داود: ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥusayn ibn Dāwūd says they give thanks in ease and patience in hardship.

positions.position: Al-Ḥusayn ibn al-Faḍl understands the favor as God completing His blessing upon them.
positions.reasons: THALABI reporting الحسين بن الفضل: Al-Ḥusayn ibn al-Faḍl understands the favor as God completing His blessing upon them.

positions.position: ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAṭāʾ al-Khaffāf transmits from Abū ʿAmr a kasra on hāʾ and a lightly articulated ḍamma on mīm.
positions.reasons: THALABI reporting عبد الله بن عطاء الخفاف: ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAṭāʾ al-Khaffāf transmits from Abū ʿAmr a kasra on hāʾ and a lightly articulated ḍamma on mīm.

positions.position: ʿAmr ibn Ḥāmid reads the word with kasra on both hāʾ and mīm.
positions.reasons: THALABI reporting عمرو بن حامد: ʿAmr ibn Ḥāmid reads the word with kasra on both hāʾ and mīm.

positions.position: Misguidance is the opposite of guidance.
positions.reasons: MAWARDI: Misguidance is the opposite of guidance.

positions.position: Another view identifies them as believers in earlier scriptures.
positions.reasons: MAWARDI reporting unattributed: Another view identifies them as believers in earlier scriptures.

positions.position: Waki‘ identifies them as Muslims.
positions.reasons: MAWARDI reporting وكيع: Waki‘ identifies them as Muslims.

positions.position: Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd identifies them as the Prophet and his Companions.
positions.reasons: MAWARDI reporting عبد الرحمن بن زيد: Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd identifies them as the Prophet and his Companions.

positions.position: One interpretation takes God’s wrath in its familiar sense as anger among people.
positions.reasons: MAWARDI reporting unattributed: One interpretation takes God’s wrath in its familiar sense as anger among people.

positions.position: One account understands divine anger as the anger known among human beings.
positions.reasons: MAWARDI-FULL: One account understands divine anger as the anger known among human beings.

positions.position: Another description of the favored is that they fulfill God's rights without turning aside to secure their own interests.
positions.reasons: QUSHAYRI: Another description of the favored is that they fulfill God's rights without turning aside to secure their own interests.

positions.position: They are also described as purified of their own traces so that they reach God through God.
positions.reasons: QUSHAYRI: They are also described as purified of their own traces so that they reach God through God.

positions.position: The favored preserve proper etiquette in service and remain aware of reverent awe.
positions.reasons: QUSHAYRI: The favored preserve proper etiquette in service and remain aware of reverent awe.

positions.position: The suns of their knowledge do not extinguish the lights of their scrupulousness, and they never neglect a rule of the Law.
positions.reasons: QUSHAYRI: The suns of their knowledge do not extinguish the lights of their scrupulousness, and they never neglect a rule of the Law.

positions.position: Those under wrath forgot divine enabling and closed their eyes to the sight of divine support.
positions.reasons: QUSHAYRI: Those under wrath forgot divine enabling and closed their eyes to the sight of divine support.

positions.position: Those under wrath also neglect the etiquette of service and fall short in fulfilling the conditions of obedience.
positions.reasons: QUSHAYRI: Those under wrath also neglect the etiquette of service and fall short in fulfilling the conditions of obedience.

positions.position: They can also be people cut off in the deserts of absence, scattered by worries through valleys of conjecture.
positions.reasons: QUSHAYRI: They can also be people cut off in the deserts of absence, scattered by worries through valleys of conjecture.

positions.position: The strongest means for the needy is continual seeking of God's aid, expressed through sincere supplication and disavowal of one's own power and ability.
positions.reasons: QUSHAYRI: The strongest means for the needy is continual seeking of God's aid, expressed through sincere supplication and disavowal of one's own power and ability.

positions.position: “Guide us” asks God to remove the darkness of one's states and the shadow of one's striving so that His holiness and generosity become lights by which one finds Him.
positions.reasons: QUSHAYRI: “Guide us” asks God to remove the darkness of one's states and the shadow of one's striving so that His holiness and generosity become lights by which one finds Him.

positions.position: The straight path is proved by Scripture and Sunna; innovation has no authority or route upon it.
positions.reasons: QUSHAYRI: The straight path is proved by Scripture and Sunna; innovation has no authority or route upon it.

positions.position: It is also the path validated by signs of monotheism, witnesses of realization, the early Muslim community, and lessons drawn from evidence.
positions.reasons: QUSHAYRI: It is also the path validated by signs of monotheism, witnesses of realization, the early Muslim community, and lessons drawn from evidence.

positions.position: The path separates its travelers from self-interest and its seekers from claims to personal entitlement.
positions.reasons: QUSHAYRI: The path separates its travelers from self-interest and its seekers from claims to personal entitlement.

positions.position: The path leads to monotheism and lets its traveler witness divine care and generosity, so effort is not mistaken for a claim that reward is owed.
positions.reasons: QUSHAYRI: The path leads to monotheism and lets its traveler witness divine care and generosity, so effort is not mistaken for a claim that reward is owed.

positions.position: A singular indeclinable relative gains case marking in the dual because particles are not dualized, but the plural is again a single form like hāʾulāʾ and remains indeclinable.
positions.reasons: WAHIDI-BASIT: A singular indeclinable relative gains case marking in the dual because particles are not dualized, but the plural is again a single form like hāʾulāʾ and remains indeclinable.

positions.position: God's inʿām is His favor and gift; niʿma is a verbal noun used in place of the infinitive inʿām, as nafaqa stands for infāq.
positions.reasons: WAHIDI-BASIT: God's inʿām is His favor and gift; niʿma is a verbal noun used in place of the infinitive inʿām, as nafaqa stands for infāq.

positions.position: Sībawayh says wāw was added after masculine hāʾ just as alif was added after feminine hāʾ, balancing their added endings.
positions.reasons: WAHIDI-BASIT reporting سيبويه: Sībawayh says wāw was added after masculine hāʾ just as alif was added after feminine hāʾ, balancing their added endings.

positions.position: Al-Zajjāj says wāw was added to make the faint throat-produced hāʾ clearer with a labial long vowel; the connecting wāw drops in pause and changes to yāʾ after kasra.
positions.reasons: WAHIDI-BASIT reporting الزجاج: Al-Zajjāj says wāw was added to make the faint throat-produced hāʾ clearer with a labial long vowel; the connecting wāw drops in pause and changes to yāʾ after kasra.

positions.position: Warsh lengthens before an open hamza rather than transferring its fatḥa to mīm, which could make the plural resemble the dual; he follows the same pattern before other hamza vowels.
positions.reasons: WAHIDI-BASIT: Warsh lengthens before an open hamza rather than transferring its fatḥa to mīm, which could make the plural resemble the dual; he follows the same pattern before other hamza vowels.

positions.position: Ḥamza and al-Kisāʾī pronounce hāʾ and mīm with ḍamma at a following hamzat al-waṣl: mīm returns to its original vowel to break two sukūns, then hāʾ follows it.
positions.reasons: WAHIDI-BASIT reporting حمزة والكسائي: Ḥamza and al-Kisāʾī pronounce hāʾ and mīm with ḍamma at a following hamzat al-waṣl: mīm returns to its original vowel to break two sukūns, then hāʾ follows it.

positions.position: Abū ʿAmr uses kasra for mīm as the usual vowel when breaking two sukūns and also gives hāʾ kasra to avoid a heavy kasra-to-ḍamma transition.
positions.reasons: WAHIDI-BASIT reporting أبو عمرو: Abū ʿAmr uses kasra for mīm as the usual vowel when breaking two sukūns and also gives hāʾ kasra to avoid a heavy kasra-to-ḍamma transition.

positions.position: Readers who keep hāʾ kasra but give mīm ḍamma restore mīm to its original vowel without restoring hāʾ, which was not forced by the context.
positions.reasons: WAHIDI-BASIT: Readers who keep hāʾ kasra but give mīm ḍamma restore mīm to its original vowel without restoring hāʾ, which was not forced by the context.

positions.position: ʿIkrima says God favored them by keeping them firm in faith and steadfast.
positions.reasons: WAHIDI-BASIT reporting عكرمة: ʿIkrima says God favored them by keeping them firm in faith and steadfast.

positions.position: Ibn al-Sarrāj additionally allows accusative as an implied aʿnī, I mean; al-Khalīl reportedly allowed it as a detached form of praise.
positions.reasons: WAHIDI-BASIT reporting ابن السراج: Ibn al-Sarrāj additionally allows accusative as an implied aʿnī, I mean; al-Khalīl reportedly allowed it as a detached form of praise.

positions.position: Apposition differs from an adjective because an indefinite can replace a definite and an expressed noun can replace a pronoun, neither of which is allowed for modifiers.
positions.reasons: WAHIDI-BASIT reporting صاحب الحجة: Apposition differs from an adjective because an indefinite can replace a definite and an expressed noun can replace a pronoun, neither of which is allowed for modifiers.

positions.position: Apposition also repeats the understood governing case factor, while both apposition and adjective clarify the first noun.
positions.reasons: WAHIDI-BASIT reporting صاحب الحجة: Apposition also repeats the understood governing case factor, while both apposition and adjective clarify the first noun.

positions.position: A parallel is the definite al-rajul described by mithluka: the article does not identify a particular man, so the description remains nonspecific.
positions.reasons: WAHIDI-BASIT reporting صاحب الحجة: A parallel is the definite al-rajul described by mithluka: the article does not identify a particular man, so the description remains nonspecific.

positions.position: Some allow added lā only after a preceding negation, but the author rejects that restriction and cites Saʿida al-Hudhalī's affirmative example.
positions.reasons: WAHIDI-BASIT reporting some grammarians: Some allow added lā only after a preceding negation, but the author rejects that restriction and cites Saʿida al-Hudhalī's affirmative example.

positions.position: Examples of the compound include min lā shayʾ and bi-lā māl; lā plus noun functions as a single expression, like fifteen.
positions.reasons: WAHIDI-BASIT: Examples of the compound include min lā shayʾ and bi-lā māl; lā plus noun functions as a single expression, like fifteen.

positions.position: The non-compounding negator leaves case untouched, as in al-Nābigha's no uncle and al-Shammākh's sleepless night.
positions.reasons: WAHIDI-BASIT: The non-compounding negator leaves case untouched, as in al-Nābigha's no uncle and al-Shammākh's sleepless night.

positions.position: He illustrates the disambiguating role with a poem: lā before ʿUmar keeps him inside the Prophet's disapproval clause instead of starting a new sentence praising Abū Bakr and ʿUmar.
positions.reasons: WAHIDI-BASIT reporting صاحب النظم: He illustrates the disambiguating role with a poem: lā before ʿUmar keeps him inside the Prophet's disapproval clause instead of starting a new sentence praising Abū Bakr and ʿUmar.

positions.position: Aḍalla can mean to hide or bury something, as in al-Mukhabbal's poem about Banū Qays losing their leader.
positions.reasons: WAHIDI-BASIT: Aḍalla can mean to hide or bury something, as in al-Mukhabbal's poem about Banū Qays losing their leader.

positions.position: Readers vary between kasra and ḍamma on the hāʾ, and between a vowelless, kasra, or ḍamma mīm of the plural, especially before a following hamzat al-waṣl; the author lists each school’s distributions.
positions.reasons: JISHUMI: Readers vary between kasra and ḍamma on the hāʾ, and between a vowelless, kasra, or ḍamma mīm of the plural, especially before a following hamzat al-waṣl; the author lists each school’s distributions.

positions.position: Ḍamma on hāʾ restores its underlying form; kasra is influenced by the preceding yāʾ, avoiding a heavy shift from ḍamma beside yāʾ, while ḍamma on mīm restores its base and appended wāw lengthens it.
positions.reasons: JISHUMI: Ḍamma on hāʾ restores its underlying form; kasra is influenced by the preceding yāʾ, avoiding a heavy shift from ḍamma beside yāʾ, while ḍamma on mīm restores its base and appended wāw lengthens it.

positions.position: Yaʿqub uses ḍamma on each hāʾ preceded by a quiescent yāʾ in dual and plural forms, except in “between their hands and feet.”
positions.reasons: BAGHAWI reporting يعقوب: Yaʿqub uses ḍamma on each hāʾ preceded by a quiescent yāʾ in dual and plural forms, except in “between their hands and feet.”

positions.position: Other readers use kasra on the hāʾ, following the preceding quiescent yāʾ, which is the sister of kasra; ḍamma returns to the hāʾ's isolated form.
positions.reasons: BAGHAWI: Other readers use kasra on the hāʾ, following the preceding quiescent yāʾ, which is the sister of kasra; ḍamma returns to the hāʾ's isolated form.

positions.position: Warsh uses ḍamma before hamzat al-qaṭʿ.
positions.reasons: BAGHAWI reporting ورش: Warsh uses ḍamma before hamzat al-qaṭʿ.

positions.position: Before hamzat al-waṣl, Hamza and al-Kisa'i use ḍamma after kasra or silent yāʾ; Abu ʿAmr uses kasra on both letters, as does Yaʿqub when the preceding letter is kasra.
positions.reasons: BAGHAWI reporting حمزة والكسائي وأبو عمرو ويعقوب: Before hamzat al-waṣl, Hamza and al-Kisa'i use ḍamma after kasra or silent yāʾ; Abu ʿAmr uses kasra on both letters, as does Yaʿqub when the preceding letter is kasra.

positions.position: The remaining readers use a ḍamma on mīm and kasra on hāʾ throughout, owing to the yāʾ or preceding kasra and the mīm's original ḍamma.
positions.reasons: BAGHAWI: The remaining readers use a ḍamma on mīm and kasra on hāʾ throughout, owing to the yāʾ or preceding kasra and the mīm's original ḍamma.

positions.position: Ikrima says they are the prophets, whom God kept firm in faith and uprightness.
positions.reasons: BAGHAWI reporting عكرمة: Ikrima says they are the prophets, whom God kept firm in faith and uprightness.

positions.position: Ibn ʿAbbas says they were the followers of Moses and Jesus before they changed their religion.
positions.reasons: BAGHAWI reporting ابن عباس: Ibn ʿAbbas says they were the followers of Moses and Jesus before they changed their religion.

positions.position: ʿAbd al-Rahman identifies them as the Prophet and those with him.
positions.reasons: BAGHAWI reporting عبد الرحمن: ʿAbd al-Rahman identifies them as the Prophet and those with him.

positions.position: Abu al-ʿAliya identifies them as the Messenger, Abu Bakr, and ʿUmar.
positions.reasons: BAGHAWI reporting أبو العالية: Abu al-ʿAliya identifies them as the Messenger, Abu Bakr, and ʿUmar.

positions.position: ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Zayd says they are the Messenger and his household.
positions.reasons: BAGHAWI reporting عبد الرحمن بن زيد: ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Zayd says they are the Messenger and his household.

positions.position: Shahr ibn Hawshab says they are the Prophet's Companions and his household.
positions.reasons: BAGHAWI reporting شهر بن حوشب: Shahr ibn Hawshab says they are the Prophet's Companions and his household.

positions.position: In the same report, Ibn Abbas says the basmala was reserved for this community and not disclosed to anyone before it.; cited verses: 15:87
positions.reasons: BAGHAWI-FULL reporting ابن عباس: In the same report, Ibn Abbas says the basmala was reserved for this community and not disclosed to anyone before it. | mentions 15:87

positions.position: Ibn Abbas identifies them as the people of Moses and Jesus before they changed their religion.
positions.reasons: BAGHAWI-FULL reporting ابن عباس: Ibn Abbas identifies them as the people of Moses and Jesus before they changed their religion.

positions.position: Abd al-Rahman b. Zayd says they are the Prophet and those with him.
positions.reasons: BAGHAWI-FULL reporting عبد الرحمن ابن زيد: Abd al-Rahman b. Zayd says they are the Prophet and those with him.

positions.position: Abu al-Aliya identifies them as the Prophet’s family, Abu Bakr, and Umar.
positions.reasons: BAGHAWI-FULL reporting أبو العالية: Abu al-Aliya identifies them as the Prophet’s family, Abu Bakr, and Umar.

positions.position: Shahr b. Hawshab says they are the Prophet’s Companions and household.
positions.reasons: BAGHAWI-FULL reporting شهر بن حوشب: Shahr b. Hawshab says they are the Prophet’s Companions and household.

positions.position: The readers differ on hāʾ and plural-mīm vowels before a hamzat al-waṣl: Warsh lengthens at hamzat al-qaṭʿ, while Hamza, al-Kisaʾi, Abu Amr, and Yaʿqub follow the stated preceding-vowel conditions.
positions.reasons: BAGHAWI-FULL reporting ورش وحمزة والكسائي وأبو عمرو ويعقوب: The readers differ on hāʾ and plural-mīm vowels before a hamzat al-waṣl: Warsh lengthens at hamzat al-qaṭʿ, while Hamza, al-Kisaʾi, Abu Amr, and Yaʿqub follow the stated preceding-vowel conditions.

positions.position: Umar’s reading says ‘the path of those You favored, not those under wrath, and not the straying ones.’
positions.reasons: BAGHAWI-FULL reporting عمر بن الخطاب: Umar’s reading says ‘the path of those You favored, not those under wrath, and not the straying ones.’

positions.position: Ayyub reads with hamza; Amr ibn Ubayd also uses a hamza form.
positions.reasons: KASHSHAF reporting أيوب السختياني: Ayyub reads with hamza; Amr ibn Ubayd also uses a hamza form.

positions.position: The hamza dialect avoids meeting two quiescent consonants, as in Abu Zayd's shaʾba and daʾba.
positions.reasons: KASHSHAF reporting أبو زيد: The hamza dialect avoids meeting two quiescent consonants, as in Abu Zayd's shaʾba and daʾba.

positions.position: The apposition reinforces and explains the straight path as the Muslims' path, certifying its uprightness emphatically.
positions.reasons: KASHSHAF: The apposition reinforces and explains the straight path as the Muslims' path, certifying its uprightness emphatically.

positions.position: Silent recitation is reported from the Prophet by Abdullah ibn Mughaffal and Anas.
positions.reasons: KASHSHAF reporting عبد الله بن مغفل وأنس والنبي: Silent recitation is reported from the Prophet by Abdullah ibn Mughaffal and Anas.

positions.position: Hudhayfa reports that when a child recites al-Fatiha amid certain punishment, God hears and lifts it for forty years.
positions.reasons: KASHSHAF reporting حذيفة بن اليمان والنبي: Hudhayfa reports that when a child recites al-Fatiha amid certain punishment, God hears and lifts it for forty years.

positions.position: Ibn Abbas identifies them as Moses's companions before they changed.
positions.reasons: KASHSHAF reporting ابن عباس: Ibn Abbas identifies them as Moses's companions before they changed.

positions.position: Another view identifies them as the prophets.
positions.reasons: KASHSHAF reporting قيل: Another view identifies them as the prophets.

positions.position: The phrase is an explanatory substitute for the straight path and virtually repeats the verb, emphasizing and identifying the straight way with the Muslims' way.; cited verses: 7:75
positions.reasons: KASHSHAF-FULL: The phrase is an explanatory substitute for the straight path and virtually repeats the verb, emphasizing and identifying the straight way with the Muslims' way. | mentions 7:75

positions.position: The repeated, first-general-then-specific description makes the believers a clear, emphatic example of those who possess the praised qualities.
positions.reasons: KASHSHAF-FULL: The repeated, first-general-then-specific description makes the believers a clear, emphatic example of those who possess the praised qualities.

positions.position: The first عليهم is parsed as an object and the second as a subject.
positions.reasons: KASHSHAF-FULL: The first عليهم is parsed as an object and the second as a subject.

positions.position: Hudhayfa reports that God lifts an imminent calamity from a people for forty years after a child recites al-Fatiha and God hears it.
positions.reasons: KASHSHAF-FULL reporting حذيفة بن اليمان: Hudhayfa reports that God lifts an imminent calamity from a people for forty years after a child recites al-Fatiha and God hears it.

positions.position: A group of commentators takes them to be the believers among the Children of Israel, appealing to the command to remember God’s favor on Israel.; cited verses: 2:40, 2:47, 2:122
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA reporting فرقة من المفسرين: A group of commentators takes them to be the believers among the Children of Israel, appealing to the command to remember God’s favor on Israel. | mentions 2:40, 2:47, 2:122

positions.position: Ibn ʿAbbās also identifies them as Moses’ people before they changed their way; the author says this is the same as the preceding Israelite interpretation.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA reporting ابن عباس: Ibn ʿAbbās also identifies them as Moses’ people before they changed their way; the author says this is the same as the preceding Israelite interpretation.

positions.position: Qatāda restricts the favored people to the prophets.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA reporting قتادة بن دعامة: Qatāda restricts the favored people to the prophets.

positions.position: The author says Abū al-ʿĀliya’s identification makes the straight path the way of Muḥammad, Abū Bakr, and ʿUmar; this is stronger because calling the persons themselves a path is figurative.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA: The author says Abū al-ʿĀliya’s identification makes the straight path the way of Muḥammad, Abū Bakr, and ʿUmar; this is stronger because calling the persons themselves a path is figurative.

positions.position: Ḥamza reads the pronoun with ḍamma on hāʾ and a quiescent mīm; the other readers use kasra on hāʾ and differ over mīm.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA reporting حمزة: Ḥamza reads the pronoun with ḍamma on hāʾ and a quiescent mīm; the other readers use kasra on hāʾ and differ over mīm.

positions.position: The remaining readers pronounce hāʾ with kasra, while differing over the mīm.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA reporting الباقون: The remaining readers pronounce hāʾ with kasra, while differing over the mīm.

positions.position: Reports give Nāfiʿ a choice between mīm with ḍamma and sukūn; since he did not object to ḍamma, the author infers his own reading used sukūn.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA reporting نافع: Reports give Nāfiʿ a choice between mīm with ḍamma and sukūn; since he did not object to ḍamma, the author infers his own reading used sukūn.

positions.position: Ibn Kathīr links the mīm with a wāw when it is pronounced with ḍamma, whether the preceding hāʾ has ḍamma or kasra.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA reporting عبد الله بن كثير: Ibn Kathīr links the mīm with a wāw when it is pronounced with ḍamma, whether the preceding hāʾ has ḍamma or kasra.

positions.position: Warsh uses kasra on hāʾ and pauses on mīm, but supplies a pronounced wāw when an original alif follows the mīm.; cited verses: 2:6
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA reporting ورش: Warsh uses kasra on hāʾ and pauses on mīm, but supplies a pronounced wāw when an original alif follows the mīm. | mentions 2:6

positions.position: Abū ʿAmr, ʿĀṣim, Ibn ʿĀmir, and al-Kisāʾī use kasra on hāʾ and sukūn on mīm in the basic form.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA reporting أبو عمرو وعاصم وابن عامر والكسائي: Abū ʿAmr, ʿĀṣim, Ibn ʿĀmir, and al-Kisāʾī use kasra on hāʾ and sukūn on mīm in the basic form.

positions.position: Before a following consonant, ʿĀṣim, Ibn Kathīr, and Nāfiʿ retain kasra on hāʾ but put ḍamma on mīm.; cited verses: 2:61, 3:112
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA reporting عاصم وابن كثير ونافع: Before a following consonant, ʿĀṣim, Ibn Kathīr, and Nāfiʿ retain kasra on hāʾ but put ḍamma on mīm. | mentions 2:61, 3:112

positions.position: Before a following consonant, Abū ʿAmr uses kasra on both hāʾ and mīm.; cited verses: 2:61, 3:112, 36:14
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA reporting أبو عمرو: Before a following consonant, Abū ʿAmr uses kasra on both hāʾ and mīm. | mentions 2:61, 3:112, 36:14

positions.position: Before a following consonant, al-Kisāʾī uses ḍamma on both hāʾ and mīm.; cited verses: 2:61, 3:112, 28:23
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA reporting الكسائي: Before a following consonant, al-Kisāʾī uses ḍamma on both hāʾ and mīm. | mentions 2:61, 3:112, 28:23

positions.position: He says hāʾ varies between kasra and ḍamma only when preceded by kasra or a quiescent yāʾ; otherwise hāʾ is ḍamma.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA reporting أبو بكر أحمد بن موسى: He says hāʾ varies between kasra and ḍamma only when preceded by kasra or a quiescent yāʾ; otherwise hāʾ is ḍamma.

positions.position: When no hāʾ preceded by kasra or quiescent yāʾ comes before mīm, he allows only mīm with ḍamma or sukūn, as in منكم and أنتم.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA reporting أبو بكر أحمد بن موسى: When no hāʾ preceded by kasra or quiescent yāʾ comes before mīm, he allows only mīm with ḍamma or sukūn, as in منكم and أنتم.

positions.position: He catalogs forms with a wāw after mīm, without the wāw, with mīm ḍamma, and with kasra and yāʾ, reflecting several combinations of vowels.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA reporting صاحب الدلائل: He catalogs forms with a wāw after mīm, without the wāw, with mīm ḍamma, and with kasra and yāʾ, reflecting several combinations of vowels.

positions.position: Ibn Jinnī transmits from Aḥmad ibn Mūsā forms with an extended wāw, unextended ḍamma, and mīm sukūn; Ḥasan and ʿAmr ibn Fāʾid also read with an extended yāʾ.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA reporting ابن جني: Ibn Jinnī transmits from Aḥmad ibn Mūsā forms with an extended wāw, unextended ḍamma, and mīm sukūn; Ḥasan and ʿAmr ibn Fāʾid also read with an extended yāʾ.

positions.position: Additional transmitted forms include kasra on mīm without yāʾ-lengthening and al-Aʿraj’s kasra on hāʾ with ḍamma on mīm without lengthening.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA reporting الحسن وعمرو بن فائد والأعرج: Additional transmitted forms include kasra on mīm without yāʾ-lengthening and al-Aʿraj’s kasra on hāʾ with ḍamma on mīm without lengthening.

positions.position: The combinations amount to ten forms: five with hāʾ ḍamma and five with hāʾ kasra, though only six are transmitted from canonical readers.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA: The combinations amount to ten forms: five with hāʾ ḍamma and five with hāʾ kasra, though only six are transmitted from canonical readers.

positions.position: The author calls the genitive reading the clear choice, noting it is the reading of the majority and is also reported from Ibn Kathīr.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA: The author calls the genitive reading the clear choice, noting it is the reading of the majority and is also reported from Ibn Kathīr.

positions.position: الذي is an indefinite, deficient relative noun requiring a clause and a resumptive pronoun; its singular is indeclinable, while its dual forms decline.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA: الذي is an indefinite, deficient relative noun requiring a clause and a resumptive pronoun; its singular is indeclinable, while its dual forms decline.

positions.position: Al-Ṭabarī also cites ما منعك أن لا تسجد and a poem after an earlier negation, where lā may be omitted because the opening negation governs the later clause.; cited verses: 7:12
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA reporting الطبري: Al-Ṭabarī also cites ما منعك أن لا تسجد and a poem after an earlier negation, where lā may be omitted because the opening negation governs the later clause. | mentions 7:12

positions.position: Some Arabs inflect the plural relative, using اللذون in the nominative.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA: Some Arabs inflect the plural relative, using اللذون in the nominative.

positions.position: Ayyūb al-Sakhtiyānī reads الضألين with a short hamza to avoid two adjacent sukūns, treating it as a dialect form.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA reporting أيوب السختياني: Ayyūb al-Sakhtiyānī reads الضألين with a short hamza to avoid two adjacent sukūns, treating it as a dialect form.

positions.position: The form الذي is conventionally written with one lām in singular and plural because it is so frequent.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA: The form الذي is conventionally written with one lām in singular and plural because it is so frequent.

positions.position: Some Arabs shorten it to أمين, as in a line attributed to Jubayr ibn al-Aḍbaṭ.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA reporting جبير بن الأضبط: Some Arabs shorten it to أمين, as in a line attributed to Jubayr ibn al-Aḍbaṭ.

positions.position: A second unnamed explanation takes it to mean sincerity of intention.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA: A second unnamed explanation takes it to mean sincerity of intention.

positions.position: A third unnamed explanation takes it to mean agreement in timing.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA: A third unnamed explanation takes it to mean agreement in timing.

positions.position: The author prefers agreement in timing together with sincere intention and wholehearted turning to God; the response follows from this state.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA: The author prefers agreement in timing together with sincere intention and wholehearted turning to God; the response follows from this state.

positions.position: He concludes that a person in this state is upon the straight path.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA: He concludes that a person in this state is upon the straight path.

positions.position: Ibn ʿAbbās also glosses the favored people simply as the believers.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA reporting ابن عباس: Ibn ʿAbbās also glosses the favored people simply as the believers.

positions.position: Nafiʿ is reported with a choice of ḍamma on the hāʾ and a silent mīm; the author infers that his customary reading was with mīm silent.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA-FULL reporting نافع: Nafiʿ is reported with a choice of ḍamma on the hāʾ and a silent mīm; the author infers that his customary reading was with mīm silent.

positions.position: Ibn Jinni reports readings with and without a lengthened wāw and with mīm silent.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA-FULL reporting ابن جني: Ibn Jinni reports readings with and without a lengthened wāw and with mīm silent.

positions.position: Al-Aʿraj reads the hāʾ and yāʾ with kasra and mīm with ḍamma, without lengthening the yāʾ.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA-FULL reporting الأعرج: Al-Aʿraj reads the hāʾ and yāʾ with kasra and mīm with ḍamma, without lengthening the yāʾ.

positions.position: Ibn Kathir joins a ḍamma-bearing mīm to a wāw after the hāʾ, whether that hāʾ is pronounced with ḍamma or kasra.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA-FULL reporting ابن كثير: Ibn Kathir joins a ḍamma-bearing mīm to a wāw after the hāʾ, whether that hāʾ is pronounced with ḍamma or kasra.

positions.position: Warsh reads hāʾ with kasra and leaves the mīm unvocalized, except when it precedes an original alif, when he inserts a wāw in pronunciation.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA-FULL reporting ورش: Warsh reads hāʾ with kasra and leaves the mīm unvocalized, except when it precedes an original alif, when he inserts a wāw in pronunciation.

positions.position: Abu ʿAmr, ʿAsim, Ibn ʿAmir, and al-Kisaʾi read the hāʾ with kasra and the mīm silent; before a following consonant, their treatment of hāʾ and mīm vowels differs.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA-FULL reporting أبو عمرو وعاصم وابن عامر والكسائي: Abu ʿAmr, ʿAsim, Ibn ʿAmir, and al-Kisaʾi read the hāʾ with kasra and the mīm silent; before a following consonant, their treatment of hāʾ and mīm vowels differs.

positions.position: Abu ʿAmr keeps both hāʾ and mīm with kasra in the same environment.; cited verses: 36:14
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA-FULL reporting أبو عمرو: Abu ʿAmr keeps both hāʾ and mīm with kasra in the same environment. | mentions 36:14

positions.position: Al-Kisaʾi gives both hāʾ and mīm ḍamma in the same environment.; cited verses: 2:61, 28:23
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA-FULL reporting الكسائي: Al-Kisaʾi gives both hāʾ and mīm ḍamma in the same environment. | mentions 2:61, 28:23

positions.position: Abu Bakr Ahmad ibn Musa says variation in hāʾ depends on whether it follows kasra or a quiescent yāʾ; elsewhere only ḍamma occurs, while mīm may be silent or have ḍamma in the stated contexts.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA-FULL reporting أبو بكر أحمد بن موسى: Abu Bakr Ahmad ibn Musa says variation in hāʾ depends on whether it follows kasra or a quiescent yāʾ; elsewhere only ḍamma occurs, while mīm may be silent or have ḍamma in the stated contexts.

positions.position: The Dalāʾil source lists five transmitted combinations of hāʾ and mīm vowels, with or without a lengthened wāw or yāʾ.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA-FULL reporting صاحب الدلائل: The Dalāʾil source lists five transmitted combinations of hāʾ and mīm vowels, with or without a lengthened wāw or yāʾ.

positions.position: Qatada ibn Diʿama restricts the favored to prophets.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA-FULL reporting قتادة بن دعامة: Qatada ibn Diʿama restricts the favored to prophets.

positions.position: Taken together, the source counts ten readings of the hāʾ-and-mīm sequence, in forms with ḍamma or kasra and differing ways of joining the vowel.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA-FULL: Taken together, the source counts ten readings of the hāʾ-and-mīm sequence, in forms with ḍamma or kasra and differing ways of joining the vowel.

positions.position: Al-Tabari calls la redundant, parallel to a rajaz line and a verse by al-Ahwas.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA-FULL reporting الطبري: Al-Tabari calls la redundant, parallel to a rajaz line and a verse by al-Ahwas.

positions.position: Reports explain the Prophet's promise about matching the angels as agreement in response, sincerity, or timing; Ibn Atiyya prefers matching the time with sincere, attentive supplication, after which the response follows.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA-FULL: Reports explain the Prophet's promise about matching the angels as agreement in response, sincerity, or timing; Ibn Atiyya prefers matching the time with sincere, attentive supplication, after which the response follows.

positions.position: Sibawayh explains kasra on hā after yā or kasra as phonetic lightening and likens it to imāla; a following silent wāw changes to yā after kasra.
positions.reasons: TABRISI reporting سيبويه: Sibawayh explains kasra on hā after yā or kasra as phonetic lightening and likens it to imāla; a following silent wāw changes to yā after kasra.

positions.position: Other interpreters take both descriptions as applying to all unbelievers, with the two attributes conveying different benefits.
positions.reasons: TABRISI: Other interpreters take both descriptions as applying to all unbelievers, with the two attributes conveying different benefits.

positions.position: Al-ḥamdu lillahi rabb al-alamin is described as the utterance of Paradise's people when they thank God for their good reward.
positions.reasons: TABRISI: Al-ḥamdu lillahi rabb al-alamin is described as the utterance of Paradise's people when they thank God for their good reward.

positions.position: Universal grace and provision lead to the name Rahman; despite people's shortcomings, God forgives, delays punishment, and does not withdraw His blessings, so He is Rahim.
positions.reasons: TABRISI: Universal grace and provision lead to the name Rahman; despite people's shortcomings, God forgives, delays punishment, and does not withdraw His blessings, so He is Rahim.

positions.position: Because people oppress one another, the worshiper acknowledges a future day when the wronged receive justice from the wrongdoer and says Malik yawm al-din.
positions.reasons: TABRISI: Because people oppress one another, the worshiper acknowledges a future day when the wronged receive justice from the wrongdoer and says Malik yawm al-din.

positions.position: Knowing God as Creator, provider, and merciful giver establishes that He alone is worthy of worship; the speaker shifts to direct address as if seeing a king face-to-face.
positions.reasons: TABRISI: Knowing God as Creator, provider, and merciful giver establishes that He alone is worthy of worship; the speaker shifts to direct address as if seeing a king face-to-face.

positions.position: Conflicting desires, doubts, and opinions leave no helper but God, so the worshiper requests assistance for obedience with all its causes.
positions.reasons: TABRISI: Conflicting desires, doubts, and opinions leave no helper but God, so the worshiper requests assistance for obedience with all its causes.

positions.position: Gabriel says that whenever a Muslim says 'Lord of the Worlds', God and the inhabitants of heaven affirm him.
positions.reasons: TABRISI reporting جبرائيل: Gabriel says that whenever a Muslim says 'Lord of the Worlds', God and the inhabitants of heaven affirm him.

positions.position: Iyyaka naʿbudu expresses pure worship, iyyaka nastaʿīn is the best way to seek needs, and the straight path is the path of the prophets.
positions.reasons: TABRISI: Iyyaka naʿbudu expresses pure worship, iyyaka nastaʿīn is the best way to seek needs, and the straight path is the path of the prophets.

positions.position: Al-Halabi reports that al-Sadiq read Malik yawm al-din and ihdina ṣirāṭ al-mustaqīm; another narration interprets the latter as referring to Ali, the Commander of the Faithful.
positions.reasons: TABRISI reporting أبو عبد الله: Al-Halabi reports that al-Sadiq read Malik yawm al-din and ihdina ṣirāṭ al-mustaqīm; another narration interprets the latter as referring to Ali, the Commander of the Faithful.

positions.position: Jamil reports al-Sadiq's instruction that a follower behind an imam should say al-hamdu lillahi rabb al-alamin when the imam finishes al-Fatiha.
positions.reasons: TABRISI reporting أبو عبد الله: Jamil reports al-Sadiq's instruction that a follower behind an imam should say al-hamdu lillahi rabb al-alamin when the imam finishes al-Fatiha.

positions.position: Fudayl ibn Yasar reports al-Sadiq's instruction to say al-hamdu lillahi rabb al-alamin after finishing al-Fatiha.
positions.reasons: TABRISI reporting أبو عبد الله: Fudayl ibn Yasar reports al-Sadiq's instruction to say al-hamdu lillahi rabb al-alamin after finishing al-Fatiha.

positions.position: The sura's sequence begins with recognition of God's visible favors, so the worshiper starts with the basmala as invocation and acknowledgment of the benefactor's divinity and mercy.
positions.reasons: TABRISI: The sura's sequence begins with recognition of God's visible favors, so the worshiper starts with the basmala as invocation and acknowledgment of the benefactor's divinity and mercy.

positions.position: Recognition of God's favors to oneself and others leads to praise and recognition that He is Lord of all creatures.
positions.reasons: TABRISI: Recognition of God's favors to oneself and others leads to praise and recognition that He is Lord of all creatures.

positions.position: The worshiper asks to join God's chosen beneficiaries and be protected from those who oppose truth, blind themselves to guidance, or doubt clear proofs and stray from the right way.
positions.reasons: TABRISI: The worshiper asks to join God's chosen beneficiaries and be protected from those who oppose truth, blind themselves to guidance, or doubt clear proofs and stray from the right way.

positions.position: Other transmitted forms vary the hā and mīm, add or omit a linking wāw, or connect it only before a following consonant; the regions and readers differ in these choices.
positions.reasons: TABRISI: Other transmitted forms vary the hā and mīm, add or omit a linking wāw, or connect it only before a following consonant; the regions and readers differ in these choices.

positions.position: They read the phrase as 'the path of those on whom You bestowed favor'; this form is also reported from the Prophet's household.
positions.reasons: TABRISI reporting عمر بن الخطاب وعمرو بن عبد الله الزبيري: They read the phrase as 'the path of those on whom You bestowed favor'; this form is also reported from the Prophet's household.

positions.position: Hamza singles out these forms because their preceding yā was historically an alif, which does not permit a kasra on the hā.
positions.reasons: TABRISI: Hamza singles out these forms because their preceding yā was historically an alif, which does not permit a kasra on the hā.

positions.position: Some reciters connect the hā's ḍamma to a wāw, while forms without wāw lighten the ending; other variants assimilate or preserve vowels according to ease and the preceding yā.
positions.reasons: TABRISI: Some reciters connect the hā's ḍamma to a wāw, while forms without wāw lighten the ending; other variants assimilate or preserve vowels according to ease and the preceding yā.

positions.position: Lexically, ni'ma is what gives a person enjoyment in life.
positions.reasons: IBNJAWZI-NUZHA: Lexically, ni'ma is what gives a person enjoyment in life.

positions.position: A sixth sense is mercy, as in the phrase 'bounty from God and favor.'; cited verses: 49:8
positions.reasons: IBNJAWZI-NUZHA reporting بعض المفسرين: A sixth sense is mercy, as in the phrase 'bounty from God and favor.' | mentions 49:8

positions.position: A seventh sense is beneficence, as in the statement that no one has a favor owed to be repaid.; cited verses: 92:19
