positions.position: A ninth sense is Islam, in God's favor upon Zayd in the al-Ahzab passage.; cited verses: 33:37
positions.reasons: IBNJAWZI-NUZHA reporting بعض المفسرين: A ninth sense is Islam, in God's favor upon Zayd in the al-Ahzab passage. | mentions 33:37

positions.position: A tenth sense is emancipation: God's favor to Zayd was Islam, while the Prophet's favor was freeing Zayd ibn Haritha.; cited verses: 33:37
positions.reasons: IBNJAWZI-NUZHA reporting بعض المفسرين: A tenth sense is emancipation: God's favor to Zayd was Islam, while the Prophet's favor was freeing Zayd ibn Haritha. | mentions 33:37

positions.position: The noun can mean a favor or gracious benefaction, and can also mean wealth; al-na'ama is a gentle wind.
positions.reasons: IBNJAWZI-NUZHA: The noun can mean a favor or gracious benefaction, and can also mean wealth; al-na'ama is a gentle wind.

positions.position: With an open initial n, ni'ma denotes luxurious living; a mutana'im is one living in luxury, and to favor one's children is to make them live luxuriously.
positions.reasons: IBNJAWZI-NUZHA: With an open initial n, ni'ma denotes luxurious living; a mutana'im is one living in luxury, and to favor one's children is to make them live luxuriously.

positions.position: The entry also distinguishes the verb نعم as 'yes' (opposed to لا), with a variant vowel, and as the opposite of بئس.
positions.reasons: IBNJAWZI-NUZHA: The entry also distinguishes the verb نعم as 'yes' (opposed to لا), with a variant vowel, and as the opposite of بئس.

positions.position: The first Qur'anic sense is gracious favor, illustrated by the command to remember God's favor and its parallel in al-Ahzab.; cited verses: 5:11, 33:9
positions.reasons: IBNJAWZI-NUZHA reporting بعض المفسرين: The first Qur'anic sense is gracious favor, illustrated by the command to remember God's favor and its parallel in al-Ahzab. | mentions 5:11, 33:9

positions.position: A second sense is religion and Scripture, as in warnings against exchanging God's favor after it came.; cited verses: 2:211, 14:28
positions.reasons: IBNJAWZI-NUZHA reporting بعض المفسرين: A second sense is religion and Scripture, as in warnings against exchanging God's favor after it came. | mentions 2:211, 14:28

positions.position: A third sense is Muhammad, whom people recognize as God's favor and then deny.; cited verses: 16:83
positions.reasons: IBNJAWZI-NUZHA reporting بعض المفسرين: A third sense is Muhammad, whom people recognize as God's favor and then deny. | mentions 16:83

positions.position: A fourth sense is reward, as believers rejoice in a favor from God and bounty.; cited verses: 3:171
positions.reasons: IBNJAWZI-NUZHA reporting بعض المفسرين: A fourth sense is reward, as believers rejoice in a favor from God and bounty. | mentions 3:171

positions.position: Ḥamza reads those pronouns with ḍamma on hāʾ; Ibn Kathīr joins the ḍamma of mīm with a following wāw.
positions.reasons: IBNJAWZI-ZAD reporting حمزة: Ḥamza reads those pronouns with ḍamma on hāʾ; Ibn Kathīr joins the ḍamma of mīm with a following wāw.

positions.position: Abū Ḥanīfa says al-Fātiḥa is not specifically required, a position also reported from Aḥmad.
positions.reasons: IBNJAWZI-ZAD reporting أبو حنيفة ورواية عن أحمد: Abū Ḥanīfa says al-Fātiḥa is not specifically required, a position also reported from Aḥmad.

positions.position: Razi sketches the sūra’s sequence: seek refuge from sins, begin good works in God’s name, praise and recognize his lordship and mercy, heed judgment, worship and seek help, ask guidance, and avoid ignorance and error.
positions.reasons: RAZI: Razi sketches the sūra’s sequence: seek refuge from sins, begin good works in God’s name, praise and recognize his lordship and mercy, heed judgment, worship and seek help, ask guidance, and avoid ignorance and error.

positions.position: Razi presents the path of those favored by God as a station of extraordinary rank, whose beginnings become visible through the preceding exposition.
positions.reasons: RAZI: Razi presents the path of those favored by God as a station of extraordinary rank, whose beginnings become visible through the preceding exposition.

positions.position: Razi supplements Ibn Jinnī with all six permutations of ل غ و and suggests their shared sense is deep engagement or immersion in something.; cited verses: 37:47
positions.reasons: RAZI: Razi supplements Ibn Jinnī with all six permutations of ل غ و and suggests their shared sense is deep engagement or immersion in something. | mentions 37:47

positions.position: Razi says the disagreement applies to إن كلمتك فأنت طالق; with إن تكلمت بكلمة, إن نطقت, إن تلفظت بلفظة, or إن قلت قولا, Zufar's view should prevail unanimously.
positions.reasons: RAZI: Razi says the disagreement applies to إن كلمتك فأنت طالق; with إن تكلمت بكلمة, إن نطقت, إن تلفظت بلفظة, or إن قلت قولا, Zufar's view should prevail unanimously.

positions.position: Used expressions divide into a simple form, a compound whose parts signify only in another analysis, and a composed expression whose parts signify independently in every analysis.
positions.reasons: RAZI: Used expressions divide into a simple form, a compound whose parts signify only in another analysis, and a composed expression whose parts signify independently in every analysis.

positions.position: At the furthest epistemological stage, he asks how the unknown can be judged contrary to the known if its nature is unknown, since that judgment would make it known.
positions.reasons: RAZI: At the furthest epistemological stage, he asks how the unknown can be judged contrary to the known if its nature is unknown, since that judgment would make it known.

positions.position: Not every essence can receive a name, because essences are unlimited and an unapprehended item cannot be individually conceived for naming.
positions.reasons: RAZI: Not every essence can receive a name, because essences are unlimited and an unapprehended item cannot be individually conceived for naming.

positions.position: A second method counts every proof, objection, reply, and separately stated linguistic alternative as its own question, multiplying the issues extracted from a short passage.
positions.reasons: RAZI: A second method counts every proof, objection, reply, and separately stated linguistic alternative as its own question, multiplying the issues extracted from a short passage.

positions.position: A speaker's mental judgment can differ from belief: someone may say the world is eternal while believing it is not, showing the two are distinct.
positions.reasons: RAZI: A speaker's mental judgment can differ from belief: someone may say the world is eternal while believing it is not, showing the two are distinct.

positions.position: Some say specifying the path of the favored shows that a seeker needs a guiding shaykh, since most people lack sound judgment and need a perfected guide's intellect.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL reporting بعضهم: Some say specifying the path of the favored shows that a seeker needs a guiding shaykh, since most people lack sound judgment and need a perfected guide's intellect.

positions.position: Razi says the surah sets out the covenants of lordship and servitude together, as in God's promise to fulfill each side of His covenant.; cited verses: 2:40
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: Razi says the surah sets out the covenants of lordship and servitude together, as in God's promise to fulfill each side of His covenant. | mentions 2:40

positions.position: The law, path, and reality complete human ascent: worship, reliance on God, and guidance culminate in fellowship with the pure and distance from the wretched.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: The law, path, and reality complete human ascent: worship, reliance on God, and guidance culminate in fellowship with the pure and distance from the wretched.

positions.position: Worldly benefits are negligible beside everlasting afterlife punishment, as a small sweetness is not counted a benefit when mixed with much poison.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: Worldly benefits are negligible beside everlasting afterlife punishment, as a small sweetness is not counted a benefit when mixed with much poison.

positions.position: The opposing evidence includes the command that all people worship their creator, who prepared the earth and sky for them, presenting these as universal blessings.; cited verses: 2:21, 2:22
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL reporting المعتزلة: The opposing evidence includes the command that all people worship their creator, who prepared the earth and sky for them, presenting these as universal blessings. | mentions 2:21, 2:22

positions.position: Another definition adds that the benefit must be good, since only a good act merits gratitude.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL reporting بعضهم: Another definition adds that the benefit must be good, since only a good act merits gratitude.

positions.position: The giver must intend kindness to the recipient; an apparent benefit pursued for the giver's own profit is not a blessing.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: The giver must intend kindness to the recipient; an apparent benefit pursued for the giver's own profit is not a blessing.

positions.position: Some blessings appear to come through another person, but God creates the gift, recipient, and benefactor's impulse; the human instrument is thanked while God is the true benefactor.; cited verses: 31:14
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: Some blessings appear to come through another person, but God creates the gift, recipient, and benefactor's impulse; the human instrument is thanked while God is the true benefactor. | mentions 31:14

positions.position: Life is God's first blessing: nothing can be enjoyed without life, and the Qur'an mentions bringing people to life before worldly provisions.; cited verses: 2:28, 2:29
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: Life is God's first blessing: nothing can be enjoyed without life, and the Qur'an mentions bringing people to life before worldly provisions. | mentions 2:28, 2:29

positions.position: Razi therefore identifies the favor in the verse specifically as faith.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: Razi therefore identifies the favor in the verse specifically as faith.

positions.position: A believer cannot remain eternally in Hell, since the verse praises this gift as a great favor; a favor with no effect on endless punishment would be insignificant.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: A believer cannot remain eternally in Hell, since the verse praises this gift as a great favor; a favor with no effect on endless punishment would be insignificant.

positions.position: If that knowledge is new, God would be subject to temporal events and its creation would require a prior knowledge indefinitely; Razi answers that God does what He wills.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: If that knowledge is new, God would be subject to temporal events and its creation would require a prior knowledge indefinitely; Razi answers that God does what He wills.

positions.position: The surah begins by praising God and ends by censuring those who reject faith and obedience, showing that turning to God brings good while turning away brings affliction.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: The surah begins by praising God and ends by censuring those who reject faith and obedience, showing that turning to God brings good while turning away brings affliction.

positions.position: This world is obscure and the afterlife pure: worldly realities need an afterlife original, while afterlife realities need a worldly example, or they would be empty illusion or unsupported claim.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: This world is obscure and the afterlife pure: worldly realities need an afterlife original, while afterlife realities need a worldly example, or they would be empty illusion or unsupported claim.

positions.position: Knowing God turns one away from caprice, treated as a rival deity; a saying to Moses urges resisting desire because it contests God's sovereignty.; cited verses: 45:23
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: Knowing God turns one away from caprice, treated as a rival deity; a saying to Moses urges resisting desire because it contests God's sovereignty. | mentions 45:23

positions.position: Knowing God as the Merciful removes anger, which arises from seeking rule; sovereignty belongs to the Merciful.; cited verses: 25:26
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: Knowing God as the Merciful removes anger, which arises from seeking rule; sovereignty belongs to the Merciful. | mentions 25:26

positions.position: Knowing God as Merciful calls a person to imitate mercy and so avoid self-wrong and animalistic behavior.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: Knowing God as Merciful calls a person to imitate mercy and so avoid self-wrong and animalistic behavior.

positions.position: Desire produces greed and stinginess, anger produces vanity and pride, and caprice produces unbelief and innovation; their combination produces envy, the worst human trait.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: Desire produces greed and stinginess, anger produces vanity and pride, and caprice produces unbelief and innovation; their combination produces envy, the worst human trait.

positions.position: Human knowledge grows through one's own reasoning or through receiving predecessors' discoveries: “guide us” asks for the first, and the path of the favored for the second.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: Human knowledge grows through one's own reasoning or through receiving predecessors' discoveries: “guide us” asks for the first, and the path of the favored for the second.

positions.position: A prophetic report says God has seventy veils of light; if unveiled, the splendor of His face would burn everything perceived by sight, and only prophetic light reveals the number.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL reporting النبي: A prophetic report says God has seventy veils of light; if unveiled, the splendor of His face would burn everything perceived by sight, and only prophetic light reveals the number.

positions.position: Raising the hands signals leaving both worlds and directing all inner faculties toward God; “God is greatest” means He exceeds all beings, knowledge, comparison, and even the claim that He is simply greater.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: Raising the hands signals leaving both worlds and directing all inner faculties toward God; “God is greatest” means He exceeds all beings, knowledge, comparison, and even the claim that He is simply greater.

positions.position: “Exalted is Your majesty” signifies that God's knowledge and greatness exceed every stated measure.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: “Exalted is Your majesty” signifies that God's knowledge and greatness exceed every stated measure.

positions.position: “There is no god but You” means every attribute of majesty and perfection belongs only to God; ultimately reason, speech, understanding, and imagination fail before Him.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: “There is no god but You” means every attribute of majesty and perfection belongs only to God; ultimately reason, speech, understanding, and imagination fail before Him.

positions.position: The names al-Rahman and al-Rahim signify the gates of hope, while Master of Judgment signifies fear.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: The names al-Rahman and al-Rahim signify the gates of hope, while Master of Judgment signifies fear.

positions.position: The declaration that God alone is worshipped and sought for help is the gate of sincerity, grounded in knowing servanthood and lordship.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: The declaration that God alone is worshipped and sought for help is the gate of sincerity, grounded in knowing servanthood and lordship.

positions.position: The request for the straight path is the gate of supplication and humble appeal, supported by Qur'anic calls to pray.; cited verses: 27:62, 40:60
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: The request for the straight path is the gate of supplication and humble appeal, supported by Qur'anic calls to pray. | mentions 27:62, 40:60

positions.position: This greeting anticipates the angels entering upon the believer in paradise from every gate and welcoming their patient arrival.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: This greeting anticipates the angels entering upon the believer in paradise from every gate and welcoming their patient arrival.

positions.position: Space and time are the most imposing created realities: space is boundless expanse, while time is an imagined span from eternity past to eternity future.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: Space and time are the most imposing created realities: space is boundless expanse, while time is an imagined span from eternity past to eternity future.

positions.position: First and last describe time, and manifest and hidden describe space; God encompasses both dimensions and is therefore beyond space and time.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: First and last describe time, and manifest and hidden describe space; God encompasses both dimensions and is therefore beyond space and time.

positions.position: The Throne is associated with time and the Kursi with space; there is no space beyond the Kursi or time beyond the Throne.; cited verses: 2:255, 11:7, 9:129
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: The Throne is associated with time and the Kursi with space; there is no space beyond the Kursi or time beyond the Throne. | mentions 2:255, 11:7, 9:129

positions.position: Divine highness and greatness are levels of perfection, with greatness above highness and majesty above both; the report makes grandeur God's garment and greatness His mantle.; cited verses: 2:255
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: Divine highness and greatness are levels of perfection, with greatness above highness and majesty above both; the report makes grandeur God's garment and greatness His mantle. | mentions 2:255

positions.position: Majesty is God's unique reality, beyond resemblance to any possible being, and the ground of His divinity.; cited verses: 55:27, 55:78
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: Majesty is God's unique reality, beyond resemblance to any possible being, and the ground of His divinity. | mentions 55:27, 55:78

positions.position: The degrees of purification are many and unequal, like the differing ranks of those oriented toward the primordial religion.; cited verses: 30:30
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: The degrees of purification are many and unequal, like the differing ranks of those oriented toward the primordial religion. | mentions 30:30

positions.position: The contemplation includes angels filling every handbreadth of the heavens, the Throne's attendants, and God's forces beyond the created world.; cited verses: 74:31
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: The contemplation includes angels filling every handbreadth of the heavens, the Throne's attendants, and God's forces beyond the created world. | mentions 74:31

positions.position: The first meaning of Allahu akbar is that God brought all things into existence and perfected their qualities, while remaining incomparable to them and beyond rational comparison.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: The first meaning of Allahu akbar is that God brought all things into existence and perfected their qualities, while remaining incomparable to them and beyond rational comparison.

positions.position: A third meaning is that God surpasses the reach of human intellect, imagination, and understanding; Ali defines divine unity as not imagining God.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: A third meaning is that God surpasses the reach of human intellect, imagination, and understanding; Ali defines divine unity as not imagining God.

positions.position: God's greatness, exaltedness, and majesty exceed all sensory images, imagined forms, and human descriptions.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: God's greatness, exaltedness, and majesty exceed all sensory images, imagined forms, and human descriptions.

positions.position: God is not great by bodily size, high by spatial direction, or great by duration: He transcends body, location, and time, while time itself is created.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: God is not great by bodily size, high by spatial direction, or great by duration: He transcends body, location, and time, while time itself is created.

positions.position: A prophetic supplication says thought cannot reach God's depth and no observer's gaze reaches Him; created descriptions fall beneath His majesty.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: A prophetic supplication says thought cannot reach God's depth and no observer's gaze reaches Him; created descriptions fall beneath His majesty.

positions.position: A report from the Prophet says Abraham asked the reward for praising God; God answered that praise begins and ends gratitude, and so begins revelation and ends the speech of paradise's people.; cited verses: 10:10
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: A report from the Prophet says Abraham asked the reward for praising God; God answered that praise begins and ends gratitude, and so begins revelation and ends the speech of paradise's people. | mentions 10:10

positions.position: Al-Rahman and al-Rahim name God's mercy; Muhammad and Ahmad likewise imply being shown mercy and being most merciful through their relation to praise.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: Al-Rahman and al-Rahim name God's mercy; Muhammad and Ahmad likewise imply being shown mercy and being most merciful through their relation to praise.

positions.position: Some reports add al-Hamd, al-Hamid, and al-Mahmud among the Prophet's names, making five names associated with mercy; paired with five divine mercy terms, they give the sinner ten oceans of mercy.; cited verses: 15:49, 21:107, 7:156
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: Some reports add al-Hamd, al-Hamid, and al-Mahmud among the Prophet's names, making five names associated with mercy; paired with five divine mercy terms, they give the sinner ten oceans of mercy. | mentions 15:49, 21:107, 7:156

positions.position: The five divine names in Fatiha correspond to five human acts: worship, seeking help, guidance, steadfastness, and asking for blessing.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: The five divine names in Fatiha correspond to five human acts: worship, seeking help, guidance, steadfastness, and asking for blessing.

positions.position: Fasting under the name al-Rahim evokes the poor person's hunger and loosens attachment to sensory pleasures, easing their departure at death.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: Fasting under the name al-Rahim evokes the poor person's hunger and loosens attachment to sensory pleasures, easing their departure at death.

positions.position: Pilgrimage corresponds to Master of Judgment because leaving home and family and traveling barefoot resembles the journey and condition of resurrection.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: Pilgrimage corresponds to Master of Judgment because leaving home and family and traveling barefoot resembles the journey and condition of resurrection.

positions.position: The five senses receive moral discipline from verses about reflection, listening well, wholesome food, Joseph's scent, and chastity; divine-name lights help repel their harms.; cited verses: 59:2, 39:18, 23:51, 12:94, 23:5
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: The five senses receive moral discipline from verses about reflection, listening well, wholesome food, Joseph's scent, and chastity; divine-name lights help repel their harms. | mentions 59:2, 39:18, 23:51, 12:94, 23:5

positions.position: The first half of Fatiha sends the lights of five divine names down and the second half sends the servant's five petitions upward, with the transition at Master of Judgment and You alone we worship.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: The first half of Fatiha sends the lights of five divine names down and the second half sends the servant's five petitions upward, with the transition at Master of Judgment and You alone we worship.

positions.position: Human requests include worldly benefit and protection, escape from hell and attainment of paradise, plus the highest aim of worshipping God for His own sake.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: Human requests include worldly benefit and protection, escape from hell and attainment of paradise, plus the highest aim of worshipping God for His own sake.

positions.position: The five names direct different requests: God alone, paradise, worldly goods, protection from afterlife harms, and protection from worldly sins that lead to punishment.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: The five names direct different requests: God alone, paradise, worldly goods, protection from afterlife harms, and protection from worldly sins that lead to punishment.

positions.position: The names also map to five familiar remembrances: Subhan Allah, al-hamdu lillah, la ilaha illa Allah, Allahu akbar, and la hawla wa-la quwwata illa billah.; cited verses: 17:1, 3:1, 29:45, 9:72
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: The names also map to five familiar remembrances: Subhan Allah, al-hamdu lillah, la ilaha illa Allah, Allahu akbar, and la hawla wa-la quwwata illa billah. | mentions 17:1, 3:1, 29:45, 9:72

positions.position: The five names correspond to stages of human life: creation, worldly nurture, knowledge of origin, knowledge of return, and transfer from bodies to the abode of recompense.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: The five names correspond to stages of human life: creation, worldly nurture, knowledge of origin, knowledge of return, and transfer from bodies to the abode of recompense.

positions.position: God, Lord, al-Rahman, al-Rahim, and King respectively govern those five stages; arrival at the final stage turns speech from third-person reference to direct address.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: God, Lord, al-Rahman, al-Rahim, and King respectively govern those five stages; arrival at the final stage turns speech from third-person reference to direct address.

positions.position: The repeated pairing of worship and seeking help relates each divine name to its fitting role as creator, provider, merciful giver, or sovereign.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: The repeated pairing of worship and seeking help relates each divine name to its fitting role as creator, provider, merciful giver, or sovereign.

positions.position: Because the Day of Judgment is a long journey, worship is its provision; the servant admits personal deeds are insufficient and asks for God's store of mercy.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: Because the Day of Judgment is a long journey, worship is its provision; the servant admits personal deeds are insufficient and asks for God's store of mercy.

positions.position: The difficult journey has many paths, so the servant asks God to guide him along the straight path and chooses the prophets, truthful, martyrs, and righteous as guides and companions.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: The difficult journey has many paths, so the servant asks God to guide him along the straight path and chooses the prophets, truthful, martyrs, and righteous as guides and companions.

positions.position: Al-Hallaj's verse depicts people lost in the name Allah and unable to reach its reality without the one who first disclosed it.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: Al-Hallaj's verse depicts people lost in the name Allah and unable to reach its reality without the one who first disclosed it.

positions.position: Fatiha's two phrases attached to God's name serve the beginning and end of actions: the basmala is remembrance, praise is gratitude, and each merits mercy from a different divine name.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: Fatiha's two phrases attached to God's name serve the beginning and end of actions: the basmala is remembrance, praise is gratitude, and each merits mercy from a different divine name.

positions.position: Lordship marks the beginning of human existence, al-Rahman its middle, and the King its end, from the primordial covenant to the final declaration of God's sole sovereignty.; cited verses: 7:172, 40:16
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL: Lordship marks the beginning of human existence, al-Rahman its middle, and the King its end, from the primordial covenant to the final declaration of God's sole sovereignty. | mentions 7:172, 40:16

positions.position: The Prophet's interpretation is transmitted in Adi ibn Hatim's report; al-Qurtubi calls it best and most authoritative. No grading is stated.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI reporting النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم: The Prophet's interpretation is transmitted in Adi ibn Hatim's report; al-Qurtubi calls it best and most authoritative. No grading is stated.

positions.position: Another view assigns wrath to followers of innovations and error to those straying from prophetic practices; al-Qurtubi calls it good but prefers the Prophet's explanation.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI reporting قيل: Another view assigns wrath to followers of innovations and error to those straying from prophetic practices; al-Qurtubi calls it good but prefers the Prophet's explanation.

positions.position: Dalal is departure from the intended course and truth; milk disappearing into water illustrates it, as does 32:10 for being lost in earth through death and becoming dust.; cited verses: 32:10
positions.reasons: QURTUBI: Dalal is departure from the intended course and truth; milk disappearing into water illustrates it, as does 32:10 for being lost in earth through death and becoming dust. | mentions 32:10

positions.position: The request means “Keep guiding us”: a person may be guided to a road and then cut off from it.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI: The request means “Keep guiding us”: a person may be guided to a road and then cut off from it.

positions.position: Duldula means a smooth stone rolled along by water in a valley; ghadba can mean a differently colored mountain rock, illustrated by poetry.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI: Duldula means a smooth stone rolled along by water in a valley; ghadba can mean a differently colored mountain rock, illustrated by poetry.

positions.position: Al-Tabari regards la in “nor the astray” as extra, as in 7:12.; cited verses: 7:12
positions.reasons: QURTUBI reporting الطبري: Al-Tabari regards la in “nor the astray” as extra, as in 7:12. | mentions 7:12

positions.position: Makki and al-Mahdawi say la is emphatic, preventing the assumption that the astray are joined to those favored.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI reporting مكي والمهداوي: Makki and al-Mahdawi say la is emphatic, preventing the assumption that the astray are joined to those favored.

positions.position: The underlying form is al-dallilin: the first lam loses its vowel and assimilates into the next.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI: The underlying form is al-dallilin: the first lam loses its vowel and assimilates into the next.

positions.position: Ayyub al-Sakhtiyani reads with an unlengthened hamza to avoid two adjacent vowelless sounds; al-Qurtubi calls it a dialect.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI reporting أيوب السختياني: Ayyub al-Sakhtiyani reads with an unlengthened hamza to avoid two adjacent vowelless sounds; al-Qurtubi calls it a dialect.

positions.position: Abu Zayd heard Amr ibn Ubayd use the dialectal hamza in 55:39; Arabs also say da'bah and sha'bah.; cited verses: 55:39
positions.reasons: QURTUBI reporting أبو زيد: Abu Zayd heard Amr ibn Ubayd use the dialectal hamza in 55:39; Arabs also say da'bah and sha'bah. | mentions 55:39

positions.position: Abu al-Fath cites Kathir's form ahma'arrat as evidence for the same dialect.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI reporting أبو الفتح: Abu al-Fath cites Kathir's form ahma'arrat as evidence for the same dialect.

positions.position: Ja'far ibn Muhammad offers another path: knowledge of God and understanding from Him.

positions.position: Ibn Sawwar reports differing lengths for separated madd: some Hijazi and Basran routes articulate without lengthening, while Hamza, al-Aʿsha, and Qutayba use full length; the rest use a lesser extension. He calls madd before hamza or idghām…
positions.reasons: NASHR reporting ابن سوار: Ibn Sawwar reports differing lengths for separated madd: some Hijazi and Basran routes articulate without lengthening, while Hamza, al-Aʿsha, and Qutayba use full length; the rest use a lesser extension. He calls madd before hamza or idghām especially good.

positions.position: Ali b. Faris says Hijazi and Basran readers, al-Wali from Hafs, and Qutayba do not extend one letter for another; the remaining readers use full madd, longest with Hamza and al-Aʿsha.
positions.reasons: NASHR reporting علي بن فارس: Ali b. Faris says Hijazi and Basran readers, al-Wali from Hafs, and Qutayba do not extend one letter for another; the remaining readers use full madd, longest with Hamza and al-Aʿsha.

positions.position: Abu Ali al-Maliki ranks Hamza, al-Aʿsha, and Ibn Amir as longest in separated madd, followed by Asim outside al-Aʿsha's route, then al-Kisa'i, though Qutayba is longest among al-Kisa'i's transmitters.
positions.reasons: NASHR reporting أبو علي المالكي: Abu Ali al-Maliki ranks Hamza, al-Aʿsha, and Ibn Amir as longest in separated madd, followed by Asim outside al-Aʿsha's route, then al-Kisa'i, though Qutayba is longest among al-Kisa'i's transmitters.

positions.position: In al-Mabsut, Ibn Mihran says Abu Jaʿfar, Nafi, Ibn Kathir, Abu Amr, and Yaqub do not extend across words; listed others do, with Warsh longest, followed by Hamza and Asim via al-Aʿsha. No one disputes extending within…
positions.reasons: NASHR reporting ابن مهران: In al-Mabsut, Ibn Mihran says Abu Jaʿfar, Nafi, Ibn Kathir, Abu Amr, and Yaqub do not extend across words; listed others do, with Warsh longest, followed by Hamza and Asim via al-Aʿsha. No one disputes extending within one word, though degrees differ.

positions.position: Al-Hasan and Amr b. Fa'id pronounce the hāʾ with kasra and connect the mīm with a yāʾ.
positions.reasons: NASHR reporting الحسن وعمرو بن فائد: Al-Hasan and Amr b. Fa'id pronounce the hāʾ with kasra and connect the mīm with a yāʾ.

positions.position: Ibn Hurmuz also transmits two unconnected forms: ḍamma on both hāʾ and mīm, or kasra on hāʾ with ḍamma on mīm; these and the standard three forms make seven dialect forms.
positions.reasons: NASHR reporting ابن هرمز: Ibn Hurmuz also transmits two unconnected forms: ḍamma on both hāʾ and mīm, or kasra on hāʾ with ḍamma on mīm; these and the standard three forms make seven dialect forms.

positions.position: Among readers, only al-Azraq lightens an open rāʾ after kasra or a silent yāʾ in a medial or final position; he normally does so without restriction, but tafkhīm returns in stated exceptions, including ṣirāṭ before an istiʿlāʾ…

positions.reasons: BIQAI reporting الحرالي: Only God can be called upon with this confidence, since every other being is subject to inability or obstruction.

positions.reasons: BIQAI: The divine names that follow praise encompass the Qur'an's theoretical doctrines and practical rulings, so the brief Fātiḥa is the Qur'an's mother and title, whose contents the rest unfolds.

positions.reasons: BIQAI reporting الحرالي: Al-Harali maps the stages of creation's unfolding onto successive scrolls, books, and tablets: scrolls concern what changes quickly, books what endures, and tablets what lasts for a time.

positions.reasons: BIQAI: The Egypt and Damascus example distinguishes coordination, which excludes the second group from the first, from ghayr, which treats the excluded wrongdoers as part of the first group.

positions.position: Sura endings match the beauty of openings, signal that speech is ending, and leave the listener anticipating what follows; they may conclude with varied rhetorical forms.
positions.reasons: ITQAN: Sura endings match the beauty of openings, signal that speech is ending, and leave the listener anticipating what follows; they may conclude with varied rhetorical forms.

positions.position: Al-Fatiha affirms lordship, seeks guidance in Islam, and protection from Judaism and Christianity; al-Baqara lays out religion's foundations, while Al Imran answers opponents' doubts, especially Christian reliance on ambiguous verses.; cited verses: 2:1, 3:7
positions.reasons: ITQAN reporting بعض الأئمة: Al-Fatiha affirms lordship, seeks guidance in Islam, and protection from Judaism and Christianity; al-Baqara lays out religion's foundations, while Al Imran answers opponents' doubts, especially Christian reliance on ambiguous verses. | mentions 2:1, 3:7

positions.position: Al Imran makes pilgrimage obligatory, whereas al-Baqara establishes it and commands completion after beginning; Al Imran addresses Christians more and al-Baqara Jews more, reflecting the Torah's priority to the Gospel.; cited verses: 2:196, 3:97
positions.reasons: ITQAN reporting بعض الأئمة: Al Imran makes pilgrimage obligatory, whereas al-Baqara establishes it and commands completion after beginning; Al Imran addresses Christians more and al-Baqara Jews more, reflecting the Torah's priority to the Gospel. | mentions 2:196, 3:97

positions.position: Al-Zamakhshari says the Fatiha encompasses praise, worship through commands and prohibitions, and promise and warning; every Qur’anic verse falls under one of these topics.
positions.reasons: ITQAN reporting الزمخشري: Al-Zamakhshari says the Fatiha encompasses praise, worship through commands and prohibitions, and promise and warning; every Qur’anic verse falls under one of these topics.

positions.position: Al-Ghazali lists three essential Qur’anic aims—knowing God, the straight path, and the return in the Hereafter—and three supplementary aims: the obedient, deniers’ speech, and the stations of the path, all signaled by the Fatiha.; cited verses: 1:4,…
positions.reasons: ITQAN reporting الغزالي: Al-Ghazali lists three essential Qur’anic aims—knowing God, the straight path, and the return in the Hereafter—and three supplementary aims: the obedient, deniers’ speech, and the stations of the path, all signaled by the Fatiha. | mentions 1:4, 1:5, 1:6, 1:7

positions.position: A second explanation counts three kinds of rights—God’s claim on servants, servants’ claim on God, and people’s claims on one another—and says the Fatiha explicitly covers the first two, hence two-thirds.
positions.reasons: ITQAN reporting ناصر الدين بن الميلق: A second explanation counts three kinds of rights—God’s claim on servants, servants’ claim on God, and people’s claims on one another—and says the Fatiha explicitly covers the first two, hence two-thirds.

positions.position: The early Successor exegetes mostly received their interpretations from Companions.
positions.reasons: ITQAN: The early Successor exegetes mostly received their interpretations from Companions.

positions.position: Later collections gathered reports from Companions and Successors; al-Tabari's major commentary surpasses them by weighing views and including grammar and inference.
positions.reasons: ITQAN: Later collections gathered reports from Companions and Successors; al-Tabari's major commentary surpasses them by weighing views and including grammar and inference.

positions.position: Subsequent exegetes shortened chains and copied statements piecemeal, allowing fabricated material in and making sound reports hard to distinguish from weak ones.
positions.reasons: ITQAN: Subsequent exegetes shortened chains and copied statements piecemeal, allowing fabricated material in and making sound reports hard to distinguish from weak ones.

positions.position: Later commentaries often follow one author's specialty: grammarians multiply syntactic possibilities, storytellers collect reliable and unreliable narratives, and jurists expand into legal disputes unrelated to the verse.
positions.reasons: ITQAN: Later commentaries often follow one author's specialty: grammarians multiply syntactic possibilities, storytellers collect reliable and unreliable narratives, and jurists expand into legal disputes unrelated to the verse.

positions.position: A further reading of guidance is to turn from everything besides God and wholly obey Him, even under Abraham's, Ishmael's, Jonah's, Moses', or John and Zechariah's severe commands.; cited verses: 6:153
positions.reasons: BURSEVI: A further reading of guidance is to turn from everything besides God and wholly obey Him, even under Abraham's, Ishmael's, Jonah's, Moses', or John and Zechariah's severe commands. | mentions 6:153

positions.position: The Prophet said that Surah Hud and its sisters made him gray because he was commanded to remain steadfast.; cited verses: 11:112
positions.reasons: BURSEVI reporting رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم: The Prophet said that Surah Hud and its sisters made him gray because he was commanded to remain steadfast. | mentions 11:112

positions.position: The Prophet advised a would-be ascetic to fast and break fast, pray and sleep, because his self, wife, and visitors each had rights.
positions.reasons: BURSEVI reporting رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم: The Prophet advised a would-be ascetic to fast and break fast, pray and sleep, because his self, wife, and visitors each had rights.

positions.position: The path belongs to God by law and choice, and to servants as something they follow and obey; both attributions express its relationship to each side.; cited verses: 42:13
positions.reasons: BURSEVI: The path belongs to God by law and choice, and to servants as something they follow and obey; both attributions express its relationship to each side. | mentions 42:13

positions.position: Repeating path indicates two journeys: the frightening way from servant to Lord, where caravans and mounts are lost, and the way from Lord to servant.
positions.reasons: BURSEVI: Repeating path indicates two journeys: the frightening way from servant to Lord, where caravans and mounts are lost, and the way from Lord to servant.

positions.position: Mentioning both groups after the favored expresses full fear alongside the hope of favor; the Prophet says a believer's fear and hope balance.
positions.reasons: BURSEVI: Mentioning both groups after the favored expresses full fear alongside the hope of favor; the Prophet says a believer's fear and hope balance.

positions.position: Anger also purifies, like a doctor cutting a diseased limb or fire separating gold from lead and copper.
positions.reasons: BURSEVI: Anger also purifies, like a doctor cutting a diseased limb or fire separating gold from lead and copper.

positions.position: Al-Rāghib defines bestowal as conveying beneficence to another rational being, so one does not say that someone bestowed a favor on his horse.
positions.reasons: ALUSI reporting الراغب: Al-Rāghib defines bestowal as conveying beneficence to another rational being, so one does not say that someone bestowed a favor on his horse.

positions.position: Another view restricts those blessed to the prophets.
positions.reasons: ALUSI reporting قيل: Another view restricts those blessed to the prophets.

positions.position: Another view means the followers of Moses and Jesus before textual alteration and abrogation.
positions.reasons: ALUSI reporting قيل: Another view means the followers of Moses and Jesus before textual alteration and abrogation.

positions.position: Another view names Muḥammad, Abū Bakr, and ʿUmar as those blessed.
positions.reasons: ALUSI reporting قيل: Another view names Muḥammad, Abū Bakr, and ʿUmar as those blessed.

positions.position: The unrestricted blessing embraces every blessing, in line with the verse saying that people cannot enumerate God’s blessings.; cited verses: 14:34
positions.reasons: ALUSI: The unrestricted blessing embraces every blessing, in line with the verse saying that people cannot enumerate God’s blessings. | mentions 14:34

positions.position: One view says God blessed them by creating them for felicity.
positions.reasons: ALUSI reporting قيل: One view says God blessed them by creating them for felicity.

positions.position: The linguists list ten forms: hāʾ ḍamma/kasra with variable mīm and optional wāw or yāʾ. Attributions name Ḥamza, the majority, al-Ḥasan, ʿUmar b. Khālid/Fāʾid, Ibn Kathīr/Qālūn, al-Aʿraj, Muslim b. Jundub, Ibn Hurmuz, and al-Khaffāf from Abū ʿAmr.

positions.position: An alternative analysis calls the second phrase an adjective of the first ṣirāṭ.
positions.reasons: ALUSI reporting قيل: An alternative analysis calls the second phrase an adjective of the first ṣirāṭ.

positions.position: Al-Akhfash permits the accusative as either a disconnected or connected exception if bestowal is understood generally.
positions.reasons: ALUSI reporting الأخفش: Al-Akhfash permits the accusative as either a disconnected or connected exception if bestowal is understood generally.

positions.position: The root of anger denotes intensity; the word is also used for a hard rock, a vicious snake, and a scowling she-camel.

positions.position: Abū Ayyūb al-Sakhtiyānī reads al-ḍāʾallīn with hamza, avoiding two adjacent quiescent letters although their meeting is permissible.

positions.reasons: ELMALILI: For Muslims, Muhammad and his Companions form an unambiguous historical example of the blessed community, whose worldly and otherworldly success had no historical parallel.

positions.reasons: ELMALILI: When Umar seemed shaken on the Prophet's death, Abu Bakr emerged and guided him and the community back onto Muhammad's path.

positions.reasons: ELMALILI: During the Hijra cave crisis, Muhammad reassured the grieving Abu Bakr that God was with them, citing Qur'an 9:40. | mentions 9:40

positions.reasons: ELMALILI: Grammatically, the relative phrase qualifies those under wrath and indicates the source of Islam's quality of piety.

positions.reasons: ELMALILI: Elmalılı says Ibn Hibban and Hakim judged the relevant reports sound, Tirmidhi judged them fair, and many hadith scholars transmitted them.

positions.reasons: ELMALILI reporting Resûlullah: The Prophet says that if a person cannot give even half a date, a kind word can serve as protection; he reassures the audience that God's help removes fear of poverty.

positions.position: Adi recalls thinking about how the Prophet's assurances compared with the bandits of the Tay mountains.
positions.reasons: ELMALILI reporting Adî b. Hâtim: Adi recalls thinking about how the Prophet's assurances compared with the bandits of the Tay mountains.

positions.reasons: ELMALILI: Because an external-reference reading is plausible without restricting the Qur'an to non-mutawatir reports, both interpretations of the hadiths should be applied; the external reading implies comprehensive exclusion.

positions.reasons: ELMALILI: The generic reading excludes all others explicitly, while the external-reference reading excludes other unbelievers implicitly; Elmalılı finds the latter more consistent with the Qur'anic context because it distinguishes polytheists from People of the Book.

positions.reasons: ELMALILI: Although Christians then ruled major powers and could appear blessed, Elmalılı says their true condition and afterlife were perilous.

positions.position: God gave Muslims Islam as a safe path to complete blessing; its rapid early success established the promise, and those steadfast on it will have the same outcome eternally.
positions.reasons: ELMALILI: God gave Muslims Islam as a safe path to complete blessing; its rapid early success established the promise, and those steadfast on it will have the same outcome eternally.

positions.position: Religious practice begins by knowing God and making a fully monotheistic covenant, then asking for guidance to a straight divine law that teaches duties and enables their steadfast practice.; cited verses: 1:5
positions.reasons: ELMALILI: Religious practice begins by knowing God and making a fully monotheistic covenant, then asking for guidance to a straight divine law that teaches duties and enables their steadfast practice. | mentions 1:5

positions.reasons: ELMALILI: Human beings make the request and practice; God gives religion, law, and two forms of guidance: intellectual instruction from the Qur'an and practical enabling through accepting it.

positions.position: Christianity abandoned divine unity for the Trinity and idols, though its recognition of a Father-God retained a limited unitarian element compared with Manichaeans and Zoroastrians.
positions.reasons: ELMALILI: Christianity abandoned divine unity for the Trinity and idols, though its recognition of a Father-God retained a limited unitarian element compared with Manichaeans and Zoroastrians.

positions.position: Elmalılı says Christians derailed inherited sciences and abandoned proof for emotional inclination, using psychology and popular sentiment to influence ordinary people and rationalize excess.
positions.reasons: ELMALILI: Elmalılı says Christians derailed inherited sciences and abandoned proof for emotional inclination, using psychology and popular sentiment to influence ordinary people and rationalize excess.

positions.position: Christian legal thought severed right and law from truth, treating law neither as divine or scientific nor as dependent on the people's will.
positions.reasons: ELMALILI: Christian legal thought severed right and law from truth, treating law neither as divine or scientific nor as dependent on the people's will.

positions.position: Clergy and councils made law by will rather than knowledge or interpretation, allowing arbitrary rules and joining divine and human realms incoherently.
positions.reasons: ELMALILI: Clergy and councils made law by will rather than knowledge or interpretation, allowing arbitrary rules and joining divine and human realms incoherently.

positions.position: This arbitrary law denied non-Christians a right to live, undermined social order, and eventually collapsed because emotional pleasures cannot sustain injustice to human rights.
positions.reasons: ELMALILI: This arbitrary law denied non-Christians a right to live, undermined social order, and eventually collapsed because emotional pleasures cannot sustain injustice to human rights.

positions.position: Elmalılı sets aside sins not arising from doctrine, distinguishing personal misconduct from the religious traits under discussion.
positions.reasons: ELMALILI: Elmalılı sets aside sins not arising from doctrine, distinguishing personal misconduct from the religious traits under discussion.

positions.position: The Prophet and his Companions provide a visible historical example of the greatness and sanctity of divine blessings attained through Islam.
positions.reasons: ELMALILI: The Prophet and his Companions provide a visible historical example of the greatness and sanctity of divine blessings attained through Islam.

positions.position: Because the Qur'an is preserved letter for letter and Prophetic practice is preserved, Islam has suffered no deviation; the Qur'an is Muhammad's clearest miracle and history testifies to his truth.
positions.reasons: ELMALILI: Because the Qur'an is preserved letter for letter and Prophetic practice is preserved, Islam has suffered no deviation; the Qur'an is Muhammad's clearest miracle and history testifies to his truth.

positions.position: Religious knowledge joins reason and transmitted tradition; societies that apply it sincerely can expect the same results confirmed by experience, and denying this is to reject induction.
positions.reasons: ELMALILI: Religious knowledge joins reason and transmitted tradition; societies that apply it sincerely can expect the same results confirmed by experience, and denying this is to reject induction.

positions.position: Europeans mislead inquiry by testing Islam among currently declining Muslims instead of investigating its genuine sources and comparing present practice with past practice.
positions.reasons: ELMALILI: Europeans mislead inquiry by testing Islam among currently declining Muslims instead of investigating its genuine sources and comparing present practice with past practice.

positions.reasons: ELMALILI: Those who genuinely follow the straight path advance, while those who do not decline; the divine law is true even when religious practice is incomplete or insincere.

positions.reasons: ELMALILI: Failure to apply arithmetic or hygiene does not discredit those sciences; likewise, people are responsible for conforming to true law rather than bending it to themselves.

positions.position: Those who knowingly disobey incur divine wrath, while the unwitting are misguided and ultimately face the same consequence.
positions.reasons: ELMALILI: Those who knowingly disobey incur divine wrath, while the unwitting are misguided and ultimately face the same consequence.

positions.position: Modern people seek to fit true law to themselves, causing human distress to grow despite advances in science; only following the right path can end that distress.
positions.reasons: ELMALILI: Modern people seek to fit true law to themselves, causing human distress to grow despite advances in science; only following the right path can end that distress.

positions.reasons: ELMALILI: Ibn Jarir uses the following worship covenant to construe the implied object as obedience and worship; Elmalılı instead finds the path itself the more apparent object. | mentions 1:5

positions.reasons: ELMALILI: This construal makes the path itself a supreme blessing, its bestowal a supreme divine aid, and the path theirs through divine gift and their following it.

positions.position: The knowing rebel is more culpable than the ignorant because knowledge followed by denial brings a graver sin and punishment.

positions.position: Unrestricted praise and the enduring nominal descriptions of the angry and astray all suggest timeless, lasting states.
positions.reasons: SAMARRAI-LAMASAT: Unrestricted praise and the enduring nominal descriptions of the angry and astray all suggest timeless, lasting states.

positions.position: Anyone who does not devote worship and reliance to God alone, or follow the straight path of the blessed, is angry upon and astray.; cited verses: 1:5, 1:6
positions.reasons: SAMARRAI-LAMASAT: Anyone who does not devote worship and reliance to God alone, or follow the straight path of the blessed, is angry upon and astray. | mentions 1:5, 1:6

positions.position: The straight path is known through prophets and messengers; acceptable worship comes from revelation, not from each person’s preference.
positions.reasons: SAMARRAI-LAMASAT: The straight path is known through prophets and messengers; acceptable worship comes from revelation, not from each person’s preference.

positions.position: Past أنعمت encompasses earlier and later generations who join the already favored; the present تنعم could suggest only a smaller group favored at one time.
positions.reasons: SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT: Past أنعمت encompasses earlier and later generations who join the already favored; the present تنعم could suggest only a smaller group favored at one time.
